THE LADY BLANCHE. The Lady Blanche was young and fair, A beauty known to fame, And gallants to herafather'S court rull many a courliug came. • Suitors a•many came to woo, The gallant and the gay; Barons and lords came aery week, And knights came every day! At 'ength Count Stephen of Toulouse Knelt low anti whispered " Fair ! llv suit must fit—don't try it on ! Eefuse me if you dare! " Refuse me, lady, yet I'll gain • Your hand by force of arms; • My guard, now keeTing watch beluw, Shall fasten on this charms. • • "Your sire is in the Holy Land ; In vain to him your prayer; Appealing, lady, ne'er can touch The heart of that old pjre ! "Then say you'll wed me, Lady Blanche; Nay, ne'er despise me so ! Let us become good friends, fair maid, 'Twill be quite comme ci fact!" " Think'st thou by threats to gain my heart. When love in vain might try— e lhat bang's of low men e'er can me In bands of Hymen tie! • •. Thou coward I defy your power, Your suit I hate, refuse ; My hand by threats you count to win, You sha'n't, then, Count Toulouse!" Then you refuse me Madness! rage! 'Thou know'st not what I am! I'll drown my good resolves in wine— Three scruples to a dram! '1 Of rage and jealousy I have A mountain so to speak ; 4, And now I feel that I have reached The summit of my pique." He left her. Then the Lady Blanche Looked forth, and saw with joy . A youth come riding—" Of my hopes This youth must be the buy." Sir Raymond 'twas, her uncle's son, From o'er the Rhine so free; Although a German cousin, scarce A cousin•german he. • "Oh, Lady Blanche!" Sir Raymond cried, "Say, why those deep-drawn sighs— Those frighted looks—nay, why those tears Li ke dots upon your eyes ?" "Oh, cousin," said the Lady Blanche, • ely wretched lot assist ; Since I am your relation, now To my relation list." • • She told him all her sad complaint; And then exclaimed the youth, " Can this be so ?" The maid realied, " This story is the truth !" "Fair cousin, hither have I come By love of thee possessed ; Just now I felt my heart was rent, And I was sore distressed! "Then say you love rne, cousin fair, And plight your love to me. And from your present evil plight I'll strive to set you free. I' My dapple-grey is fleet and strong; How proud and tall he stands What powers of speed ! what four stout legs, And nearly sixteen hands.'" • She's gone. A moment more the Count, Exulting, came again. And, quite resolved to "come it strong," He'd mustered all his men! A word, a blow, and in they go, Burst op 3 the door that's shut ; One glance sufficed—the Count exclaimed, " She's precious sharp I She's cut ! " Away, away Sir Raymond's steed Went faster than the wind ; He laughed and said, "We're right befure ; Count Stephen's left behind!" On. on they rode through hill and dale They crossed, nor dare refuse. The Same, poetic stream, which pays Its tribute to the Meuse! They swam the madly rushing flood Which people call the Seine, Bat till the town of Rheims was reached Sir Raymond ne'er drew rein. There by the bishop they were wed— Fond hope of all their dreams ! With choral service, for there are Full twenty choirs in Rheims ! Full long they lived through every change Of seasons, time, and weather, To reap the fruits of love—ln short, They lived for years together ! —Harper's New ..llonthly.

Castle is said to have once pos. sessed a very noted ghost, in the form of a large black spaniel with shaggy hair, which used to appear in every pert of the castle, but especially in the guard-chamber. where it was seen at candle-light time to come and lie down before the fire iu the presence of the seldiers, who at last became so much accustomed to their ghostly visitor as to pay little heed to it, so long as they were not alone. It always appeared and disappeared by a particular passage, through which the solOiers had to go with the keys of the castle. On this account they never ventured along it alone. One night, however, a eoldier, fired by Dutch courage, re- fused a companion, declaring that he defied the Moddey dhoo, as it was called. He presently returned sobered and speechlese, and died on the third day without uttering a word. After this the apparition was sten no more.— Our Own Country. A CURIOUS COSTOM.—Provionsiv to the year 1859, when it was discontinued, a curious ancient tenure custom had been for centuries performed, on the occasion of the pre- , sshtation of the sheriffs of Lendoa and U!4l.ll,Petfec in the Cr; of gxCh3clu'r, After ;be cqeony of preaentatiell. jerociam ti;on fies made by the Crier of the Court for the service as follows :—" Oyez! oyez! oyez ! Tenants and ozcupiers of a piece of waste ground called The Moors,' in the county of Salop, come forth and do your service, upon pain and peril that shall fall thereon!" The senior alder- man below the chair then cut one fagot (small twigs) with a hatchet, and another wide a billhook! The crier then rcieele this proclamation—" Oyez! oeez ! ayez ! Tenaets 'ited oeedelerre of a ceriain ieuement called 'The Forge,' in the parish of St. Clement Danes, in the county of Middle- sex, come forth and do your service." The alderman then counted certain horse-shoes and hobnail", and was Sl' es- tion ed by the Queen's Remembrancer thus :—" How many have you ?" "Six shoes." Then the alderman counted the nails. "now many have you ?" "Sixty-one nails— good number." And so the ceremony ended.—Frona Cas- sell's " Old and Yew London." Our OF Dooas es. RIYY.—Not a breath of air is stirring, and under the iofituence of the July heat our little out-of- the.world hamlet—drowsy always—is now absolutely still. Even the cows on the trim little green are too lezily in- clined to do more than lie abont chewing the cud. Up on the hillside, where the foxeloves make such glorious die. play, the old donkey has ceased from his prickly repast, and sits calmly looking down upon the scattered cluster of cot. tages below. The birds have hushed their songs, the lambs. refrain from play, and all things seem to be enjoying a siesta. As we pass the little red-tiled school-house, with its garden full of tempting currants and gooseberries, a drowsy ham denies that the children are quite asleep; but the only other definite sounds are the long drawn out " caw " of al languid rook floating over us and the crazy tinkle of a sheep tankard in the meadow below. Come with me over the moor, all dotted with white eyebright and nodding lilac scabious. Now up the hillside by the donkey-path among the gorse and brambles, where luscious raspberries bashfully hide beneath the white downy under-surface of the pinnate leaves. On where the noble willow-herb flaunts its great Mass of rosy blossoms, near to the spring that nourishes a colony of healthy lady.ferns protected by the endless clumps of bramble. Little do the hamlet-folk know of the treasures that abound up here upon the sandy platforms and recesses a little higher than their church steeple. . . . Bat now you have rested long enough. I want to take you through the pine wood, where the tall straight ruddy shafts are all aglow in the slanting rays. The paths are red with the fallen fir-needles and bordered by tall growths of "hurts," or blaeberries, and our ever-present friend, the despised and common bracken. Beneath the trees the ground is thickly covered with the long-trailing stems and yellow stars of wood-looeestrife or yellow pimpernel. And now look around you. We have reached the brow of the hill, and to left and right and away in front the wood drops down; ansl frem this spot we look sheer over the tops of the pines that grow on the steep precipitous flanks. We descend by the wind- ing path and, passing through a coppice at the foot, are soon cut again upon the common.— Good Words. EPPS'S CoCOA.—GRATEFEL AND COMFORTING. The 'thamen Chemical Society is raleiug a sub- ; scription to commemorate the event. 1 UM11.1.: Or A. CAT AT WO R KINGTON. While some alteraticnis wen being made in an old house in Nock-street, Workirigten, the other day, Mr. Porter, joiner, discovered the body of a mummified cat between the joists of the flooring. The cat must have been imprisoned when the floor was laid down. Its skin had become quite dried and tough, and it is halieved the cat mutt have been in that position over a century.— White/maven Free Press. RABBIT DEVOURING WORMS.— rX. few daye since I ob- served, with considerable surprise, a common tame rabbit devouring earth-worms with evident relish, eating them in precisely the same way as he was in the habit of eating i pieces of straw or hay. The worms were being administered I by a boy, who informed me that he occasionally gave the i animal a-few worms to eat, and was of opinion that they produced no harmful effect.--Tield Naturalist. We learn from the Lancet that Babesin, of Pestle, records some observations cm the nature of the red masses sometimes found adhering to the hairs and giving a red colour to the cutaneous excretion. They were made on four patients. In all the cases the results of microscopical examination were the same. The axillary hairs wets found to be brittle and thin, and surrounded by a thick and rough coating of red matter. This coating wascomposed of masses of spheri- cal or ovoid bacteria, united by a reddish material, and so j arranged as to give a radiating striation to the ernes sections lof the hairs. The same bacteria were found infiltrating the hairs in places, and also free in the sweat, to which they j gave the red colour; they did not penetrate to th 3 roots of I the hairs. The bacteria could be cultivated in sterilised solutions, but they multiplied only slowly. Mr. T. Jamieson, Fordyce Lecturer in the University of Aberdeen, has issued an appeal to agricultnral chemists, manure merchants, and farmers, "arm the analysis of phos- phates and methods of expressing the results." In this he sets forth the grounds of his dislike for the plan need by the "high" chemist. "Phosphatic manures do not, as a rule, contain the proportion of phosphate represented by the analysia by about 3 per cent." This would be equal to.an annual error of £20,000 in the article of imported bones alone. Mr. Jsmieson suggests as remedies the uniform use of the molybdenum process, checked by the uranium pro- cees, the uniform method of expressing results, that is the percentage of the element phosphorus in the three forms of ! insoluble phosphate of lime, and phosphates of iron and alumina, and finally, reference la caeca of need, to a canape. tent chemist. HEALTH OF SCOTCHMEN AND ElsentisztorEN.—The lower average of temperature in Scotland as compared with Eng- land appears, from the Registrar-General's Report, not to occasion any very striking aifference in the number of deaths from diseases of the respiratory organs. In Scotland the proaortion of deaths from bronchitis during the last year under review is 246 in every hundred thousand of the population ; in England, 245. In the case of that terrible malady, phthisis, however, the disparity is someehtt etreati-r, being 239 in Scotland, to only 213 in England. On the other band, fatal attacks of heart disease are rather lees common in the north, being annually in the nroportion of 140 in Scotland per 100,000 inhabitants, to 143 in Etpgland. It is curious that while 139 persons out of the hundred thousand in Scotland-are put do-wn as iving tf old age, the figure in the case of England is only 111. For some unex- plained reason consumption or tubercular diseases, though, as elsewhere appears, mere fatal than any of those enumer- ated, do not figure in the Registrar's comparative table of "The twenty most fatal diseases in S.cotlacd and ngland, ' arranged in the order of their fatality." LIFE HISTORY OF THE TRICIIIN A.—The mature and re- procinctive Trichina inhabits the intestinal canal of Marn• malia, including man, and its life lasts from four to five ! weeks, and they attain their full development and ability to reproduce on the second day of their introdncl.ion to their locality. The eggs of the female are batched, as it were, within her uterus, and prcduce minute hair-shaped embryos there, and there may be from ten to fifteen thousand of them. The embryos are expelled from the body of the i mother whilst in the intestines of the victims, and they soon drill their way through the mucous and muscular tissues of the parts, and then, traversing even serous membranes, get into the muscles. There they assume the form khown as Trichina spiralis. The importance of the discovery of this seties of changes is great, for it is clear that if the ihieltiree can be kept out of the digestive ore.,ene of an animal, it can- not suffer from the painful and dangerous disease which is , set up by the young worms, as they grow to a certain life- Istage in the muscles. And, moreover, the only matiner in which the Trichirm can get into the digestive system it by their being swallowed alive, with pieces of improperly ,- cooked muscle in 'which they aie encysted. Men are infeeted j by eating badly. cooked pork, the pig bappening to suffer• I from the presence of the worm in its muscles. Leucliatt stated that, as a rule, "swine obtain their Triehiem from I rats, to which latter we also, as natural bearers, have to con- vey them." Cobbold has shown the stupendous number of I Trichical an animal may have within its muscles at one time, and he proved that 80,000 were in an ounce of pig's 'flesh belonging to an animal part of which had been unfortu- nately eaten, and had produced an epideatic.—Cassell's .Xatural History. POISONING FROXI GAS —Some weeks ago I began to

suffer from peculiar symptonee. I felt at times drowsy ,1 during the day without any apparent reason, and aeon upon that I had a sense of nausea and giddiness, followed by a sense of coldness of the body, feebleness, and ieaptitude for work. At first I imagined that these symp- toms were due to derangement of the stomach- or indiges- j flop ; but this did not fully account for them, and in a day or two I noticed that they invariably came on in the library, after I had been sitting in it for an hour or so, and that they were soon relieved when I went out of the room. At last the addition of another symptom led ms to feel sure that the air of the 11,,rary was the source of the mischief, and that I was suffering from the effects of inhaling car- benic oxide. I compared the symptons I was now under- going with those I experienced when inhaling cerbenic oxide in experiment, and I had no doubt as to the identity. There was but one source for carbonic oxide in the place, and that was the coal-gas. In the room at large there was no odour of the gas. We sought for escape of gas from the burners of the chandelier and from the pipes leading to it, but without result. At lest, on opening a small cupboard at the lower part of the room, in the corner to the right of the fireplace, a faint odour of gas waa perceptible, for the moment, after the door of the cupboard was opened. This recess was below the Wok -shelves, and I,here was no supply of gas anywhere near to the spot. A farther eearcb was therefore carried out in the basement below the library, and ultimately it was discovered that a sin 11l portion of gas-pipe passed over a partition wall, between the upper part of the wall and the ceiling. On cutting down to that concealed pipe—the existence of which had not been suspected—it was found to leak, and a minute jet of gas was detected Issuing from it into the FtlCB above it and into my room. Entering into the roam at the base of a large set of book- shelves, it diffused behind the books and gradually into the air, not in sufficient quantity to be detectable by the tenses, but in quite sufficient quantity to be detectable by one who. from the re:inlt of exceptional work, to have ex- inented with it, and to have learned, bv this purely m ceptional experience, the action of one of 113 noustlinents oa life and health.—De. Richard!on, in C Our Homes, and How to nzake them Healthy."

Lt week an aceident befell Mr. Efeczilson, of Prior Rigg, Kirklinton, a kriner.• Mr. Hewitson, in stepping across a thrashing machine while it was in motion, slipped, and his foot fell into the drum, where it was crushed, and was with great difficulty extricated. A celebrated French agriculturist, especially noted for his success in fattening sheep, when urged to divulge his secret, rep Led ;—" Secret! I have none ; it is only a question of fare. Induce the animals to eat abundantly by a large, choice variety and good preparation of food ; that is all there is to it."

The apple, pear, and plum trees in parts of Kent have put forth fresh leaves and blossoms in place of the foliage which was destroyed by the extraordinary cold wind which occurred on the 29i.h of April. The blossoms on the tops and sides of the pear trees especially present a curious spectacle at this time of the year. Amos Acteaerser A GARDENER.—At the Chelmsford County Coin; recently, a singular action was decided by Dr. A Ay, the judge. It appears that at a floral exhibition at Chelmsford in July last a flowering plant, technically termed Phcenocoma prolifera Barnesii, was exhibited by Mr. Duffield, solicitor, of Chelmsford, and gained a prize. Be- fore it was removed from the exhibition, however, it sus- tained damage which rendered reproduction from it impos- sible. Rewards were offered for the discovery of the offender, but without avail. Subsequently circumstances transpired which induced Mr. Duffield to believe that the injury had been inflicted by Thomas Simpson, head gardener to Mr. H. Wells, J.P., Chelmsford, himself also an exhibitor and a member of the Horticultural Committee. An action was therefore brought against him to recover the estimated value of the plant, £2. Judgment was found for the plain- tiff, and an application for a new trial was refused. QuArarr OF STRAW.—An opinion is generally prevalent that a great difference in the quality of the straw is effected by climate, and to a small extent this is the case; but far greater differences arise from the condition of the soil as to manurial matter for the nourishment of the crop, and from careful harvesting, by which the scorching heat of the sun and bleaching effect of wet are avoided. The truth of this may be inferred from the small value put upon straw as fodder in those districts where the slovenly system of mow- ing and carting barley and cats as loose corn obtains. It is to be hoped that the high price of mutton and beef may cause those farmers to see the vast value of wellesaved straw as the most economical means of supplying those fibrous elements of food which are indispensable for ruminating animals. It must be admitted that in a fine harvest barley and oats are more quickly, though more expensively, saved when loose, because if the crop is tied up and ehocked it will require three times as much fielding before it is fit for of w the stack and safe from risk of heating. am (for we are his countrymen) deeignated by a phrase as offensive as the abandaut vocabulary of his eloquent con- federate could supply—l cannot help thinking that he ought to have recollemed the many fields of fight in which we have been contrieutors to his renown. The battles, selges, fortunes that he has passed' ought to have come back upon him. He ought to have remembered that from [. his earliest achievement in which he displayed that military I genius which has placed him foremost in the annals of modern warfa:e, down to that last and surpassing combat which has made his name imperishable. From Assays to Waterloo the Irish soldiers, with whom your armies are ailed, were the inseparable ausidary of the glory with which his unparalleled successes have been crowned. Whose were the arms that drove your bayonets at Vimiera through Phalanxes that never reeled in the shock of war before ? What desperate valour climbed the steeps and filled the moats at Badajos ? All his victories should have rushed and crowded back noon his memory—Vimiera, Badajos, Salamanca, Albaera, Toulouse, and last of all, the greatest tell me, for you were there—l appeal to the gallant soldier before me (sir Henry Hardinge), from whose opinions differ, but who bears, I know, a generous heart in an in- trepid breast—tell me, for you must needs remember on that day, when the destinies of mankind were trembling in the balance—while death fell in showers—when the artillery of France was levelled with the precision of the most deadly science—when her legions, incited by the voice and inspired by the example of their mighty levier, rushed again and again to the onset—tell me if for an instant, when to hesi- tate for the instant was to be lost, the aliens blanched? And whin at length the moment for the last and decisive move- ment had arrived, and the valour which had so long been wiselei checked was at last let loose—when with words, fealidar but immortal, the great captain commanded the great assault, tell me if Catholic Ireland, with less heroic valour than the natives of your own glorious country, pre- cipitated herself upon the foe? The blood of Eagland, Scotland, and of Ireland flowed in the same stream, and drenched the same field. When the chill morning dawned, their dead lay cold and stark together—in the same deep pit their bodies were deposited—the green corn of Spring is now breaking from their commingled dust—the dew falls from Heaven upon their neien in the grave. Psi-takers in every peril—in the glory shall we not be pertnitted to par- ticipate, and shall we be told as a requital that we are estranged from the noble country for whose salvation our lifeblood was poured out ?' The effect produced by the, speech from which the above is an extract was tremendous—probably greater than any since the memorable denunciation of Napoleon uttered by William Pitt in 1804. Lard Lyndhurst was present during the delivery of the speech, and upon the marked allusion of his too well-known words of the preceding year, every eye was turned upon him. Kindling with the excitement he himself produced, and yielding to the dramatic impulse of the moment, as he indignantly reiterated the word Aliens the orator waved his heed reproachfully towards the spot where lewd Lyndhurst was sitting. Tee effect of the tone in which the word was uttered, and the gesture by which it was accompanied, is saki to hive beau indescribable. Toe whole House gave way to conflicting emotions. and as no intelligible sound could be heard for many minutes in the storm n of cheers and exclamations, tneny on both sides arose from their seats in their curiosity to observe the expression of the sneaker's countenance and that of the distinguished object of his rebuke. Order was not without difficulty re- stored, and when, at the termination of the splendid passage with which the orator concluded, he sank back exhausted into his seat, the enthusiasm and applause broke forth anew, and continued without intermission for an unprecedented time. The effect of this speech was irresistible. The ill- starred taint of alienaee rendered resistance to the creation of municipal institutions in Ireland almost impossible. In the following Session the controversy was-indeed renewed, bat a section of the Conservatives led by Lord Eliott seceded from their party on the question, and with some reserva- tions, moot ef which were 'subsequently swept away, core°. rate Privileges were in 1840 made the same on both sides the Channel. Notwithstanding his success in debate, Shiel remained without any acknowledgment of his services until Lord Melbourne offered him the Commissionership of Greenwich Hospital. His acceptance of this office was much disproved of by many of his warmest friends; while to those who dis- liked him it furnished occasion for many an ill-natured comment and witless sneer. Afterwards under Lord Mel- bourne's Government he was made Jadee-Advocate—an office which he held till 1841. Again in 1845 he was made Master of the Mint. Bat his political career was fast draw- ing to a close. For twenty years he bed occupied a promi- nent place in the varied, controversies of the Senate, hut now he seemed to he hoeing much of his old power. "The glitter of the blade was still unsullied by any indications of mat, but the handle somehow seemed to have grown loose when graved, and it Use was gradually felt to he more la- borious and exhansting." He died in Italy in 1850, whither a Government appointment had taken him. His realties were borne in a British ship of war ta Ireland, where he had expressed a wish to be interred, and they were deposited in their final resting place at Long Orchard, on the 24th of February, 1350. I; must be admitted that very little is remembered of this Illustrious Irishman, and Justin al'esetley ac mnnts for the evanescent nature of his power by the fact that he was no more than an orator. As an orator he stood unrivalled daring his lifetime. Lord Plunkett, when speaking of the comparative merits of celebrated speakers, said that he had thought Curran hail a greater choice of words than Any min he had ever listened to until he had heard Shiel. Lead Beaconsfii-ld, in one of his novels, speaks of Saiel's elo-. I querme in terms of the highest praise. A few years ago Mr. I Gladstone selected Shad as one of the three remarkable ll- lustrations of great success achieved in spite of serious de- fects of voice and delivery; the other two examples being Dr. Chalmers and Dr. Newman. After describing Shielie peculiar voice, which he likened to "the sound produced by a tin kettle battered about from place to place," and it effect upon the House, he says: "Although it is now thirty-five years since I heard Mr. Shiel, my recollection of him is just as vivid as if I had been listening to him to-day." Yet this man, whom so many wellequelified authorities declared to be a genuine orator, has left no mark on Parliament or on 1 Politics. And the historical student, studying his life and I times, simply sees in this Illa.etrioue Irishman an agitator whose career, beginning in stormy oppoeition to the English I Government, fades away after a while into a second class Ministerial office, arid closes at last somewhat prematurely in the little Court of Florence, whither he had been sent as I.representative of England. With Richard Later Shiel we close oarsketches of "Illus- trious Irishmen." Our readers may not have admired all our heroes, but they will edinit that some of the illustrious ones whose characters we hare endeavoured to pourtray have been such as create an epidemic of nobleness, and with whom it does U 3 good to become acquainted. Men become much better and greater from gazing at their examples— more ready to do and dare—more willing to lift their eyes out of the mire of selfishness and the duet of anxiety and toil—more brave to try whether they, too, cannot "scale the toppling Vigil Of detea" and hold converse with those their loftier brethra npOii Iho

UNSHOD HOESSES. —The capability of the horn of an un- I shod horse's foot to withstand the wear of paved roads has I been made the subject of a communication to the Irish' Farmers' Gazette by Mr. F. F. Collins, F.R.C.V.S., who, in the course of his remarks, makes the following statements: —For many years during my regimental career I worked ' the whole of the remounts. annually purchased, without shoes, and I always found I could do so with the greatest benefit to the feet, so long as they remained at school work and for some time after they had joined the ranks, provided the weather remained -fine. A wet road I always found acted like a whetstone in its action upon the horn, which at once succumbed to the attrition, the toe being the vulnerable point, and lameness would follow unless the feet received immesliate protection. In every instance this untoward re- snit took place. During my service in India I- never used shoes to any of 'my own horses, and they travelled bare footed through into Afghanistan and.back without any ill effects; but I must confess I was dubious as to the result when starting, and carried shoes with the fall expectation that they would be required before I returned. The native cavalry never shoe the hind feet, and one regiment at my suggestion discarded shoes altogether, but it was found about six per cent. of the horses, from some peculiarities, had to continue their shoes. I can fully understand, there- fore, where grass abounds and but little macadam exists. shoes can be dispensed with, provided the ham is in its na- tural condition, but not otherwise. We may as well expect a man who has worn shoes all his life to travel without them as well as a man who never knew the use of ehoes. Shod and unshod horn are as intrinsically different as it is possible for them to be. It is instructive to note the change that takes place in the appearance of the crust of the foot, if untouched, whenever any decided change of season affects the soil. In India the dry and wet seasons are each indi- cated by a ring round the hoof, and the dietance between I these rings will give a pretty accurate time how long each Season liaa lasted. Similar changes may be noted when a . horse is brought up from, or turned out upon, grass, or, in fact, when any change acts upon the caroller, such as a I blister, and it is these marks that cause the knowing one to I have the whole of the front of the crust rasped. The.secret- ing membranes of the foot are particularly susceptible of receiving intrinsic as well as extrinsic ieflaences in the de- velopment of horn, either for good or eeil, and the less they are artificially interfered with the greater tha ease and corn- fort that will accrue to our poor social and mercantile slave. There is a description of shoe, or rather plate, that I have seen used in India, but I have never heard of it elsewhere. It stretches across the foot, and protects the qu alas, chiefly, leaving the toes, frog, and heels entirely free. I have used this plate in acate cases of latninitis (founder),• where we find the front of the foot mainly implicated, and its application has certainly been magical, by allaying the inflarnmatiou through the weight of the animal being thrown on the quarters and heels. I cannot but think, from what I have seen of this plate, that it would fully meet all ordinary requirements of country life, and its simplicity is less likely •to interfere with the ordinary functions of the font. It will be seen from the very interesting and useful facts supplied . by Mr. Collins that it is not the hardness of the road, nor its roughness, that militates against the practicability of ,working horses unshod, but its condition with _regard to moisture. This agrees perfectly with the broad fact that 1 the records we possess of the successful working of unshod horses come chiefly from the East, where the sail and i climate s dry for the greater part of the year.

THE STATE OF IRELAND.

A parliamentary return issued on Wednesday shows that during the five months ended March last, 1,048 tenants were evicted in Ireland who have not been re-admitted as tenants. Twenty men were taken to Dublin on Tuesday from Loughrea under the Protection Act, being suspected of com- plicity in the late murders there. Some were placed in Kilmainham Gaol, and the rest forwarded to Dundalk and Enniskillen. Michael Devitt was to have spoken at Worcester, Massachusetts, on Sunday night, but was so prostrated by overwork that he merely appeared for a few minutes at the meeting, and did not attempt to speak. His condition, how- ever, is not serious. "The Provisional Committee for Inaugurating the Move- ment for " Paying the Members '" have issued a manifesto to the people of Ireland, in which they give the following reasons why the Irish members ought to be paid :-Ist, they work ;.2ad, they are under considerable expense ; 3rd, ' they are men of slender means ; 4th, they are honest; sth, they have no prospect of other reward; and 6th, if not paid they must die out. • An extraordinary statement was tnade at Mass in a Roman Catholic church at Castleisland last Sunday. It is not quite clear from the account we have whether the speaker was the Bishop of Kerry or one of his archdeacons, but in tither case the words are remarkable. "He complained," s,eys the re- port, " of the outrages committed in his parishes during the last two years, and what gave him most pain was that so sure as he denounced them from the altar of Ged that very night there was a fresh one committed in one spot, especially in the parish of Call. Riotous proce2dings are reported from L'stowel. While Mrs. Moore, of the Dublin Ladies' Land League, was addressing a crowd of people the other night, the police, under Captain Massey, RM., armed with revolvers, arrived and dispersed the meeting. Mrs. Moore sebsequently attempted to address a crowd at the railway station, but the police again appeared. Stones were then thrown, and, the Riot Act having been read, the police were ordered -to disperse the crowd. Revolver shots were fired, and a few peeple hurt, Several persons were arr3Bted. Mr. Gladstone has published another "Treasury Minute" on the subject of the arrears of rent in Ireland. The right hon. gentleman, addressing his colleagues at the Treasury, says he is anxious that the sum to be raised shall be "at all ,events sufficient," and he reckons the number of persons to whom the Arrears Bill will extend at 430,000, occupying holdings valued at £4,560,000, and paying a rental of £G,500,000. He lays before the Board information which justifies him in coming to the conclusion that the moiety of arrears up to November, 1880, which will constitute the liability of the State, will not exceed .wo millions sterling. THE MURDER OF MR. BLAKE.

A great number of arrests 'lava been mada in connection with the murder of Mr. Blake and Thady Ryan near Loughrea, but few further details of the crime are given. There is, indeed, little to tell. Mrs. Blake, who was with her husband when he was shot, has given an account of the tragedy which shows that Mr„ Blake was struck by the first shot that was fired, and that a second shot killed the driver of the car, who fell uport ,Mrs. Blake's arm, and was sup- ported by her until Lowirhrea was nearly reached. Then a priest and some policemen ssera met, and the lady, who is herself wounded, was conveyed to an hotel. Mr. Blake is described as having been a very indulgent agent. ANOTHER MURDER IN DUBLIN. • SUPPOSED FENTANISM.

Another horrible murder, supposed to be the result of I Feniani3na, was committld in Dublin on Tuesday morning, I the victim being John Kenny. The Irish Ti;nes thus reports the murder :—lt appears that at about 20 minutes to one o'clock an altercation was heard in Seville Place, in the vicinity.of the railway arches of the Great Northern line. I 'I he incident did not attract much attention at the moment, 1 as it was snapased to be merely a street brawl. A !eenlenian I who was within a short distance of the spot heard high words and a sound which appeared to him like the stroke of a stick. A voice also cried, " Oh, flout." Immediately afterwards the report of firearms was heard by the same gentleman, accompanied by a flash. That was repeated three or four times, and then one of the men fell to the ground and two others were seen to, run away. No oppor- tunity was, however, afforded of seeing the latter with sufficient distineness to lead to their identineation. The shots were also heard by several other people who happened to be within a short distance of the scene. Two men, whose names were reported to the police as Edward Ennis, of 70, Amiens-street, and Patrick Egan, of 32, Lower (Mel-street, who were among those attracted to the place by the explo- sions, ran down Seville Place from the direction of Amiens- street, and when they had proceeded to within a few yards of the railway arch they found a man on his hands and knees. He was unable to speak, and blood was flowing freely from him. The man haying been left in charge of one of the bystanders, Ennis and Egan ran to the Summer Hill Police Station, which is hard by, and reported tile occurrence. All the available Men were at once turned out and hastened to the place where the man was lying. On reaching Seville Place the police at once got a c tr, and the body, for by this time it was evident that the unfortunate victim had breathed his last, was placed on it, and in charge of Acting Inspector M'Crarry and several policemen driven off at a rapid pace to the nearest hosaital—Jervisestreet. Dr. Chance and the regular pupils were in attendance, and a superficial examination of the body was at once made. From a number of wounds the blood had copiously flowed. It was just one o'clock when the policemen came to the hos- pital, and 'a short time afterwards Chief Superintendent Cerr arrived from the Castle, and Superintendent Entwistle was also Trickly on the spot. The ; medical staff learned by an examination of the body and of the clothing that the deceased was apparently, of the artisan class, but be was so poorly clad that he cannot have been fra any lucrative employment. The body was that of a stout, strongly built man of about . thirty years of age. He wore a reddish moustache closely clipped, and an imperial. He was slightly abave- the middle , height. He wore an outer coat of brownish plaid pattern, I which was in tolerably goad condition. ,It was marked in several Places by bloodstains, and the punctures made by the bullets were easily discernible in three or four places. The edges of these perforations appeared as if singed, and that fact would lead to the inference that the revolver must have been fired very close to his person. There were also several clean cuts, as if effected by Some sharp instru- ment. undercoat was tattered almost beyond des- cription, and the trousers, which were of a brown tweed pattern' were also in a state of dilapidation. The deceased wore a belt, and this article furnishes a suggestion as to the character the crime is likely to be found to possess. It was a leathern belt, well worn, and had a brass buckle with the words, in a circular band around the ring into which the plate fitted, "God save Ireland ; " and on the plate is a harp and sunburst. There are bullet wounds on the left side of the body, and on the left shoulder, and two similar wounds on the back of the head. Western Railway Company, at their docks at Garston, has North Shield& resulted in some disturbance since Monday last, when about GOO men in a body refused to work under 4s. per _day. All labour was brought to a standstill for the remainder of the day, and it was found necessary to bring labourers from towns at a distance. These, however, encountered Some difficulty in approaching their work on Tuesday, and many

of them decided not to be engaged. Those who proceeded to work did so under difficulties, having to be protected by the police, who were themselves assailed in several instances, not, however, leading to any very serious consequences. A deputation from the men on strike waited upon the heads of departments at the docks on Tuesday, and the result was so unsatisfactory that in order to prevent any further display in the place it was found necessary to have at immediate call more than 100 constables from other parts of the county in addition to those available in the surrounding neighbour- hood. These men arrived at Garston and reported them- selves at a late hour on Tuesday night, and all was then quiet.

' The LASOUIt Meaum.---The labour market remains in a fairly satisfactory condition, and there is no marked want of employment in any important district. In some agricultural parts of the Midlands labour for the hay harvest is reported as somewhat deficient, but large numbers of labourers from Ireland have come over during-the last few weeks.. At Bir- mingham the miscellaneous industries remain fairly em- ployed, and orders from the colonies are good. The edge- tool trade in the same town is somewhat quiet. At Newcastle-on-Tyne there is some slackness, but at Barrow- in-Furness, the Hartlepools, and Middlesborough local industries are well employed. The textile trades show some- what more activity, and prospects are g'ood. The boot and shoe trade at most centres is fairly busy, and at Leicester the hosiery branch is active. Several important works, in- cluding the new docks at Tilbury, will soon be entered on, and railway contractors in several parts are advertising for hands. In Cornwall the mining market is decidedly more active, and at Plymouth there is a fair amount of building going on. Emigration to the United States is not quite so high as it has been for some time past, and recent advices indicate that labour is stilLvery unsettled in many of the American industries. Railway works both in Mexico and Brazil are being pushed vigorously forward, and some mechanics for the latter country have lately been adver- tised for. Meanwhile the Canadian North-West cenfinues to attract much attention, and the railway system is being rapidly.extemled both On the British and American side. Domestic servants are in demand in all parts.—Labour • Nem, .

-T-RE LANCASHIRE COAL AND IR )N TRADES : MINCHESTER, WEDNNsuLT.The coal trade of this district cantinues depressed, except for house fire coals, which of course only meet with a very slow sale owing to the season of the year, other classes of fuel for ironmakiog and manufacturing pur- poses are in fair demand, but the large output of the pits more than covers all the rEquirements of consumers, and the pressure of stocks in the market keeps down prices at a very low point. The average quotations at the pit mouth remain at about Bs. to 83. 6d. for best coals, Os. to 6s. 9d. for seconds, 4s. 9d. to ss. 6d. for burgy; 33. 61. to 3s. 91. for good slack, and 23. 941. to 33. 31 for inferior sorts, but with holders of stocks in many cases open to offers actual selling prices are irregular. The depression in the trade is bringing to the front the question of wages; and the action now being taken by Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., of St. Helens, one of the largest coal owning concerns in Lancashire, in reducing the wages of their men 10 per Cent, at some of their pits will, if successful, no doubt ba followed more or less generally throughout Lancashire. At present, however, the reduction seems likely to meet with the most strenuous opposition on the part of the men, and a serious strike in the district is probable.—ln the iron trade there has been rather a lull during the week. In Lancashire pig iron a moderate business has been done at full rates, and local makers are firm at 455. to 465., less 21, per cent. for forge and foundry qualities delivered equal to Manchester. Outside brands in a few exceptional oases are being offered at comparatively low figures, and the recent advance is scarcely being realised to the full extent,' but sellers as a rule are firm, at from 465. up to 475. 61, less 24--. for, Lincolnshire- iron delivered _here, with Derbyshire brands in some cases quoted at is. to Is. 61. per ton above these figures. Finished ironmakers generally are reported to be better off for orders, and although local bars delivered into the Manchester district can still be beught at £6 7s. 61. per ton, prices are gradually stiffening up to £6 103. The posi- tion of the engineering trades is unchanged, and most of the works about this district continue well employed.

XXVII.-RICURD LALOR SHIM,: "O'CONNELL'S IMPASSIONED LIEUTENANT."_

At one of the earliest meetings of the Catholic Assecie• tiun, a yoang man, carelessly dressed, whose appear- ance was unknown to the majority of those present, asked for a hearing. The tone of. his vice, and something wild and unsettled in his look, did not at first favourably impress his qaestioning, auditory: As he proceeded, his earnestness began to win its way, and some few gave him a cheer. The effect of this was to render hie manner more collected, and his articulation more clear. When he sat down much ap- plause greeted the young orator.: That orator wee Richard Lelor Shiel, who, joining "Erin's Uncrowned King" in his bloodless crueede against intolerance and bigotry, was known in after years as " O'Connell's Impassioned Lieutenant." The young lawyer who thus had entered the lists as the champion of civil and religious liberty. soon distinguished himself by the fearlessness of his attacks upon the strong- holds, and his Rupert-like charges upon the forces of the O. opoeition. The freedom with which he incessantly assailed the whole system of intolerance and misrule, and the pitiless Irony in which he held up to ridicule the inconsistency and errors of those in power rendered hio-npre-eminently obnox- ious, if not peculiarly vulnerable to the weapons of official- enmity. During this period—the period in which O'Connell and he were engaged in the advocacy of Catholic: Emancipa- tion—he occupied the most exposed position of any man, for he went further than alt others to provoke the attacks of the Crown. At length the Castle authori- ties opened tire. Shiel delivered a speech on the published memoirs of Wolfe Tone, which appeared in the Morning Register on the 22nd January. Is was of more than ordinary length, and bore the evident marks of careful and minute cerrectien. Few, if any, of those by whom it was read with jest and impartial eyes ever thought of aecribing to its acthor unconstitutional designs. But the Dionysian vigi- lance of the Home Office discerned insidious treason in the delineation of events which had occurred thirty years be- fore, and ,the earnest depreciation wherewith their recital had been 'accompanied. "Beneath the luxuriant verbieee of the orator, deadly sedition," it was .said, 'lay ceilel" The Government resolved that a proeecution should be Nab with instituted against the publisher, and if possible againet the svelter. VlThereupen the Crown Solicitor wrote to Mr. Staunton, the proprietor of the Morniv Register, to the effect that unless the name of the author of the speech in question were given up, he would be prosecuted for its publication. Shiel at once acknowledged its authorship, and begged as a favour that Plankett, the Attorerey-General, should conduct the prosecution in person. Bed he done ere Shiel intended to "cut down Goliath with his own sword" by citing passages from his speeches on the Union which at least excelled in violence any passage which occurred in the oration on Tone. The jury found a true bill against Shiel, and a lively passage of arms was expected to take place be- tween rival lawyers. But the Government dissolution pre- veeted the prosecution, and Charming, who became Prime Minister, refused to continue it. The brilliant but short-, lived Premier declared that the obnoxious spveh allght have Lem dtljire7o in Parliament without even eliciting e call to order.

At the Go'd;:ral Election on the death of Cleerae IV. Shiel untested Louth. The struggle WAS a severe one, and Mr. Shiel was defeated. Had anyone, during the protracted struggle for Emancipation, ventured to foretell that upon the first opportunity that should occur he who had done so much towards its accompliehment would be left without a seat in Parliament—the only recompense he ever sought at the hands of his fellow counfrymem—the prognostic would have been treettd as a calumny or as the ebullition of envy and of spleen; and yet it so fell out, and the matter seemed to cause little astonishment or coneern. Soon after the Whig Government had been formed, Lord Angle:ea, who was about to resign the Lord-Lieutenancy of Ireland, hiforrned him that he was willing that he should be returned for Mil. borne Port. For this borough he was accordingly elected, and on the Bth of March he took the oaths and his seat as a Member of the House of Commons. The long day dream of his youth and manhood was at length fulfilled. This wee for him Catholic Emancipation. Nor was the "little Gascon figure" long in the House be- fore he attracted the Speaker's eye. His maiden speech was delivered on the second reading of the Reform Bill. It hardly equalled the niches of his friends, but in come re- spects it exceeded their anticipations. With all the ardour of his nature he threw himself into the wordy free which fol. lowed the passing of that Bill. As we read the Parliamentary annals of that somewhat monotonous period, we discover that the speeches of this Illustrious Irishman relieve with their flashing wit and sparkling imagery the darkness of speeches in ordinary. With the exception of Lord Stanley, he stood without a rival as a speaker. One of his oratorical achieve- ments has become historical, and we introduce it here be- cause it illustrates the power and genius of the man from Whose speeches we have had from time to time to make quo- tations. The Irish Municipal Question was before the House. Lord Lyndhurst in the preceding year had Opposed the granting of municipal privileges to the Irish on the ground ! that" they were aliens—aliens in race, in country, and in re- ligion." The attorney-General having introduced the Bill, O'Connell, adverting to Lord Lyndhurst's plea, argued that if it were held good every idea of cementing an incorporate union of the two countries must be abandoned. Lord Stan• ley rejected his pretension to speak in the name of Ireland, admitted that the old municipalities could no longer be maintained, but deprecated the creation of new ones, which would prove as exclusively Catholic as the existing bodies had been exclusively Protestant. In reply Shiel delivered the greatest of his speeches to a crowded and excited House. He stake.i the whole issue of the question—Were the hulk of the Irish people aliens, and to be treated as such by law? "There is, however, one man of great abilities not a member of this House," said the orator (referring to Lord Lynd- hurst, who, however, was present under the gallery), "hut whose talents and whose boldness have placed him in the topmost place of his e arty—who, diAaining all imposture, and thinking it the best course to appeal directly to the re- ligious and national antipathies of the people of this country—abandoning all reserve and flinging off the slender veil by which his political associates affect to cover, al- though they cannot hide their motives—dietinctly and audaciously tells the Irish people that they are not entitled to the sense privileges as Englishmen, and pronounces them in every particular which could enter his minute enumera- tion of the circumstances by which fellow-citizenship is created in race, identity, and religion—to be aliens, to le aliens in race to be aliens in country, to be aliens in religion. Aliens! Good God! Was Arthur, Duke of Wellington, in the House of Lords, and did he not start up and exclaim, ' Hold ! I have seen the aliens do their duty: His mind is of a cast too martial to be easily moved, but notwithstanding his habitual inflexibility, I cannot help 'thinking that when he heard his Reman Catholic country-

div.head: COBDEN CLUB DINNER.
div.p: THE COBDEN CLUB DINNER.

The 'Earl of Derby presided on 'Saturday night, at the annual dinner of the Cobden Club, held in Willis's rooms, and was supported by a strong gathering of guests. In pro- posing the toast of the evening, he asserted that "Fair Trade" was a ghost mely and not a reality, and that Protec- tion could not be revived. ' The controversy, which had been closed at home, remained open in the colonies, and Protection -was accepted and believed as a system by a large part of the colonial communities. He did not think they would be converted by reasoning, but the test of experience was a sure one. He did not See that we could do anything as regards the colonies directly to check the growth of the Protectionist spirit; all we cOuld do was not to encourage f..r advise ate increased colon:al expenditure, which would pro- bably be mid for out of the Protective duties. Although to Free-traders the sky was at this moment overcastilight came to Us from the East, and we saw that the Finance Minister of India had taken a bold step as well as a wise one, and that we had now in India a nearer approximation to absolute Free Trade than exists anywhere except in England. On the subject of commercial treaties the world of Free Traders had long been divided, but the pestion was one of pratical expediency rather than of abstract theory, and if through the machinery of a treaty we could get better terms than without one most people would be content to put their objections in .their pockets. The noble earl proceeded to urge that there was nothing more certain than this, that the great preventive of war was trade. Religion had not served to check wars, ferries of government had not suffierd, and not even the general increase of intelligence had done much to make men peaceable ; but if we could so connect two countries that neither could injure the other without equally injuring itself at the same time, we ihad a better guarantee than any other yet devised against quarrels. On all these grounde he dented that 'the policy of Cobden Wad been a failure. fie desired' to avoid any direct reference to the circumstances of the moment, as to which we have not the materials on which to form a judgment; but no Ministers who had ever held power in this country were less likelybe eri on the side of aggression or of panic than Mr. Gladstone and Lord Granville. Sir C. Dilke returned thanks on behalf of the Club, and expressed his conviction that Russian Nihilism, German Social De- mocracy, and French Anarchism were in a high degree the children of Protection. Referring to the present condition of France the hon. Bafonet controverted the. belief abroad that French opinion,, which had once been Free Trade, had gone back to Protection: That was not the cue: The now French tariff was not ton the average of, a retrograde character, and there was a possibility of a further advance in the direction of Free Teade. The toast of "Our Colonial Guests" was proposed by the Earl of Kimberley, and the health of the Chairman was propesed by Mr. T. B. Potter.

POLITICAL ITEMS. Lord Randolph Churchill has recovered so far that he has resumed his seat in the House of Commons.

From Monday next the Arrears Bill will be proceeded with from day to day till it is through Committee. The Select Committee-on Burial Fees will meet for the consideration of their Report on July 14. Sir Alexander Gordon, who was the last witness examined, will, as chair- man of the Committee, prepare the draft Report. In suspending the Irish members at the sitting of the House of Commons, on Saturday, Mr. Lyon Playfair was, the Observer is inform, actuated by considerations of the conduct of the suspended members, not merely .through the ninteen hours of the sitting, but of the twenty-three days during which the committee has been engaged in endeayou - ing to pass the Crime B 11.

„ . The addittional rule framed by the Speaker for the re- gulation of the business of the House whilst the state of public business is urgent merely confers upon the Chairman of tommittees the power, already enjoyed by the Speaker under the rules, to declare his view of "the sense of the House ” that the question be now put. This, it will be seen, is the Closure with the stipulation that the resolution to close -the debate can be passed only by a majority of three to one. - •

In the division on Monday night:on the motion for the suspension of Mr. O'Donnell, the following members, in addition to the Particilite section, voted in the minorities of 35 and 33 John Hay, Sir H. Tyler, Captain Nolan, Captain O'Shea, Messrs. W. Cunliffe Brooks, P. Martin, Blake, and Whalley; Mr. Cowen aod Mr. Lthouchere were -tellers for the minority. In the minority ot 36 against the Ministerial vote, in addition to the usual contingent of Land League members were Messrs. Storey, Thompson, O'Shea, Hill, Cowen, Nolan, and Blake. Messrs. Redmond and Power were the tellers. When the house agaia went into committee on the Prevention of Crime Bill the Solicitor- General occupied the chair in place of Dr. Lyon Playfair, and was loudly cheered by the Irish members on taking that position. Few Members had expected the urgency rule wouldehave,been voted early enough to prevent any other business being taken last night.

div.head: • FENIANISM IN AMERICA. ALLEGED PLOT TO SEIZE THE PRINCESS LOUISE.
div.p: • FENIANISM IN AMERICA. ALLEGED PLOT TO SEIZE THE PRINCESS LOUISE.

A New York correspondent throws some light upon Fenian operations in America. According to him there was a design some time ago to seize the Princess Louise while she and the Marquis of Lorne were visiting Manitoba; but as the Princess stayed at home it was concluded that the plot had leaked out. Several other projects in which dynamite was to be used also fell through because of their becoming known to the British authorities. Then it occurred to someone that time would be saved, and possibly opportunity also, by manufacturing explosives near the proposed scene of action, and an establishment for secretly tekiching people to prepare explosives was opened. A good many students, some of whom were from Ireland, attended these lessons, and presumably became efficient. The dyna- mite party also had ag,ents in England, and endeavoured to send over infernal machines, much in the same way as Walsh has shipped arms to Fenians in Ireland, but the detective system was so well organised that little success attended these efforts. The dynamitists, however, continue to be actively plotting; and if they do not succeed in doing more harm, it will not be from lack of effort.

div.head: All' i
div.p: All' i

Ministt.r lucidly e:r,plained the scope and purpose of the measure, and left to the decision of the House the impnr- tant points as to whether the ability or inability of the tenant to discharge his arrears of rent was to be considered in granting relief under the Act, and as to whether the in- terest such tenant might have in his holding was to be re- garded as an available asset.. He appealed for a prompt settlement of the arrears question, which was necessary for the peace and security of Ireland. He frankly admitted that the tendency of a bill of this kind must be to check the payment of rent, yet be was certain the House would not undertake the responsibility of rejecting the measure._ Mr. CHAPLIN moved an amendment that the House declined to proceed with a measure which imposed taxation for objects which must tend to demoralise the people of Ireland. He gravely stated six separate charges against the Govern- ment, among the least terrible of which were financial bungling and deliberate confiscation.—These stock objections were retailed with more or less acerbity by various Tory members of the type of Sir Walter Barttelot and Mr. A. J. Balfour.—Mr. DILLotc, in the course of the discussion, made a passionate and touching appealing on behalf of the small tenants in Ireland.—Mr. ARNOLD spoke in support o'f Mr. Gladstone's motion.—The CHIEF SECRETARY for IRELAND denied that the block in the Land Court was likely to inter- fere with the working of this measure, and stated that the clearing off of arrears of applications in that Court for the fixing of a fair rent was proceeding at the rate of 4,000 a month.—Mr. Trevelyan was speaking when the kour arrived for the adjournment of the debate.

div.head: HOUSE OF LORDS.-THURSDAT.
div.p: HOUSE OF LORDS.-THURSDAT.

TRH EARTHWORKS AT ALEXANDRIA. --- The Marquis of SALISBURY asked for information with respect to the earth- works and fortifications at Alexandria, and whether orders had been given to our Admiral to enable him to act with promptitude in case of danger arising to thq fleet.—Earl GRANVILLE replied that instructions had been given of a character which appeared to Her Majesty's Government to be ample to deal with the emergency. The Government had no officil informatisn at present as to whether the Egyptian preparations had been stopped or not. THE VAGRANCY BILL.—Earl STANHOPE moved the second reading of the Vagrancy Bill, which has passed through the House of Commons, and explained that its object was to enable Guardians to retain vagrants who come into the workhouse as casual paupers, and to render liable to penalty persons who make a fraudulent statement when applying for relief.—The bill was epposecl by the Duke of lircinuo,ND and GORDON, and it was stated by the Marquis of SALISBURY that there was the most profound division amongst Con,servatives on the subject, arising from the difference in the amount of pauperism in various The noble Marquis stared that what used to be considered the great mainstay of the British Constitution, washing the vagrant frequently and making the water cold enough, appeared to have failed, for npw the vagrant came to his bath with entire courage.—Eirl FORTESQUE was of opinion that the bill would have a beneficial effect.—The Earl of KIMI3ERLEY explained that the measure would be an op- tional one so far as Guardians are concerned, and there was nothing iii it which would be a .hardship.—The bill was then read a second time.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.-7TnunspAy.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.-7TnunspAy.

THE AMEER.—The Marquis of HARTINGTON informed Mr. Stanhope that it is not intended to give any further subsidy to the Ameer of Afghanistan. THU SUEZ CANAL—The PRIME MINISTER informed Sir W. Lawson that in the question of the results which might follow to the Suez Canal in case of any attack on Egypt it was not possible for the Government to be governed by the exclusive judgment of Mode Leeseps. The policy of the Government, which must be judged as a whole, involved considerations not apparent on tiee face of the question put by the hon.baronet. THE BANKRUPTCY BILL.—The PRESIDENT of the BOARD of TRADE informed Mr. E. CLARKE that the Bankruptcy Bill promoted by the Associated Chambers of Commerce, and which was read a second time in a thin House, did not in his opinion form a basis on which a satisfactory altera- tion of the law was possible, and therefore he .could not as- sent to a discussion being taken at a time when no adequate opportunity could he afforded to the House for its proper consideration. In the present state of public business he could not set apart a day for the discussion of the measure. THE SUGGESTED VOTE OF CREDIT.—THE INSTRUCTIONS TO ADMIRAL SErerouß.—The PRIME MINISTER stated that the Government had not any intention of prcposing a vote of credit with respect to warlike operations. If a state of facts should arise calling for such a measure the earliest information would be given to the House.—Sir C. DILKE declined to state what instructions had been given to Admiral Sir B. Seymour, remarking that they were Ad- miralty and not War Office instructions. THE MURDER OF MR. BLAKE.—The CHIEF SECRETARY informed Mr. Dillon that during the day he had been going through the evidence upon which 23 persons had been arrested on suspicion of being accessory to the murder of Mr. Blake at Loughrea, but he had not yet arrived at any final judgment on the matter. THE ARREARS (IRELAND) BILL.—The debate on the Arrears (Ireland) Bill was resumed by Mr. TREVELYAN, who made a brief explanation as to leases.—Sit M. HICKS-BEACH contended that the section of the Land Act of 1881, which dealt with arrears had failed, and that now the Government wished to pass a measure to do that which the- section was intended to do. He attributed the failure of the clause to a belief amongst the Irish tenants that by delay and. further outrages they could obtain better terms.—Mr. JOHN BRIGIIT replied to the remarks of Sir M. H.-Beach, on the surplus from the Church Fund, emigration, the purchase clauses, and the question of gift or loan to tenants in arrears. He denied that the Land Act had been a failure. What had been a failure was the land acts and the land system previous to our thwes. Referring to the state of Ireland, the right hon.gentleman said it would be quite easy by means of military and police to overawe the people, but the Government held that it was better to take a more patient course. There was no virtue more necessary for Parliament and the nation than patience. All were not disloyal in Ireland, there were hundreds of thousands weary of the anarchy that had prevailed, and who would support the Government in any effort to restore peace to the population of that country.— Mr. ECROYD trusted that precautions would be taken to pre- vent the disloyal and unscrupulous who would apply for gifts or loans from obtaining grants of capital from the Government. A great, injustice had been done to the land- lord in depriving him of the riglit of obtaining the best price for the one thing he had to sell, which was the common right of all free citizents. He opposed the bill because he held that it offered a reward to evil-doers, and a discourage• ment to those who had done well.—The debate was continued by Lord Lymington, Mr. Grantham, Mr. Gregory, Mr. Donaldson-Hudson, Mr. Maclver, Mr. Whitley, Mr. Villiers Stuart, Mr. Guy Dawnay, Mr. Moore, Mr. Bell, Mr. Rath- bone, Mr. E. Clarke, and Mr. W. Fowler.—On a division, the amendment was negatived by a majority of 75.

div.head: REPLY TO " ANGLO-SCOTUS."
div.p: A REPLY TO " ANGLO-SCOTUS."

We are much indebted to "Anglo-Scotus " for his learned letter, and think the more he writes the better. We quite believe that whether • Mrs. Glasse wrote "sketch," "cast," or " case," she used the word she meant for " skin," being one and the same thing. It would. however, have been interesting and useful information if the authorities quoted had pursued their research just one step further, and shown us how these words gave place to "skin."' In Danish we have the word ekat, tribute, tor treasure ; and know that taxes and tribute are still paid in skins in the far north of Europe, Asia, and Americo, and this may have been the case when this word was introduced into Norfolk and Suffolk by the Northmen about the some time as when the Varungians took tribute this way in Russia. The word " cast" is simply a metathesis of "skat," and means the same thing, • in Danish ; and "case" is the effect of apocope and aphce- resis; but the puzzle is to find a raison ntre for the " ch " in skat-ch, for the Anglo-Saxon " sceat," a piece of money, price, treasnre, profit, does not supply it; but the Gothic, Skatts, and especially the Old Norse skatt-gp (tribute) do; and we offer this as our contribution to its solution. It mig,ht have been got over by supposing an apheresis and a glide by way of paragoge; but this is dubious etymology, and that we wish to avoid. But to return to the matter in hand (Revenous a nos Moutons), we mean our hares, we heard from a bee-keeper on Saturday, while looking on at the hiving of a swarm of bees, that the " queen bee " is called "tlie queen " when we have a Queen, and " the king" when Ive have a King. His employer, a few minutes after, showed the original Bee Book, and said he thought the statement was not quite true. We fancy Butler would have said, the same of his male and female hares privately. But leaving these high meta- physics we con assure him that without putting thee, shares of the company in the market, almost the whole of the money required has been obtained, and we know of several persons who wished to invest from five hundred to a couple of thousand pounds in it, who were not able to get more than two or three ten pound shares each. Stables and stands and kennels will before . long, be seen rising in palatial grandeur, to astonish and delight as the else May be, and it is quite true that the lord of the manor will receive a thousand a year: and some Say ten per cent of the profits for the use of a hundred acres or so. At the dote referred to, we know a man who , kept a cow almost for the sole use of a greyhound, its butter ! being mostly used, and sweetlard for making cokes for the canine:broed,which it had periodically eight or nine at a time its own share when training, save the mark; it never yet won a race of any consequence, being from 12 to 20 eggs ; a day, and by way of a constitutional diet had a cows head lnoiled almost weekly. Mutton was then 4d. to sd. now it is 101. to is. per pound, and if we give credit to what we hear there are many hounds batter fed than whole families. %Ve were also the legatee of a village poet whose , writings have not yet seen the light, and probably never , will, for this is a very matter of fact age, and we fear to , trust the airy nothings of a poet's imagination to a rude and rabbit running race, who do not yet realize that this is, as Chaucer says," that other hond of the devil, with five fingers to caccite the people to his vilar.ic.

div.head: LOW TON.
div.p: LOW TON.

SUDDEN DEATH OF A Cmr.D.—Early on Monday morn- ing, Charles Ingham, 15 months old, son of Peter Ingham, a labourer, residing in Church-lane, Lowton, died somewhat suddenly. The deceased had been a somewhat delicate child since birth, but had not been attended by any medical gentleman. About 12 o'clock on Sunday night, the mother noticed her child to be breathing quickly and in short gasps. She'tcok him downstairs, but he would not drink the tea which she offered. She returned to bed and slept for about three hours, when she awoke and found the deceased in a fit. A neighbour was sent for, but the child expired almost immediately.
