Br?tish subjects are to be permitted to land at Malta on Thursday. A Iteuter's telegram, received from Malta on Thursday, stat2s:—The Spanish ironclad frigate Aragon' from Cartha- gena bound for Alexandria, is arrived here. Her Majesty's ships Achilles and Northumberland have arrived from Syra- cuse. Ordnance stores are being shipped on board the Minotaur, Agincourt, Ifecla, and Humber. The hired trans- port Nerissa has shipped 1,950 toes of coal, as well as a quantity of warlike stores and provisions. She is still waiting orders. Two hundred more refugees have arrived here from Egypt, making 2,200 since the Ist inst. Most of them are still at the Lazzaretto in a destitute state.
, THE EGYPTIAN QUESTION.
THE CONFERFINCE. CONTINUED WAR PREPARATIONS,
THE EARTHWORK 1S AT, ALEXANDRIA: MESSAGE
FROM ADMIRAL SEY M OUR. THE BRITISH ADMIRAL'S ULTIMATUM. FRANCE AND THE BOMBARDMENT OF THE FORTS. - •

There is no news of importance from Constantinople with regard to the Conference on the Egyptian Question. The Powers keep their secrets well and the reports that are trans- mitted from the Turkish capital are necessarily vague and conjectural. It seems, however, that towards the close of last week a proposal was submitted by Lord Dufferin for a Turkish military intervention, and the Conference "desired to subject this intervention to such conditions as would in any case prevent it from becoming a Turkish occupation, and from restricting the liberties and independence of Egypt." On Friday a fight was occasioned at Carlo by some sus- picious movements on the part of the British fleet at Alexandria. On Friday the ships executed certain . man- oeuvres, which led to a complaint from Ourabi Pasha to Dervish Pasha. The result was that the War Minister pro- posed to send an Egyptian Rear Admiral on board the flag- ship to request an explanation. Ourabi has declared that he will oppose a European intervention, and his officers say that if the Sultan should order him to quit Egypt they would not permit him to obey the mandate. With regard to the intervention of Turkey, the corre-' spondent of the Times at Alexandria says the time has gone by when such a solution would be possible. European prestige has been shattered, and it must be restored by Europe and not by Turkey. If the fleets quit Alexandria without destroying thp forts and showing their power the natives would believe, whatever else happened, that Europe had been defeated. With regard to the means of resistance at Ourabi's disposal, a despatch from Alexandria says that no practical resistance could be offered to English troops. "A landing at Aboukir would either be unopposed or, if opposed, would leave Alexandria open to the fleets. Ourabi would, it is believed, not attempt to defend Alexandria, but would retreat to Cairo. This could be readily prevented. Five thousand men landing from each side could seize the railway and shut Ourabi in Alexandria, the entire garrison, including police' not exceeding 10,000 men. The easy de- struction of the forts, which could be effected by two ships alone of the fleet within 20 minutes, would spread such con- sternation that Ourabi would be delivered a prisoner by his own troops." This is probably too hopeful a view of the situa- tion."

A Central News telegram, dated Paris, Thursday, says : The Cabinet Council yesterday arrived at no decision as to the•extent of French intervention in Egypt. Instructions were-last night sent to the French Admiral to withdraw his ships in the event of a bombardment on the part of the British Fleet. M. Freycinet meets his ,-.tollea.gues again be- fore the commencement of the sitting, and will probably place before the Chamber certain applications for grants to enable the French to meet any emergency.

It is stated that the force to be sent from India to Egypt in case of emergency will consist of 10,000 men, in the usual proportion of one-thud British and two-thirds native troops. A Simla despatch informs us that on Saturday de- tailed preparations commenced in the Adjutant and Quarter- master Generals' departments. A telegram from Simla to the Deily Nnes states that in case of an emergency the chief command will be given to General Herbert Macpher- son, who held the second command of the Malta contingent, and led the first brigade in Roberts's march front Ca.bul to Candahar. The note of preparation for hostilities in Egypt comes from India and France as well as from our own arsenals. A Paris correspondent telegraphs that, according to the Paris, the French naval reserves have been called out, and many of the men are already on their way to Toulon. A consider- able squadron has been concentrated at Marseilles, -and transport accommodation is prepared for fifteen or twenty thousand men. From Sitnla it is now announced that with the exception of the actual issue of the order to take up transports everything is ready for despatching a division to Suez. From Woolwich and Portsmouth we have reports of active exertions to strengthen the land and sea forces in the Mediterranean. A rumour obtained currency in London the other day that the British fleet had received orders to attack and destroy the forts in Alexandria. Very few Englishmen now remain in the city, and they could defend them- selves until rescued by the fleet. Ourabi has stated that if England and France should declare war their subjects would be ordered to leave the country at once, but would not he otherwise molested. The Times correspondent describes Ourabi as " a simple fellah, of very small intelligence, labouring under the impression that he is supported by an omnipotent Sultan, and without the smallest notion of the relative fighting strength of Turkey and the Western Powers." The same correspondent says that a Turk, who is extremely well informed as to what passes at Stamboul, asked him to give in the most emphatic manner this warning, which could be proved by an authority which the Sultan will not deny :—"Every Turkish soldier that lands in Egypt—be the guarantee of Turkey what it may—will be within a month the ally of the Egyptian military party, and will be opposed to European interference in Egypt in a far more efficacious fashion than Ourabi or the whole party now in Egypt are. The day that such troops are sighted I leave behind me Egypt, Turkey, and the East, convinced that it can only result in a European war which will terminate the existence of Turkey." The Daily .Areles Alexandria correspondent telegraphed on Tuesday :—" Ti's military preparations are being re- newed on an extensive scale. Last night guns were mounted on Fort Pharos, in the East Bay. 400 soldiers have arrived from Cairo, nominally for Rosetta, but have remained in Alexandria. 1,200 soldiers have been sent from Rosetta to Aboukir. I believe that Admiral Seymour sent a polite intimation to the Governor of Alexandria to-day to dis- continue the mounting of guns, and if this request be not complied with, another message will go to-morrow, and if still unheeded decisive action will be taken directly."

Another correspondent, telegraphing from Alexandria on Wednesday, says :—There is no truth in the report that Vice Admiral Seymour has demanded the cessation of the armaments in Alexandria Harbour. In consequence, how- ever, of a rumour that it was intended to block up the, entrance to the harbour by sinking ships laden with stone, the Admiral notified to the Egyptian authorities that he would regard an attempt of this kind as an act of open hostilities. The authorities replied that they had no such intention. Active military preparations continue to be made by thee Egyptian War Department, and large stores of ammunition are being despatched by road to fortified points on the coast. Within the last few days reinforcenvnts from Damietta and Aboukir have increased the garrisons of Alexandria by 2,000 men. The Government bakery, which two months ago baked rations for 3,000 men, now bakes for ' 13,400. In both cases camp followers were included. It is calculated, therefore, that the garrison of Alexandria is now between 7,000 and $,OOO strong. Further papers on the Egyptian question were presented to Parliament on Tuesday, bringing down the official history of events to May 31. They describe the progress of the Inaval demonstration, the " irritation " of the Sultan, the attitude of the Great Powers, and the cbcumstanc,s under which the famous " ultimatum " requiring Arabi Pasha's removal came to be presented. Ws last explanation is a little curious. On May 20 Sir E. 'Valet telegraphed to Lord Granville in favour of the removal of Arabi and hca princi- pal colleagues, and the English and French Governments fell in with this proposal. Then, however, Arabi began to circulate exaggerated reports as to the demarCs of England and France, and the English and French representatives, believing that unless the false rumours were corrected serious consequences might result, presented the joint note to the President of the Council demauding Arabi's exile and the retirement of the military pashas into the interior. Sir E. Malet then sent Lord Granville an account of what had been done, and the Foreign Secretary telegraphed back the approval of her Majesty's Government. Subsquent de- patches describe the circumstances under which the Confer- ence was agreed upon. A despatch from Alexandria states that more than 40,000 people have left the country, and in another week Alexan- dria will be entirely deserted by the European colony. Close upon 30 vessels of war are now stationed inside and outside the harbour, and nine of the first-class Powers are now repre- sented there.

A telegram from Alexandria on Thursday afternoon says: —The President of the Council of Ministers has received a telegram from the Sultan announcing that the Eritish fleet would bombard the fortifications of Alexandria unless the works were stopped immediately. The Sultan holds the Khedive and the Ministry responsible for the consequences. Ragheb Paella replied that the Ministry bad already tele- graphed to Constantinople that demonstrations bad' been made, in consquence of which the Sultan's permission to resume the work of the fortifications was asked. Pending his Majesty's reply no definitive resolution had been adopted. Notwithstanding all official denials, however, work still continues on the fortifications. Admiral Seymour will delay making his formal demand for the cessation of the Egyptian armaments until the British subjects are on hoard. Thay are now embarldng in great haste. Arabi Paella is reported to be supplying arms to the native popu- lation.

The constitution of the Ist army corps has been definitely decided upon. It will consist of 25,000 men, 10,000 of whom will be drawn from Aden, India, and the Mediterra- nean stations, and 15,000 to be sent from England. This will be divided into three divisions, each of which will have its own staff distinct from the general staff of the com- mander-in-chief of the whole army corps. The troops to be sent from England are to be made up of the following: In- fantry (21 battalions) and Cavalry (6 rep.•,iments); the Royal Artillery will consist of four baterics of horse artillery, and 11 of field artillery, together with a reserve ammunition column for infantry and artillery. The Royal Engineers will have its own regimental staff, and will consist of four field companies in cl.arge of pontoon, train, and telegraph trains. The field artillery first required will ha supplred • from the fleet, all the vessels carrying eight. field pieces. The regiments composing the First Army Corps have all been selected, and are nearly all made up to war strength. Where there is any deficiency the men will be chosen from the reserves.

A letter from Malta, of July Ist, says :—H.M.S. Sultan left on the previous day for Alexandria, after receiving sealed orders, the band playing, "We don't want to fight, but," &e. The Minotaur, Northumberland, and Achilles left this morning. The Saint Romans, a lar:ze vessel capable of carrying 2,000 troops, has been cirartered by the Government, and is here waiting orders. The Herissa is loading with coals and materials for the fleet. A thousand shovels and some thousands of_sandbags, besides other war- like stores, will be sent to Alexandria in the Ms. She takes in addition a large number of supernumeraries for the fleet, and sails to-night. The Humber awaits orders, and there is la large number of invalids—over one hundred—waiting to go home. The Rhosina, with a large number of refugees, is hourly expected from Alexandria. The island Govern- ment, in consequence of the large number of refugees from Egypt at present here, have decided that none but bona fide

div.head: ZULULAND. FEARED DISTURBANCES
div.p: ZULULAND. FEARED DISTURBANCES

The Admiralty have received an application from the War Office for a troopship to be placed at their disposal, in view of the prospect of the disturbances in Zululand necessi- tating the despatch of military reinforcements to South Africa. The Indian troopship Malabar, which was expected to be utilised for conveying an expeditionary force to Egypt, is available for this service.

A Maritzburg telegram states that Cetewayo is to leave Capetown by the Arab on the 12th of this month, and that he may be expected at Plymouth about the 3rd of August. He will be accompanied by Mr. H. Shepstone, two Zulu headmen, and an assistant.interpreter.

From a Capetown telegram we learn that the Cape Parliament has been prorogued. In his allocation to the bishops at the Consistory of Monday, the Pope strongly attacked the Italian Government for its treatment of the Church.

News of the assassination by Tobas Indians of Crevaux, the French savant, with Is of his followers, while engaged in exploring the Gran Chaco, is fully confirmed. The French Government has proposed to the Powers to fix upon the 16th August for the meeting of the interna- tional conference on the protection of submarine cables. While a performance was in progress, the Opera House at St. Petersburg, which was considered fireproof, was totally destroyed, and the scenery and the wardrobes of the actors were also burnt. Fortunately, no lives were lost, but the event forms a striking commentary on flite Austrian proposed precautions against fires in theatres. There has been a " fraternisation " at Tunis between the French and the Italians, on the occasion of a commemora- tive celebration in honour of the late General Garibaldi The band of a Zourve regiment played the Italian national anthem, and an Italian band replied with the " Marseillaise." The music and the speeches are regarded as "indicating a definite reconciliation betweeh the French and Italian 14,-4- dents in Tun's."

- Bulgaria is almost a sealed book to. Western Europe, and the little news which reaches us is not of a re-assuring character. M. Zankoff, after being kept under police sur- veillance in his own house, has again been imprisoned. A telegram from Sofia says that disturbances are apprehended in consequence of the belief obtaining currency that the system of arbitrary government has derived support and en- couragement from the Prince's journey to Russia. A telegram from Simla rep-is that a rebellion has broken out at Muscat. A ship of war has been sent to the coast for the protection of British subjects. Muscat is the most powerful of the Arab States, and hie commercial importance is very considerable. The rebellion is headed by a brother of the Imaum.

The feeling against Chinese immigration has spread 'from California to the British territories on the Pacific, where the Celestials have recently arrived in large numbers. The elections of representatives of British Columllja in the Dominion House of Commons will take place in a few days, and all the candidates, without exception, have found it necessary in their appeals to the electors to "denounce" Chinese immigration. EXECUTION or GUITEAU.—Charles Louis Guiteau, the murderer of General Garfield, was hanged at Washington on the 30th ult. The crime for which he so justly suffered death was committed almost exactly a year ago. General Garfield died on September 20, and his assassin was put upon his trial on October 17. Months have elapsed since Guiteau was condemned, the law of the district of Columbia enabling hie counsel by talking against time on a particular day during the trial to throw the case over into the succeeding term, and thereby prolong his client's life. NARROW ESCAPE OF GENERAL GRANT.—The express train from Long Branch to New York, consisting of 1 Pullman car, 1 smoking carriage, and 4 ordinary passenger carriages,ran off the line on Thursday while crossing the bridge over Parker's Creek, and all the carriages were pre- cipitated into the water. The fall was about ten feet, and the water was only four feet deep. The carriages fell on their sides, and many of the passengers were injured and three killed. Twenty were cut and bruised. General Grant was in the smoking carriage, and fell into the water breast high, but was drawn out through the window. He was slightly cat about the hips, and his left knee was bruised. _ .

A secret court anartitl-held within the fortress at St. Petersburg has condemned 20 gendarmes and eight soldiers to various degrees of punishment and exile for aiding the transmission of correspondence between the prisoners and their friends, and, besides this, the captain of the gendarmes in question and the officer in command of the company to which the soldiers belong have both been deprived of their rights, and banished to a northern province. Owing to the number of recent arrests, and the state of Russia generally, it is conjectured that it will not be possible for the corona- tion of the Czar to take place this year.

According to a letter from Cabui, the reception of Colonel Afzul Khan, the British Envoy, was most cordial. The Governors of Candahar, Ghazni, and Jellalabad were all suppliants for pecuniary aid, and it was believed that, with the very largo subsidies granted to the Arneer by the Indian Government, he would be able to render the required assis- tance. The Ameer is said to have informed the British Envoy that, if properly supported by the Indian Govern- ment, he would be able to maintain his authority. NIHILISM Pr RUSSIA.—Fresh arrests of Nihilists have been made in St. Petersburg, and several naval and military officer's are among the prisoners. It is said that Count Tolstoi, the successor of General Ignatieff, has received many threatening letters since he assumed the office of Minister of the Interior. In a letter which was published on Monday, the Nihilist leader Prince Krapotkine states that the new Minister is among the educated classes the best hated man in all Russia. He is, soya the Prince, "the worst enemy of all educAtiou—not only university, but also secondary and even primary—as well as of all private initiative in education, of all freedom, of all 'control of public instruction by anybody except his own officials; while the recent disturbances on his estate proved him to be one of the most oppressive of landlot ds. He is the declared enemy of any material and intellectual improvement in the condi- tion of the peasantry, of all reforms introduced during the 14st reign ; and his name (inseparable from that of M. Katkoff, the editor of the Moscow Gazette, who is his true inspirer) merely and sitnply represents the return towards the state of things before the emancipation of the serfs—to the autocracy of Nicholas I."

OPENING OF THE NEW R ILWAY BRIDGE AT EARLESTOWN. An important improvement, and one which the inhabi- tants of Earlestown will not fail to utilise to their personal safety, was brought into use on Saturday morning last, when the britlge, recently erected by the London and North- Western Railway Co. ov.tr their lines off Earle-street was thrown open to the public. Hitherto the only means which pedestrians have had at their disposal for -crossing the line was a "level crossing" about a hundred yards to the west of the station, and near to the works of Messrs. T. and T. 'Vicars, engineers, &a. This was frequently attended with much danger to these who attempted to cross, owing to the ceaseless rapidity with which trains followed each other on the "main lines," and the somewhat less, though nane the less objectionable, forms of danger to which they were ex- posed by shunting operations. Now, however, all danger is averted, and those on foot, who are very numerous during the day, may cross with ease and comfort, and all vehicular traffic across the lines may - also be carried on in perfect safety by means of the sub- stantial bridge erected bY the railway company. The work of putting in the foundations was commenced so far back as May, 1831, though preliminary operations had been carried out for some months previous. The bridge was completed a short time ago, bat was not used by the puulic until Saturday last. The foundations are of I.)rick, as are also the supports of the arches, the iron girders of which rest upon stone copings. There are seven arches in all, the most important one, which spans the " main lines " at a height from the level of the rails of about 15ft., measuring 63ff. in length. On the north side of this are two smaller arches and there are four at the opposite end. The roadway over the bridge is about 181 t. in width, and at each side is a foot- path about 6ft. wide. Protecting walls about 6th. in height run along each footpath, with the exception of the princi- pal span alluded to, over which the protection is iron, each side of the bridge bearing the following words: "The Pear- son and Knowles Coal Iron and Company, Limited, En- gineers, Dallam Forge, Warrington." The ironwork, as may be gathered from this inscription, has come from the Dallam Forge, while the contract for the brickwork was let to Mr. Jams Fisher, of St. Helens Junction, and for the stonework to Mr. Auckland, of Warrington.

RAILWAY PASSZNGERS.—A Parliamentary return just issued shows the number of railway passengers,and the amount of passengers' fares in Great Britain in the year 1573 and 1880, and the amount of passenger duty paid in those years. In 1873 the number of first and Second-class ordinary pas- sengers and periodical ticket holders was 103,033,078, the amount of whose fares was £8,647,151, and the amount of passengers duty on which: was £432,358, the number of third-class ordinary passengers and ticket holders was 336,239.981, who paid fares amounting. to £11,38,2283, and possenger duty to the amount of £14,097. A considerable &crease was apparent in the number of and receipts from_ first and second-class passengers in 1880, the number being 93483,636, the amount of their fares £3,213,889, and the passengers duty thereon £410,694. A proportionate increase ! is however, noticeable in the statistics of the third-class passenger traffic for the same year, when 458,622,960 pas- sengers were carried in this class, whose fare amounted to £14,333,271, and the passenger duty on which amount to no leas than £339,025.

The Duchess of Connaught left London for Paris .en Thursday morning. • An Orange circular warns Orangemen that another rising ' . In. Ireland is preparing. The North Staffordshire coilmasters have resolved upon 3 reduction of &per cent in Miners' wages. The Archbishops and Bishops in Ireland have promulgated a (*cilia forbidding priests to support the Ladies' Land League or attend any public meeting without the consent of the priest of that parish. • At a meeting of the Burii, Town Council on Thursday morning, on the moron of Alderman Cook a resolution was passed adapting a pethion in 'favour of Mr. Stevenson's bill for closing public-houses on Sunday. Seventeen voted in favour of the petition and fourteen against. After the funeral -on Thursday of the man Kenny, who was murdered in Dublin this week, three men visited his widow and told her that if she did not hold her tongue she might. very soon follow her husbind. Mrs. Kenny very conrageouHy gave the rufliirns into cu 9 tody. On Thursday, at a meeting of employers, and representa- tives of the operative spinners in Chorley, a settlement of the strike which has existed for four months was effected. The operatives agreed to accept the masters' terms, namely, the adoption of the Bolton hand-mule list. The Civil List pensions of Sav per annum to Mrs. Alice Chadwick ad £9O to Mr. Edwin Waugh which weregranted jUst before.the close of last month exhausted the sum of £1,200 per annum which the Crown is empowered to con- fer upon persons distinguished in art, literature and seieroe. __

A Newcastle correspondent announces that Sir William krmstrong has given La,ooo towarcla the extensio,p of a new natnral history museum at Newcastle, while Lady Arm- strong has subscribed £l,OOO to the general building fund, in aeldithiti to the sums previously given by Sir Witliam and Lady Armstrong. Between eleven and twelve on Wednesdgy night, a fire broke out at the Atherton mime liill,Stsckseade, ht by great exertions it was confined to the scutching-room. where it originated, and the damage is therefore, fortunately, not very heavy. About GOO people are employed in the various departments of the mill, which is one of the largest in Rossendale.

William Sigley, ten years of age, was, at Leek on Wednes- day, committed to jail for 14 days, and ordered to be after- wards kept in a reformatory till he was 16, for stealing two young ducks, value Bd. It was stated that the bey had repeatedly c.used his father to be fined through his non- attendance at school, and that he had so corrupted other children in :::hool that of late no schoohnaster in the district would have him. While James M'Eivan, ated ten years, was enjoying a sail in a small boat with father and uncle, between nine and ten o'clock on Wednesday night, off the Innellan shore, Firth of ' Clyde he observed a whale and became frightened.' He fell into afit and died before his father pulled the boat to the shore. WESLEYAN RELIGtors EnucirrxoN.-We learn that the forthcoming annual report of Wesleyan sunday schools will show the following state of thoconnexional organisation Sunday schools, increase of 58; Sunday school teachers, increase of 1,506; Sunday school scholars, increase of 19,386; Sunday school scholars. members of the Wesluyan Methodist Society, increase of 141 G. A serisus fire broke out early on Thursday morning at a large private boarding-school for ladies, outside the dock- yard walls, in Old Brompton. A soldier first observed the flimes and an alarm was given. In a short time the fire engines of the Royal Marines.'lloval Engineers, and the local volunteer brigades arrived. The inmates of the burn- ing house, about thirty in number, were with difficulty rescued, amid great excitement, but the premises were totally destroyed.

At Manchester, on Thursday, Adam Holt, a "shoemeier, was sentenced to seven years' penal servitude for burglary. Prisoner was a Sunday school teacher, and apparently a most respectable man,-11Put, suspicion attaching to him, the police starched his house and found £3OO worth of property, resulting from burglaries in the neighbourhood, one of them nest door to his own house. He had :also a lot of burglars' implements and several loaded revolvers. Two families have been poisoned in Oldham through, it is alleged, eating tinned mat. Mrs. Holdaway, wife of a brass finisher, bought some tinned tongue at a retail shop, and after eating it she and her three children were seized with violent vomiting, and a doctor had to be called in. Fourachildren of another family were attacked in the same way, anti one case was looked upon as hopeless, but the party is now recovering. The meat has been seized by the sanitary authorities. The Freeman's Journal says it has learned upon reliable authority that, on the snggestion and advice of an official, a pack of trained bloodhounds are about to be brought over to Ireland—in fact, are actually ordered—to be used in the tracking and running down of persons concerned in deeds of blood. The Freeman urgently hopes that an act which would render the name of the present rule odious will, if seriously contemplated, be at once abandoned, and that the country bo not made ten limas worse by the introduction c f a degrading and revolting agency. HEROIC CONDUCT OF A RAILWAY GUARD.—Oa Thurs. afternoon a Midland Railway guard named Dando, belonging to Derby, saved two lives at Saltley. Dando was the guard of the train from Birmingham to Leicesttr, and on arrival at Saltley an alarm iva, raised that three boys were drowning in the canal under the railway. Dando, a splendid swim- mer, left his train, jumped into the water, and with great difficulty rescued two lads, and another man saved the third. Dando was so exhausted that he was unable to proceed with his train to Leicester.

The Press Association learnsthat a meeting of the ge: oral managers of the English and Scotch' railways was held on Thursday. when they finally approved the terms of the arrangement to be entered into with the Government for the establishment of the new system of parcels post, at the charges already reported—viz., for prrcels not exceeding one pound, 31; not exceeding three ponads, dd; five pounds, .9.1; and seven pounds, Is—the railway company to have 55 per cent, of the money taken for parcel stamps, and the remaining 45 per cent, to go to the Government. It was also decided to communicate with representatives of Irish railways recommending them to coucur in this arrangement, to appoint two members to the general committee, which "will now put the scheme into strict form, and arrange the necessary details. A QUESTION OF PARENTAL AUTHORITY.— The que:tion of the right of a father to take his children who had been made wards in Chancery, with him to Canada, came b. fi 0 Vice-Chancellor Bscen in the Chancery Division on Wed- nesday. A motion was made ;to restrain Mr. Collyer from takiig his eldest son, now apprenticed in the engineering department of the Adnaralty, at Devlrn or, with him to Manitoba. The defendant was an undisch ,rged bankrupt, and having no meaes-of maintaining his family in this country proposed to emigrate to Canada and take his eldest son, now eighteen years of age, with him. The executors of the will of the grandfather of the childreß, under which the children are interested, objected to the eldest son being taken away, as he was in a fair way of earning his own livelihood.—His Lordship decided that to take the son away was calculated to injure his filters prospects in life, and therefore restrained the defendant from taking his son away or cancelliras the indentures. TEMPERANCE LEAGUE JUBILEE AT PRESTON. The annual meeting of the British Temperance League was commenced on Tuesday, at Preston. The assemblage there of so many supporters of the anti-liquor traffic agitation has been taken advantage of to celebrate the jubilee of "teetotalism," it being 50 years since Mr. Joseph Livesey and six of his friends raised in Preston that watchword of the total abstinence principle. The report of the League took a hopeful view of the cause generally, and expressed the opinion that it would be impossible to resist munch longer the force of public opinion in behalf of a • Sunday Closing Bill for the whole of England. On Wednesday, Mr. Thomas Einmott, J.P., of Oldham, moved the following resolution : —"That this conference views with the deepest interest the mission work which is now being pursued with such great activity and zeal on behalf of the cause of total abstinence, and it urges upon the ailiated societies of the League to . arrange for such missionary work in their respective locali- ties." It was carried. Mr. E. Whitwell moved a resolu- tion to the effect that the conference rejoiced that the move- ment for the entire closing of public-houses througl out England on Sunday had made such rapid progress ; and he submitted a petition in favour of Sunday closing. Mr. Charles Watson, of Halifax, seconded the motion, which was carried. It was agreed that the next annual conference be held at Leicester, and the work of the conference con; eluded. . TRE SEIZURE OF Ak,IS IN CLERK:MULL—Thomas Walsh, described as of 12, Charles-sticet, Hatton-garden, was on Monday again brought up on remand before Sir Jas. Ingham, at the Bow-street Police-court, on a charge of " treason-felony," which it will be remembered was substi- tuted for that of feloniously dealing with firearms, the pro- perty or her Majesty's Government, at the last hearing. Mr. , Poland prosecuted for the Treasury (instructed by Mr. Pol- lard) ; and Mr. S. B. Abrahams defended .the prisoner. A good deal of evidence was given, showing that Walsh has been buying arms and ammunition for many years past. Be- tween July, 1880, and September, 1881, he purchased this class of goods at one shop to the value of £l2B, and in January of the present year he bought 800 central-fire re- volver cartridges. He was also in the habit of occasionally buying " instructors" such as are sold to volunteers, and which explain the use of the rifle. At another place he on . one occasion bought 500 rifles, and at another time 10,000 cartridges. He was also shown to have made other pur- chases elsewhere. Latterly, according to one witness' he had been accompanied by a gentleman wearing a soft felt bat and dressed like a curate; and another witness said that when he took away the goods he Was assisted by a young man of about twenty. Further evidence against the prisoner, given on Tuesday, shows that for many months past a detec- tive from the Royal Irish Constabulary has been watching his his operations, examining cases and eisks of arms I. t.nat various railway receiving houses by, Walsh, nod t anctr at i nnvi. of the Irish police as to the nature of their contents, i despatch, and destination. On Wednesday further was given as to Walsh leavin ammu- nition at railway booking offices, been the Irish constabulary, who had , said they had opened the tic,eaisfies tents, and then resealedt , and poiwing them out evidence packages of arms and g packnad several members of watching the prisoner, , taken samples of the con- follewing them to Waterford to the police authorities there. Several c,nstabulary otneers were called, who proved seizing the casee.on arrival at various railway stations in Ireland . and secte in the arms. Many of the cases were sent to fic- titious porsons. Mr. Fanal, merchant, Castlereagh, gave ' ' evidence to the effect that although a case of pistols was ' addressed to him he knew nothing of them nor of the sup- posed who was booked in the name of Cooper, but ,e eetwier, , was identified as the prisoner. On ;Thursday, after hearing further evidence from Ireland against Walsh, Mr. Poland applied for and obtained an additional remand of a week in order to continue inquiries.

WIDNES PARISH CHURCH ScnooLs.—Yesterday at noon, the scholars attending these schools, numbering about 1,100 had their annual treat to Hale Bank. They were accompanied by the vicar, the Rev. J. Wright-Williams, and the teachers. The weather was very favourable, and an enjoyable time was spent. Mr. A. T. Nowell, of Runcorn, who was announced last week as having taken the gold medal at South Kensington, was on Tuesday admitted by the Council as a student at the Royal Academy. The above receives five year's gratuitous teaching by the R.A.'s. There were 21 vacancies, for which there were 121 competitors. PAVILION THEATRE, WIDNES.—An attractive programme was performed at this theatre last week, the play "Streets of Widnes" being especially successful. In this piece a successful attempt at scenic effect was produced in .‘ Run- corn Bridge by night," painted by Mr. A. Conville. For next week is announced "The lights in London," in which Mr. Charles Quayle will appear, and good houses may be expected.

SPECIAL ELECTION OF THREE GUARDIANS.—In accord- ance with an order of the Local Government Board a special election of three Guardians has taken place for the town- ship of Runcorn, and no other nominations having been
sent in in addition to the nominations made at the rate.
payers' meeting, the returning-officer (Mr. H. Linaker) has certified that Messrs. William Fisher, William Handlev, and William Whittaker have been duly elected as Guardians of

FORTHCOMING BAZAAR AT RUNCORN.—Under the patron- age of his Grace the Duke of Westminster, a bazaar will be held in the National Infant School, on Tuesday, and two following days. The opening ceremony will be performed by Major J. Cavendish Orred. The object of the bazaar is to provide funds for the erection of a church in Greenway- road, which within recent years, has become a populous neighbourhood. The attractions provided are of great variety, including dramatic performances, musical and magic lantern entertainments, and marionettes ; and it is to be hoped the expectations of the promoters will be realised, and a handsome sum obtained towards the cost of the pro- posed erection.

HUTCHINSON ,ST. PRIMITIVE METHODIST SUNDAY SCHOOL, WIDNES.—About 200 scholars attending the above school, accompanied with their teachers and a few friend, had their annual treat on Wednesday. The place chosen for the day's out was Hale Hall, the residence of Colonel Ireland Blackburne, and they were conveyed there in four waggonettes and two tarries, provided by Me. Lee. Al- though the weather was very showery, a pleasant day was spent, spot ts having been organised by Messrs. Bold, Ogden, Hill and Williams. Tea was provided about five o'clock. The scholars and teachers Fere photographed during the afternoon, and as inementees of the occasion, views of the hall and church were also obtained. RUNCORN AND DISTRICT STARR•BOWKETT BUILDING SOCIETY: FOURTH APPROPRIATION.—A public meeting was held in the Girl's School, Church-street, Frodsham, on Wednesday evening, under the auspices of this society, when the Rev. H. B. Blogg, M.A., vicar, presided, but there was only a moderate attendance. Addresses were delivered by the rev, chairman and Mr. T. C. Beckett, after which the secretary, Mr. William Handley, read the minutes of the last appropriation meeting, which were confirmed_ Mr. J. Darlington and Mr. Cunnah, of Frodsham, having been appointed scrutineers, the ballot was proceeded with, a little girl named Eveline Aston being engaged to produce the lucky number. The first number drawn was 043, and a reference to the register showed that the member held four shares, but was in arrear and therefore not entitled to the appropriation A second ballot was then taken and 081 was announced as the winning number, a reference to the regis- ter showing that it consisted of two shares which have been transferrecfa short time since to Mr. John Tonks, painter* Lord-street, Runcorn; and the subscription had been duly ' paid up. A hearty rote of theuks to the chairman for pre- siding brought the meeting to a close. ISIT OF TICE SOCIETY or CHEMICAL INDUSTRY TO WIDNES.—At the present time the Society of Chemical In- dustry is holding its annual meetings in Manchester, and yesterday various excursions were made to chemical works in the district. Amongst the places to be visited was Widnes, and about GO members of the society left the Cen- tral-station, Manchester, at a quarter to ten. They arrived at Widnes about half an hour later, and under the couduc- torship of Mr. A. E. Fletcher, one of Her Majesty's alkali , works inspectors, visited the Tbarsis Sulphur and Copper Works. Having viewed the interesting process carried on here, they went to the alkali works of Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon and Co., where they witnessed the manufacturing of sulphuric acid, sulphate of soda and hydrochloric acid, carbonate of soda, and bleaching powder. Of their kind these works are about the most extensive in the country, and a considerable time was passed in examining the plant. About two o'clock a capital lunch was provided at the Central Hotel by Mr. Fowler. The chair was occu- pied by Mr. F. 11. Gossage. Mr. Tyrer, London, secretarY of the society, made a brief speech, in which he spoke highly of the courtesy with which the members had been received by their Widnes friends. Mr. Eustace Carey and the Chair- man acknowledged the compliment in suitable terms. The members then proceeded to Messrs. W. Gossage and Sons' soap works. A visit was also paid to the works cf Messrs. Golding, Davies, and Co., for the purpose of inspecting the Hargreaves' process. The members returned to Manchester in the course of the afternoon. RUNCORN WANDERERS BICYCLE CLUB—The cham- pionship race of the Runcorn Wanderers' Bicycle Club took place on Saturday, on the Aston course. A considerable number of spectators assembled, and the race was keenly centested, the distance being accomplished in less time than upon any previous occasion. The distance was three times over the course—a macadamised road—a total length of 10i miles. The following started : T. Bate, J. Green, R. Raw- linson, W. Woodward, J. W. Temperley, S. Sherlock, and C. Hesketh. Bate (captain) was the acknowledged favourite. Temperley, however, ran him hard, and made some very fast running. The first rourd, 31 miles, was finished in the following order : Bite and Temperley, 14 mins. 2 secs. ; Sherlock, 14 mins. 15 sees.; Woodward, 14 mins. 30 sees.; Rawlinson. 15 mins.; Hesketh, 15 mins. 20 sees.; Green, 15 mins. 25 secs. Woodward and Hesketh now retired. The positions at the end of the second round were: Bate and Temperley, 14 mins. 50 secs. ; Sherlock, 16 mins.; Green, 16 mins. 35 secs.; and Rawlinson, 17 mins. 15 secs. Green now retired. In the third round Bate and Temperley still kept close company, and gradually left the Other riders. About 100 yards from home Temperley, when attempting to pass Bate, fell heavily over the handles, and for a moment lay bruised and helpless on the road. The madhine was also broken. Bate finished the round in 14 mins. 43 secs. Temperley succeeded in walking his machine to the tape, and then retired to have his wounds dressed. Sherlock finished in 16 mins. 38 secs., and Rawlinson, in 17 mins. 10 secs. The time for the whole distance is as follows: Bate, 43 mins. 35 sees.; Temperley, 43 mins. 40 secs.; Sherlock, 46 mins. 53 sees.; and Rawlinson, 49 mins. 25 secs. There were two prizes, the first being a gold centre medal, and the second a silver one. Bate, besides winning the first medal, is the champion of the club for the ensuing year. Temperley took the second medal. The prizes were presented in the evening by the president, Mr. J. D. Jones. ATTACK OF THE SALVATION ARMY ON WIDNES.— With that indifference to violence, threatened or actual, ,which characterises all their proceedings, the Salvation Army commenced an assault on Widnes early on Sunday morning. At least one third of the inhabitants of the town are Irish Rotnan Catholics, and in this fact lay danger, had the army attempted to penetrate the. Irish quarters. Happily, how- ever, they confined their perambulations to the principal streets and roads which were crowded with people. The majority appeared to be animated by no more intense feeling than that of curiosity, and the few who had any hostile in- tentions, confined their demonstration of disapproval to hoot- ing. This applies only to the morning's proceedings. In the afternoon, at half-past one, an open-air meeting on the Market Ground had been announced, and about that time the army, led by the band, and with a red flag flying, made their appearance. They were immediately surrounded by several hundreds of people, and amid great uproar, the Salva- tionists endeavoured to conduct their service. Growing bolder, persons situated at the limit of the crowd threw stones, and a rush was made to seize the instruments and the standard. The policemen, under Inspector Barnett, interfered and frustrated the attempt; but the army had been disorganised, and its members were scattered among the assembly. Coming to the wise decision not to further attempt to hold the meeting, the army with difficulty formed into processional order. Whilst on their way to the Volun- teer Hall, an Irishman rushed to the band and kicked the drum. He was at once taken into custody, but after being closely questioned at the police office, he was liberated. The army now arrived at the Hall without further disturbance, owing rrainly to the well-directed efforts of the police. The building was quickly filled, antita service of the usual des- cription was conducted. The audience was largely com- posed .of respectable townspeople, and the peoceedings.were very orderly. In the evening another service was held. At its conclusion the army was followed by a vast concourse of people along Victoria-road and Waterloo-road to the bridge. Bricks aud stones were freely thrown, and again the police, by their concerted action, were successful in- averting what would doubtless have been a serious disturbance. BISHOP O'REILLY.—In a pastoral which was read on Sunday in the churches of the Roman Catholic diocese of Liverpool, of which Warrington forms a part, the Right Rev. Dr. O'Reilly warmly acknowledged the solicitude which his people and others not connected with the Roman Catholic body showed towards him during his recent serious illness, and announced his intention to leave Liver- pool for a time, in order to 'recruit his health, so that he may tke sooner be enabled to resume his episcopal duties. GOSPEL TEMPERANCE AND BLUE RIBBON UNION.—A miscellaneous entertainment under the auspices of the Blue Ribbon and Gospel Temperance Union, and presided over by the Rev. S. Wilkinson, was given in the Co-operative Hall, on Saturday evening last. The chairman conducted praise and prayer, and the Rev. W. Mules read a portion of scrip- ture, after which the chairman opened the meeting and delivered a short but suitable address. A song by Miss Waterford was well received, and an interesting reading entitled," Not a arop more, Daniel," was next given by the Rev. W. Mules, which elicited much applause. Mr. Kirkham, an old enemy to the temperance cause, gave an account of his conversion through the army's operation, and also rendered a very facetious song. A short address by Mr. Winskill followed, and he also gave a song "Try, try, try again," which was well received ; and a pianoforte duet by the Misses Bonnell received a well-deserved encore. A recita- tion by Master Wm. Pollitt was much enjoyed ; whilst a comic song rendered by Master H. Galloway brought down the house. Short addresses by the Rev. E. Moore and Rev.i T. Rippon were listened to with very marked attention by the large and appreciative audience. A vote of thanks to the chairman for presiding brought the meeting to a close. DISTURBING AN OPEN•AIR SERVICE AT WARRINGTON.—A powerful-looking Irishman, named Stephen Mcllroy, rag gatherer, 4, Bakehouse-yard, Foundry-street, was charged before the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere) and Major Cart- wright, with being drunk and disorderly in the Fair Ground on Sunday afternoon. P.S. Bowen said he received infor- mation that there was a disturbance going on on the Fair Ground on Sunday afternoon, and on proceeding there, in company with P.C. Hennessy, he found the prisoner shout- ing at the top of his voice, and two men trying to prevent him. Prisoner's language was something frightful in try- ing to disturb these people.—The Chief .Constable : You have not said a word about "these people."—P.S. Bowen then said there was an assembly on the Fair Ground, where there was preaching, and prisoner had been trying to disturb them. Prisoner said he was a Roman Catholic; they were all going to hell, and he, was going to heaven. He had a stool, and persisted in standing upon it. They got him away, and he "carried on " all the way to the police station. It was not the first time "these people" had been disturbed.—The Mayor: Who are they ?—P:S. Bowen : They are what they call Free Gospellers.—The Chief stable: Who are the individuals themselves ?—P.S. Bowen: Mr. Bolton, Mr. Wright, and several other gentlemen--- H. Norman, inspector of nuisances, said he Saw a number of gentlemen on a hurry, and 300 or 400 peons listening to them. They were preaching the eospel. About three o'clo;:k the prisoner came up. He was very drunk indeed, and commenced cursing and using blasphemous language. He was requested several times to go away, but he refused to do so until the officers came and took him away.—The Mayor: This is a Very disgraceful thing.—The Chief Con- stable said in the neighbourhood of Silver-street and Silver- square there seemed a disposition to suppress these Free Gospel men, who go about preaching and visiting the sick, and from what had come to his knowledge he would have to be ready for any emergency that might arise.—The Mayor said cases like this, where a man forced himself on the public, were likely to create great disorder, and if he was supported by people of the same opinion as himself to create a riot.—The prisoner was fined 20s. and costs, total , 6.3 61, with the alternative of one mouth's imprison- ment. FOLLOWING IN HIS FATHER'S STEPS.—At the Borough Court on Monday, before his Worship the Mayor (Mr. Pickinere) and Major Cartwright, Robert Berwick painter, 22, Leicester-street, was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly, and assaulting P.C. Corc)ran, at the Police-station. —P.S. Cox said at 12 o'clock on Saturday night, he found the prisoner sitting on the footpath in Bewsey-street drunk. He "got him on his legs," and was persuading him to go home, when prisoner became disorderly, and followed him up the-street. Prisoner refused to go home, and he be- came again disorderly, and told witness it used to take 16 policemen in Glasgow to lock his father up. He got the prisoner to the Police-station, and when they commenced to search him he became very violent, and kicked P.C. Corcoran on the shins. They had to put prisoner on his back, and it required four policemen to hold him while he was searched.—P.C. Corcoran gave confirmatory evidence, and remarked that prisoner was the most violent person he ever saw.—Prisoner said he was drunk and he did not know what he was doing.—The Mayor: How was it you were drunk? Major Cartwright: He was showing a bit of the strength of his father- (Laughter.)—P.S. Cox: He is a very powerful man.—:The Chief Constable : I had to get up and order the police to put him in a cell by himself. He was very violent indeed. There was no sleep for anybody where he was.—The Mayor: Is he a Warrington man? The Chief Constable: No; he is a Scotchman.—Prisoner was fined 10s. and ,costs, (total 15s. 6d.) with the alternative of 14 days' imprisonment in default of payment. • A PUBLICAN OHARGED WITH PERMITTING DRUNKEN-

ICAM? MEETING AT WARRINGTON. What Was termed a united camp meeting was held in connection with the Free Gospel Churches of Warrington, on Sunday last on the New Fair ground. Service was held in the morning conducted by Mr. L. Bate, of Calcheth, and addresses were delivered by Messrs. J. Mort, of Lymm, and Wm. Twiss from a lurry, which had been improvised as a platform. Mr. George Hindley, of Leigh, conducted the afternoon meeting, and Messrs. J. Knowles, of Lymm, E. Twiss, and J. Evans preached. The weather was very fine, and the services were well attended, but some disorder was created at the afternoon meeting by a drunken Irishman who" held forth "in opposi- tion, and eventually found himself in the Bridewell, where he remained until he was sober. In the evening well-attended " lovefeasts " were held in Friars' Green and Bank Quay Workingmen's Mission Chapels, and service was also held in Academpstreet Chapel. Com- FIGHT IT WARRINGTON. —An unusual spectacle was witnessed in Peter-street, off Horsemarket-street, about three o'clock on Tuesday afternoon. Two game cocks often seen in the vicinity met, and apparently having some dis- pute proceeded to settle the matter by resorting to the use of their natural weapons—beak and spurs. No sooner had the battle begun than the feathered combatants were sur- rounded by a number of children and men who spend a good ' deal of their time at street corners on the look-out for any easy job that will enable them to earn a copper or two; and judging by the faces of the on-lookers, the contest seemed to afford them as much gratification as any fight witnessed in the cockpits at which many Englishmen used to pass their holidays and Sundays in "the good old times." However, when the fight .was becoming " interesting " a gentleman passed along the street and being more sensitive than the rest, separated the birds which ran screeching, and with ruffled feathers in different directions, and the crowd dis- persed as quickly as it had assembled. DAMAGING TREES AT BURTONWO OD. A man named Henry Charnock was brought before Messrs. H. Bleckly and S, Rigby at the Warrington County Petty Sessions on

Wednesday, charged with having maliciously cut and de- stroyed a number of trees and shrubs the property of John Fairclough, farmer, Burtonwood, and done damage to the amount of £2.—From information Mr. Fairclouglireceived on Saturday last he went to the garden belonging to his cottage and found a number of trees, 50 or more had been cut down. They consisted of currant, elder, and sycathore tree, willows, and other shrubs. They were ornamental trees. The prisoner formerly lived with his father at the house to which the garden belonged. The father was Mr. Fairclough's tenant, but on Saturday last he left the house, leaving a quarter's rent unpaid. The trees appeared to have been cut by a bill-hook—some about a foot from the ground, and others less, and were left lying about. On Saturday the prisoner was at a public-house with a man named Patrick Mullancer to whom he remarked that he had planted the .trees and could cut them down if he liked.—The prisoner, who was arrested on warrant on Tuesday, in answer to the charge, said he bought the trees and paid for them, and would have them.—He was committed' to the next quarter sessions for trial. - LANCASHIRE DANKitUPTS, &C. —FC ma Friday nigua Gazette—Liquidations by Arpangentent: J. RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS. The monthly meeting- was held at the Public Offices on Monday morning. There were present the Chairman (Dr. Steele), Messrs. W. Handley, Briscoe, Shaw, Lake, Timmins, Meadowcroft, P. Speakman, J. J. Speakman, G. S. Hazle- burst, Whitaker, Williams, Dr. McDougall, Norman, W. H. Linaker (law clerk), W. Brooks (secretary), Dr. Mouritz (medical officer), Barker (surveyor). MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT. The monthly report of the Medical Officer was read as follows : The number of deaths registered in Runcorn during the past month amounted to 28 ; two deaths occurred at llalton-within- Ruworn ; total 30; representing a death rate of 23 per 1,000 per annum. Of the above deaths 7were due to chest, Cto brain, 5 to abdominal. 3 to smrlatina affections, awl 2 to premature birth Disease of the throat, senile decay, cancer, and gangrene, and disease of the heart account for one owls. Fourteen deaths occurred among children 5 years old and sonde 8 under one year. Two inquests were held. I consider it my duty to state that during the past week nauseating exhalations have been eliminated from the glycerine works, and I understand one family h roe suffered from gastric irritation caused by the above nuisance. In answer to Mr.- W. Handley, the MEDICAL OFFICER said inquests were not included in the death rate. Mr. HANDLEY said two inquests had been held during the past month, and he thought they ought to be added. Let them know the worst. Mr. NORMAN observed that Mr. Barker kept them dis- tinct. Mr. HANDLEY: This report goes to the public and does not show the full death rate. The MEDICAL OFFICER: But cases of drowning are cer‘- thinly not diseases,—("No,")—and ought to go in a health return. If you take icquests you will have to take all accidents and sudden deaths. Mr. HANDLEY remarked that the Registrar General cer- tainly took all deaths in his return ; and unless this were done some of the healthiest districts in England would ap- pear the most unhealthy. Dr. McDouGALL said this was a ni..tter which did not admit of discussion. Inquests were held on persons whose death had resulted from violent causes, or in cases where there was a suspicion of foul play; and he did not think, in making a return of the causes of death, they could be in - eluded without making it entirely fallacious, because deaths, with regard to which inquests were held, could not possibly be recognised as the result of any disease incidental to any given locality. He quite concurred in the Medical Officer's classification of the deaths, which was the only way in which they could register them or get at the cause of death. The MEnscar. OFFICER, replying to Mr. Norman, said the death rate for the corresponding month last year was only j 11 per 1000. Mr. NORMAN observed that they could not expect the rate to remain so low as that. The matter then dropped. HIGHWAY AND StI•ZITARY Coons iTrEE. At a meeting held on the 28th ultimo, a letter was read from the secretary to the Water Com- pany with reference to the drainatte from the proposed hospital, and instructions were given to the Surveyor to reply (hereto.. Recommendation, that the reduced plans of the hospital and cottage be approved; that stne dressings be used in the elevation; and that tenders for the erection be obtained by the neort monthly meeting ot the committee. Mr. HANDLEY moved the confirmation of the minutes, and in doing so explained that the term "reduced plans " meant that the cotnmittee intended only to erect that portion of the hospital immediately neceesary, leaving the other portion until occasion demanded it. (Hear, hear.) Mr. NORMAN seconded the motion. Mr. MEADOWCROFT, having been supplied with a copy of ' the Amendment Act referred to in the minutes, &Aid it was 'at-:d at the last meeting that certain recommendations lied lven made by the Commissioners to the authotities in reference to clauses embodied in that Bill. If that were so he wished to know whether clause 5 in the sub-section was one of those recommendations. That clause stated that such part of the fees paid in respect of registration under the principal Act and of that Act, should be applied towards the expenses of any inquiry by the Lena' Government Board under that Act. He desired to draw the attention of the Commissioners to the matter, and if it had not been consi- dered, ask them whether it was not proper that they should take it into consideration. The CHAIRMAN said there was no resolution on this question, and as Mr. Meadowcroft was on the committee he had better bring it before the committee and discuss it there. He did not wish to stifle discussion, but it was a matter for discussion in committee and not at the Board. Mr. Meadow- croft was out of order. Mr. MEADowereorr replied that it was the unanimous wish of the colilalittee that he should bring the question forward that day. Some action ought to be taken with regard to this important clause. The CHAIRMAN : It is outside the minutes of the com- mittee. If there had been any recommendation, he might have discussed the subject, but he WAS decidedly out of order. He might bring it up at the end of the meeting. Mr. MEADowcttorT remarked that there seemed a desire to stifle discussion. Dr. MCDOUGALL inquired what Mr. Meadowcroft wished the Board to do, and said the authority of the chairman must be maintained. Mr. SHAw: I think be considers clause No. 4 ought not to be in the Bill. The Board might discuss it. I take it that any minute can be discussed. The LAW CLERK: There is no minute. The CHAIRMAN: It is only a report. Mr. SHAW: If it is a report you can discuss it. The CHAIRMAN ruled the subject was out of order. Mr. MEADOWCROFT remarked that if the Board did not think the clause worth attention he had done with it. The CHAIRMAN: It is quite worth discussion, bring it up at the end of the meeting. When the ordinary business of the Board was concluded. Mr. MEADOWCROFT again brought forward the subject. He said the clause he had adverted to, embodied in his opinion a proposition which the Board should consider, as there was no Board which it would affect so much as them- selves, Runcorn being the terminus of an important naviga- tion, and consequently the working of the Act and inquiries would fall upon them. He thought the expense of an inquiry such as that cefitemplated by the Act, should be borne by the Imperial Exchequer; he did not see why the Authority 'should be saddled with the expense. It was proposed also to allow the renewal of registration every twelve months. and in that ease, while the Board :night be deprived of a considerable revenue, the expense might be increased. It ' was a ratepayers' question, and he thought it ought to be raised. Mr. P. SPEAK3IAN suggested that the matter should be referred to the committee to report. Mr. MEADOWCROFT seconded the proposition. Mr. W. HANDLEY did not see the use of referring the sub- ject to the committee. They I:ad considered it fully. Mr. Meadowcroft was asked to make a proposition in committee such as would suit himself, and he refused to do so. Mr. MEADOWCROFT: I beg your pardon. I had framed one and it was suggested that I should bring it up in that form. Afterwards it was stated I hid better bring the reso- lution I do this morning. Mr. HANDLEY (continuing) said Mr. Meadowcroft seemed to consider the clause of the bill more from a boat owner's view than as a member of that Authority and declined to make any special re- commendation with regard to the clause. In fact Mr. Speakman was particularly anxious he should net be named in the matter. (A laugh.) The responsibility was thrown on the committee, who thoroughly dealt with the bill, in which they found no cause of complaint. Why, therefore, should they pass a recommendation to deprive themselves of revenue that the bill proposed to give them ? Had the committee agreed to the recommendation of Mr. Meadowcroft instead of adding to the fund for the adminis- tration of the Act, they would have been crippling it. Mr. Meadowcroft had asked whether certain recommen- dations had been mscie by the Board in regard to the bill. He (Mr. Handler) did not know whether they had or not, but he had pre- viously stated that where the Board had foand a weakness in the bill, which wanted amending, some mem- bers of the committee had made certain recommendations. The recommendations provided for the annual renewal of certificates, for it was quite evident to the members of the Board that a certificate once granted should not be con- sidered valid for whole time—(hear, hear,)—because between January 1882 and January 1883 very important alterations might be made in the boat. It was consequently asked that there should be an annual renewal of the canal boats' certifi- cates. The Board had found a great deficiency in the powers of inspections under the principal Act, bat this was amended in the bill, and greater power was given to the authority. The committee also considered it unjust that all the expenses of working the Act, so far as bringing Cases into the police courts was concerned, should fall directly upon the town, and they thought they ought to have some provision with i regard to the tines under the Canal Boats' Act as they had under the Public Health Act, and a clause was put in. The ' section referred to by Mr. Meadowcroft simply &lid that if there was a Government inquiry in the locality, the fees the Commissioners received should to some extent go towards

the expense of that inquiry. He had pointed out to Mr. Meadowcroft and to other members that it was simply such a clause as the Board had had under the Public Health Act for several years. The cost for the last seven years under the Public Health Act had been, he thought, about X 6. There was very little new matter in the administrative por- tions of the bill, which were mainly copied from the Pub:ic Health Act. The committcp dii not see anything to amend in the clause referred to by Mr. Meadowcroft, and if it were referred back it would only meet with the same arguments, and would come to the Board as bald as it had done before. ; (Hear, hear.) Dr.McDorGALL suggested that the matter be referred to the Highway and Sanitary Committee. Mr. MEADowcuorr said he was surprised, and the mem- bers of the Board would be surprised, that cettain members of the committee should make recommendations to the authority without bringing them officially before the com- mittee or the Board, and as though they represented the conclusions and opinions of the Board was a most extreme thing to do. Mr. HANDLEY: I rise to a point of order. I never said any such thing. The CHAIRMAN: I never heard you say so, Mr. Handley. Mr. MEADowcnorr was surprised at the opinions and views Mr. Handley had set upon him. They were wholly unjustified. Mr. P. SPEAR3LAN remarked that Mr. Handley must have misunderstood Mr. Meadowcroft. What Mr. Meadowcroft complained of at the last meeting was that all the recom- mendations that went to the Local Government Board did tit go from the Board, but from individual members of it, and was therefore a proper complaint tot him to bring-before the Board.
The CIIIIRMAN : I understan.l Mr. llindley d'JQsn't admit that.
Mr. MEADOWCROFT : lie said so in his speech. Mr. SPE&KMAS : It is a matter of fact that it is so. Mr. SJEA.IV : Mr. Handley said recommendations had been made.
Mr. _SPEAKMAN seconded Dr. McDougall's motion.

Dr. McDouGALL, in the course of a ft-i-w observations, said be did not think it right to throw discredit upon what Mr. Handley bad done, and to suggest that he had done it im- properly It was then decided to refer the subject to the Highway Committee.

THE BOARD AND THE WATER COMPANY. Mr. SHAW said when he saw the reference to a letter from the Water Company, he wondered whether there was some sanitary authority in the town besides the Commissioners ; or perhaps the Commissioners were unable to manage their own business. What answer was sent to the request of the Water Company. _

Mr. HANDLEY replied that the secretary to the Waterworks sent a letter asking whether the committee had adopted any system of drainage for the hospital; would it be in- imical to their interests; and bad they any objection to stating what systeni of drainage was to be adopted? The committee instructed Mr. Barker to reply and simply state that the drainage would be dealt with on the spot, and would not be allowed to contaminate anything. When there was an accumulation of sewage it would at once be removed, and would not be inimical to the Water Com- pany. Mr. SHAW said the Water Company bad waling what- ever to do with the question of sewage from the hospital, or from any other building, and the proper reply to that letter would have been that the Commissioners were dealing with the question, and that was the only reply which should be given. The only time when the Water Company coßld raise the question was when a nuisance was caused. . . . .

Mr. G. S. HAZLEHURST demurred from that statement. Suppose the drainage got round the Waterworks pipes, which became corroded, and sonic of the sewage got in the water, there would be an epidemic in the place. Mr. SIIAW : You have no water pipes near the place. The CiTAIRMAN observed that tbe sewage plea percolate through the red sandstone into the well. Mr. &taw said if the Water *Company were allowed to have some control over the hospital, as in that case, the same question could be raised against ev.ery dwelling-house in the town, and it was on that vital ground that he objected to the interference of the company in the drainage of the hospital; nor would he be any party to giving them even an assumed right of interference in the matter. He trusted the answer was going that the Board should take proper means for the disposal of the sewage. Mr. HANDLEY said it did not appear to the committee Vaat the letter was in any way officious, but simply a courteous communication asking what provision the Board were making for the drainage of the hospital in the interest. of the public and of the hospital. They ought to treat any public body in the same courteous spirit iu which they had written to the Board.

The CITAIRMAN thought Mr. Shaw was right in one sense; :.the Company had no right of interference in the matter; but a civil cpestion deserved a civil answer. There was no harm done in sending a reply. Mr. SHAW: Sometimes those answers involve you. There's the difficulty. Dr. McDouGILL: Will von, read the letter, Mr. Chair- man ? The CHAIRMAN then real the letter which was in sub- stance what was stated by Mr. Handley. The Clerk also read the reply sent by the committee. ' Dr. McDotTom.r. thought they were perfectly justified in sending the reply. Mr. Slimy: I take it that that answer has admitted the control of the company over the sewage question. It has not repudiated the interference in any shape or form.

Dr. McDotroutr. said the Water Company was constituted the water supplyin.-; authority of the township and district by Act of Parliammt with certain privileges and responsi- bilities, and it seemed to him that in discussing that ques- tion th,-,y, had tw) points to consider as far apart as the north was from the south pole. Mr. Shaw had said alloy ing the present inquiry to be made by the company was virtually admitting the right of the company to inquire as to the remora/ of sewage from any house the Board had to erect. lie should be sorry if any member of the Board was so thorouglq ignorant of the sources of water supply in Runcrn as to mire a statement like that which could not possibly be borne out by facts. The water supply of the cpmpany was not drawn from a lake—an accumulation of surface water—but absolutely from part of the earth over which the hospital was about to be built. They could not possibly have a niore courteous letter addressed to a public body than that written by the secretary of the water com- pany, and to send such a letter as suggested by Mr. Shaw would be disrespectful. Mr. Sate.w remarked that the Commissioners knew their own business; how to erect a hospital and deal with the sewage ; without the interference of any other party. ' Dr. McDouGALL said people having other rights had a right to know what was proposed to be done with the swage. The LAW CLERK 1)0 you mean legal or moral rights? Mr. HAZLEHURST : Has the letter-gone ? The LAAV CLERK: Yes.
Mr. IlezLEurnsT : It is ;:then no :use discussing the matter.

Dr. McDouGALt, : The company are the gnardians of their own rights and of the ratepayers rights too. Mr. SHAW: May we ask the Law Clerk whether he con- siders the:Water Company have any right whatever over this particular question at issue. The LAW CLERK: Not the slightest. Dr. gcDOUGALL : That is the opinion of the Law Clerk, of course. (Laughter.) The LAW CLERK : If the Water Company consider that their works will be damaged by what the Commissioners do, they can go to the Court of Chancery and restrain them from proceeding. Dr: McDotrosti.: That would be melancholy. The LAW CLERK further observed that although the com- pany had no right to interfere, they could courteously ask what was being done. Dr. MCDOUGALL : I am glad the letter has gone in the spirit it has been sent. The minutes of the Hospital Committee were then con- firmed.
