div.head: GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE.
div.p: GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE.

1119 General Purp^ses Committee recommended the payment of tcronnts amounting to £313; that the Market Inspector be allowed 14 days' holiday, and that Dr. McDougall, Messrs. Briscoe and Norman, be empowered to make arrangements for a substitute during Lis ab,ence. It was also recommended that the Board-room. staircase and lobby, ceilings. and walls, be repapered and cleated, and if necess try reyarnisited. at a cost not exceeding £3. Dr. MeDoroALL moved, and Mr. NORMAN seconded, the motion for the adoption of the minutes. After some discussion they were passed, it being decided that the Board-room &c., should be decvated at a cost not exceeding £lO. The CHAIRMAN intimated that the work would be performed for £5, he having a tender to that amount.

div.head: FINANCE COMMITTEE : CONGRATULATIONS:.
div.p: THE FINANCE COMMITTEE : CONGRATULATIONS:.

At a meeting of the Finance Committee held on the 2011 June, the following summary of accounts for the month was submitted :—Market rents and tolls, £53 163. 83. ; slaughter house rents, £1 lls. 11d.; Hospital Cottage rents, 6.7. e., £2 83. ; surcharge Bs.; H.M. Treasury contributions, .-C4 Os. ; general district rate, £849 Cs. 103.; total, £9ll lls. 11d. Accounts amounting to £BlB us. 1.1. were recommended br payment. The Treasurer's bilances were given as follows ;—General funds, £492 14s. Be.; district funds, £lO 2s. 103. ; sinking fund, £O5O 2e. 23.; loan (unspent), £2 247 4s. 73. &commended that a special committee, consisting of Messrs. Norman, McDougall, Fisher, Lake, J. J. Speakman, Briscoe and Shaw, he appointed to con- sider the duties and salaries of the officials, and report thereon to the Board.

Mr. J. J. SPEAIIMAN in moving the passing of the minutes, which was seconded by Mr. TammtNs, said the auditor had sent a very' gcod report, and there was only the sniall surcharge of £2 Bs. Dr. McDouGALL thought the Board ought to congratulate the Committee upon haying escaped with whole skins on this occasion,—the only time, be believed, sincc.t the ap- pointment of the Ciovernment auditor, that they had not been sensured or surcharged. Mr. HANDLEY remarked that the Board had not been in the difficulties described by Dr. McDougall, each year. Dr. MCPOUGALL Said it had been an exceptional circum- stance if they bad escaped. It was matter for congratula- tion that the affairs of the Board had succeeded so greatly, and been able to meet the requirements of the auditor upon so small a rate. lie hoped the current year would he equally satisfactory to the Board and to the auditor. Mr. HAZLEHURST asked how long it was since the salaries . and duties of the officers of the Board were last investi- gated. The L.kw CLERR In 1877.
Mr. HAzty.ntns-r enquired if there vas any ream for doing so again. He confessed to a feeling of specir:l

sympathy with the officials, who never seemed to know definitely What was required from them, nor what salary they were to rec3ive. It really was not a desirable course to pursue at all. Mr. P. SPEAKMAN (jeculatly) : We will increase the salaries. The CHAIRMAN said the auditor expressed himßelf on one point strongly, and it was on his sf;ecial recommendation that they were considering the re-arrangement of the officials.
Sabsequentls the names of Mr. Hazleburst and Mr. Meadowcroft were added to the committee, and the minutes passed.

WATERLOO ITOVSE : THE QUESTION TO BE RECONSIDERED. Mr. LAKE rose to move the resolution of which he had given notice, "That the recommendation of the 'Properties. Committee,' April 24, as to various properties of the Board be taken into consideration." Mr. Lake narrated at length what had taken place at the committee previously formed to deal with this matter, arid said at the second' meeting they bad the advice of the law clerk, who drafted the resolution which came before the Board. On the morning previous to the meeting of the Board the Law Clerk sent him a slip of paper, suvesting what resolution he (Mr. Like) should propose if the iecom- mendation was adopted. Unfortunately the committee were met with an objection from a gentleman who they thought would have been most anxious to urge the matter forward, that the committee's proposal was extraordinary business, and what was surprising to most gentlemen on the commit- tee, the Law Clerk supported him after he advised him (Mr. Lake) what to propose. He did not know why he changed his mind so suddenly; perhaps he had hid a consultation with a certain gentleman. But, notwithstanding the legal authority of Mr. Livaker, he was still inclined to believe that the matter was really in order; and he thought it ab- surd to call the report of a committee appointed by the Board extraordinaty business. The LAW CLERK said the objection. was that the commit- tee had exceeded the instructions given by the Board. Mr. LAKE submitted that the recommendation of the COM. mittee did not go beyond their powers; ond if they adopted it the Law Clerk was I esponsible for it. The LAW CLERK: The Law Clerk did not draw the recommendetions and, therefore, could not be responsible for it.
Mr. LAKE: The minute was drawn by the Law Clerk.
The LAW CLERK: I drew the minute appointing the committee! Keep to facts and then you can say what you like.

Mr. LAKE remarked that the committee recommended that Waterloo House be advertised for sale, and that he contended came clearly within the power of the committee. However, it was ruled otherwise. Personally he was much opposed to entering into this subject again, and he had only done it as a duty he owed to the other members of the commit- tee.
Mr. NORMAN seconded the motion, wi;ich WAS carried. It was ultimately decided that a meeting to discuss the matter should be held on the 27th inst.

The LAW CLERK, in replying to Mr. Lake's statement, said it was true he had attended the committee meeting at which the recommendation was drawn up, and that he sent the memorandum referred to to Mr. Lake, but be was net then aware of the powers of the committee. Mr. Lake was chairman of the meeting and be (Mr. Linaker) presumed he knew the scope of the committee, and it was not until his attention was called to the resolution appointing the com- mittee, that he decided they had travelled beyond the powers given to them—that they cmild not deal with the matter. Mr. LAKE: Unless my memory is tuacherous your atten- tion was called to it at the meeting. The LAW CLERK: Then your memory is treacherous. Mr. Handley was there and he will know. . _
The discUssion then ceased. - _ _ _ AN AGREEMENT. _
The seal of the Board was ordered to be affixed to an agree- ment between the Commissioners and the .Board of Guar- dians with reference to the proposed Infectious Diseases Hospital.

div.head: TIIE PUBLIC FOUNTAIN : ANALYSIS OF THE WATER.
div.p: TIIE PUBLIC FOUNTAIN : ANALYSIS OF THE WATER.
The SECRETARY (Mr. W. Brooks) read the following. analysis:—

Royal Institution Laboratory, Liverpool, June 21. 1882. Analysis of sample of water in stone jar received from Mr. Barker, June 17, sealed S.W. and Stag's Head, Irem the Runcorn Commissioners. Total residue on evaporation. 63•25 grains per gallon. The mineral constituents are :—Chloride of sodium, 3157; chloride of potassium, 073; chloride of magnesium, 2.68 ; sulphate of lime, 212; sulphate of magneda, 9 21; carbonate of lime, 1575 • carbonate of magnesia, 281 • nitrate of magnesia, 083; oxide of iron; 024; oxygen require for water (T;dy's test) in thousands, 0137 oxygen required for water in thousands. 0190; free ammonia (per million), 0.1-3 ; albumlnoid ammonia (per mil- lion), 052; hardness temporary (per million), 28; hardness permanent (per million), 140; total hardness. 348. The water when examinei had a strong smell of sulphuretted hydrogen, and evolved that gas sufficiently to blacken a lead pager held in the upper part of the jar. The water was slightly turbid, and contained some black flocculent matter. 17nuer the microscope this was found to consiat of decomposed organ;c matter, coloured. black by sulphide of iron. There was a'so a large amount of low forms of animal life. The water is slightly alkaline. The analysis snows that the water receives a large quantity of se vage, and belongs to the class of decidedly impura water. In my opinion it is totally unfit for use as a beverage in it present state, and is decidedly dangerous. In- dependently of the sewage the water- is very bard, and owing to the la--ge proportion of magnesia salts would prove rather relaxing. A 1)ottle eantainins a large quantity of black sedi- ment accompanied the sample of water. The sediment is of the same character-as that in the water, and owes its blackness to the same cause. It also evolved a large quantity of snl- phuretted hydrogen.—Eowasin DAVIES, F.e.S., F.J.C., It was decided, on the motion of Mr. NORMAN, to close the fountain for two months. This was all the public business.

div.head: FRODSITAM,
div.p: FRODSITAM,

PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL, KINGSLEY. —The anni- versary services in connection with this chapel were held on Sunday, when the sermons were preached by the Rev. J. J. Bradshaw, of Crewe, and the collections amounted to the satisfactory sum of £lB. METHODIST FREE Ciluncu, FRODSHAM. SUNDAY SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY AND TREAT.—Two sermons were preached in the Methodist Free Chi*eh on Sunday, by the Rev. J. P. Burt, of the Theological Institute, Manchester, the collections being in aid of the school funds, and amounted to £lO. The services were well attended, the musical por- tion was nicely rendered by the choir, and the congregation joined in the hymns in a very hearty manner. Mr. Harry Aston presided at the organ. The annual treat to the scholars took place on Wednesday, when tea was again pro- vided at Mr. James Percival's, of Godscroft, and although the weather was very unfavourable for those out-door games which even Sunday school teachers and scholars delight in, a very pleasant afternoon was spent, and the little ones were brought safely to Frodsham in a waggon kindly supplied by Mr. Thomas Davies.
FRODSHAM LORDSHIP SEWERAGE. GOVERNMENT INQUIRY.

A public inquiry was held in the Town Hall, Frodshana, yesterday, by Samuel Joseph Smith Esq , the inspector ap- pointed by the Local Government Board, to receive evidence relating to a further loan of £593 required for works of sewerage and sewage disposal for the lordship of Frodsham. The following were present :—S. J. Smith, Esq , inspector ; Dr. J. G. Bride, medical officer of health ; Mr. Henry Linaker, clerk to the Sanitary Authority; Mr. James Far- rington. inspector of nuisances ; Messrs. Thomas Davies, John Challoner, Thomas Riley, Thomas Andrews, Joseph Cunnah, 11.)hert Andrews, Samuel Spencer, and Samuel Aston.

The notice convening the meeting was read, and a state- ment of expenditure on account of the drainage scheme for Frodsbam and Frodsham Lordship was prolucod by Mr. Linaker, from which it appeared that a mcotgage of £3,110 for Frodsham, and £2.860 had been actually charged to Frodsham, leaving a balance of unexpended loan of £253. , With respect to Frodsbam Lordship, a mortgage of £762 had been obtained, and the amoutn charged to,that township was £1,360, leaving the sum of .£593 to be obtained, and this, it was explained, was the object of the inquiry, the additional expenditure havin.2; been incurred for two way- leaves, which in one case was by arbitration, and the other by arrangement. The Inspector inquired what further portion of the entire drainage scheme was proposed to be carried out, and Mr Challoner, as guardian for the township of Frodsham Lord- ship, stated that he did not consider that any further extension of the drainage scheme was necessary, aP.d suq- geEt-d that the water might be deferred for ten years. The MEDICAL OFFICER of HEALTH, in reply to the In- spector, said he knew the Five Crosses district, and con- sidered that works of sewerage were necessary and could not be postponed for an indefinite period. The v o at vrtion was up to the Five Crosses smithy, and he was of opinion thit "the sewer should be at once extended along Fluin-lane, to the Five Crosses smithy, and for the pr?sent the other por- tions of the scheme submitted to the Local Government Board might be deferred. Mr. CHALLONER said that the land along the line of pro- posed sewer was already built upon, and he contended that the question of an extension of the sewers could not bo raised at this inquiry, as the notice contained no ref,rence to it, but only referred to money required for works already carried out, and if the ratepayers had been aware that this course would have been taken, they would have had a town's meeting to consider the matter.

The IssPscron remarked that it NS's pertinent to the in- quiry to take the opinion of the Medical Officer of Heal'h. The CLERK to the Authority informed the Inspeet-): that the leng;th of the sewer along Fluin-lane to ToWnfield- lane was estimated by the engineer to cost £62:1 83. .24., and from Townfieldlane to Five Crosses £667 105.7 d. The cost of length of s .wet to Five Crosses smithy only, was not given separately. The INSPFCTOR pointed out that the proposed extension would have to be undertaken by the townships vf Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship jointly, and the amount afterwards apportioned by the Sanitary iutbority. ; Mr. JOHN CHALLONER.her, ap-r1 objected to the con- sideration of an extension of the drainage scheme without 'due notice. The Medical-Oflicer of Health said the Towt,field-lane should also be drained at the same time, as complaints bad been made that the water in Cobden or Water-street brook o Hated by the drainage.—The Clerk said that the 'esq.'ii-mra°ted cost .of this sewer was .£llO 185 2d.—The luspee- tor inquired if there was any obj-ction to the apportion- mc.nt as submitted by the Rural Sanitary Authority, and elicited the opinion that a portion of the costs of athitration as to wayleave should be borne by Frodsham. This the Inspector explained was not reasonable, and having Ft ttorll that he would rcport to the Local Government Board CI inquiry was declared closed.

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of the Council was held on Tuesday in the Council Chamber, Town Hall. The Mayor (Alder- Men Picamere) presided; and there were also present Alder- men Burgess, Kean, Harrison, Davies, Holmes, and Webster, Councillors Milner, Platt, Burgess, Mackie, Collin, Ashton, Woolfall, Wright, Wallington, Barker, Greening, Monks, Jeans, Fairclough, Brown, and Whittle; Messrs. W. H. Brook (town clerk), J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk), C. Cliorley (oorough treasurer), T. Longdin (borough • sur- veyor), and J. Paterso'n (gas manager). WATCU COMMITTEI3 : TUB CORPORATION ACCOUNTS. The MAYOR moved, and Alderman HARRISON seconded, the adoption of the minutes of the Watch Committee. Councillor PLArr said there seemed to be a pretty general opinion at the last meeting that the various accounts of the COMMit.L. SS. should be read out before they were passed, so that the Council would know the amounts that were being paid, to whom they were being paid, and for what purpose. Alracet everyone seemed to agree that that course would be an improvement upon the mode of procedure. It might lengthen the proceedin,,,s half an hour, but in his opinion it would be half an hour well soent. The expenditure Of the Corporation was increasing almost daily, and if they could . .

rteluee some of the accounts it would be time well spent. AldermAn 9ARRISON would like to have the opinion of the Town Cierk as to whether it would not be preferable to print the accounts on the minutes than to keep the Council while they were read out. as used to be the case on former occasiwis. On those occasions the meetings of the Council were very troublesome, whereas if the Council had the accounts printed on the minutes every gentleman would have an opportunity of studying them before he came to the Council, and the business small Le comparatively sh3rt. The MAYOR did not think the remarks applied to the -committee whose minutes were under consideration for he believed the principal items were for wages—the usual weekly wages. Probably to some committees the remarks might have more weigtt. Counc'llor Monks remarked that he could not think Councillor Platt had given an exactly correct version of what took place at the last meetinte• He thought it was e then understood that any extraordinary amounts such as those in payment of the balancteof Messrs Manlove, Fryer, and Co.'s accounts should be included in the minutes in future. (The Mayor: Yee.) He did not think it was understood every account should be printed, and he con- fessed that he had not the slightest belief if they were to print every item it would tend to lessen the expenditure one iota. This was a matter that should be left entirely in the hands of the committees. Councillor Feanceot-Gif thought some committee should be asked to take the matter in hand and report thereon to . the Council. He suggested the Finance or the General Purposes Committees whose decision would satisfy all par ties. The MAYOR thought the General Purposes Committee the best as the Finance Committee were the greatest sinners. (Laughter.) Alderman HOLMES observed that when it was customary to read out the accounts, the members amused themselves in all sorts of fashions. Alderman HARRISON said that was so no doubt, but if

the accounts were printed it would not be so. Councillor MACKIE said it struck him the suggestion was received with great unanimity at the last meeting of the Council, and the exception they seemed inclined to make was in connection with salaries—what might be called, fixed expenditure. He had a very vivid remembrance of the proceedings to which Alderman Holmes had alluded, and he was quite correct in saying the accounts were read over somewhat rapidly amid a conversational buzz. But he believed it was quite within the power of the Council to have the ordinary accounts printed and laid before the Council. He was persuaded it would not cost them ss. a month, and what was of much greater importance, the rateyayers would know something of the large sums which were totalled up in the minutes. There was no doubt a great deal being said out ef doors about the rates rising. Some said ratee were falling, and certainly there was some pleasant app,arance of reducing taxation and expenditure, for he had learned within the last half-hour that the Government official who was audit- ing the accounts of the Union was determined to make the overseers their own bill posters. Anything in the way of economy should be strongly supported. Councillor MILNER said 'one of the principal reasons for discontinuing the reading bf the various items of expendi- ture was because it was practically too late to do anything, with the accounts when they were read over. (Hear, hear.) The idea was that by acting as they had done lately more responsibility was thrown on the individual committees, and that the people who really could control the expenditure should be pressed to do so. He did not think they could gain anything at all by reading over the accounts again, more especially as large amoun-s had been already passed by the Council. There was not large amount spent by the Council that was not passed there, and the reading over of the payment of the accounts really amounted to nothing, as the payment bad eh eady been approved. Alderman HARRISON : How. do Non mean that the ac- counts have been already before the Council? Councillor MILNER said supposing the Council undertook

to give a contract for a thousand pounds they approved of the spending of the thousand pounds, and the simple read- ing over of the fact that the thousand pounds had been paid to the man who had done the work did not amount to any-. thing. The Mivron : The conversation is beyond the minutes before US. If any gentleman likes he can move, at the proper time, that the accounts be printed, or can do so at the quarterly meeting. Alderman BURGESS: You will take it at the end of the meeting, I suppose ? The MAYOR: It is a monthly meeting to-night. Alderman IlAnnisolr: I intend to move in this matter at the next meeting, because I knew it was a quarterly meeting. The minutes were agreed to. FINANCE.

In moving the adoption of the minutes of the Finance Committee, Alderm tn HOLM:2S alluded to the report which had been presented by the Borough Auditor, remarking that it reflected very grditt credit on Mr. Chorley for the manner in which the accounts were kept. Councillor MILNER seconded the motion, which was sarried,

OTETZSIGIIT OP BUILDING OPERATIONS. Councillor PLATT moved the paesing of the minutes of the Street Improvement and Lighting Committee, and in doing so observed that the committee had decided to appoint se sub-committee whose duty it would be to visit the sites of proposed buildings or alterations in property where it was thought necessary to do so. Cases had come before the committee where they were scarcely able to judge from the mere plans as to bow certain alterations would affect the property surrounding, and it was thought desirable in such eases that a cub-committee of the Street Improvement Com- mittee shoeld visit them and report to the committee on the subject. Councillor WALLINGTON: I second the motion. The MAYOR: Are the gentlemen on the sub-committee going about at their own expense 2 (Laughter.) Councillor PLATT: Most decidedly, Mr. Mayor. (Laugh- ter, and "Hear, hear.") The MAYOR: Very good of them. (Renewed laughter.) The motion was carried. TEE TAKING OVER OF STREETS BY TRE CORPORATION. Alderman KEAN moved the confirmation of the Paving 1 and Sewerage Committee's minutes, and called attention to the recommendation of the committee that the tender of Messrs. Ryder and Sons, of Sale, for the drainage of Latch- ford according to the specifination and quantities prepared by the borough surveyor, be accepted. He observed that since the recommendation had been printed they had received an amended tender from the firm which the com- mittee had decided to accept. It was found that they had made a mistake of £Bl, and he moved the adoption of the proceedings of the committee with that amendment. Councillor WoorsAtr, seconded the motion. Councillor Memetc slid be wished to ask a question on behalf of the Ratepayers' A sisociation with reference to the responsibility which he Corporation assumed when they adopted new streets. He remarked that there was some doubt among certain owners of property in the town as to their liability ; it was discussed at a late meeting, at which state- ments were made which he could scarcely think correct. It was stated that streets which had been ordered to be made hy the Corporation,and had been paid for by the owners of pro- perty, still remained at the expense of those owners of pro- . pe rty, unless buildings were erected through the whole - length of the street. He thought some authoritative state- ment should be made on the subj,ct. Alderman KEAN remarked that they had recently had two oases before the committee, in one of which the properte- owners refused to pay before their street was adopted, amid consequently it was on their hands and they had to pay for any repairs tint might be required. In the other case— which was one of litigation and in which there was a dispute about payment—it was not wise for the Corporation to take any responsibility. Councillor Lamm said that was not quite an answer to leis question. What be wished was an authoritative state- ment as to when the responsibility of property owners ceased. - The Tower CLERK said that all streets made according to the requirements of the Corporation had to be repaired by the individuals who hid been called upon to make them, hut when once they were adopted by the Corporation they had to be repaired at the expense of the ratepayers at large. Alderman NVE.I3VrEII observed that the property owners had no responsibility after a street had been accepted by the• Corporation, and the Corporation always accepted a street where it was made properly. In reply to a (position, Alderman Klux remarked that the tender of -Messrs. Ryder and Sons was the lowest tender • by far. • - The minutes of the Committee were then adopted. SCITOOL ATTT.NDANCE. Alderman WEBSTER moved the adoption of the minutea of the School Attendance Committee, Councillor Dixote seconded the motion, which was carried. The report of the Inspector ehowed that 47 cases had been enquired into by the Board of Guardiene, cud that echoel fees bad been allowed in 31 eazes for G 5 children. Also, that 34 cases were taken before the magistrates when fines were in3icted in 32 cave, one adjourned, and one boy whipped. 44 cases were brought before the committee and dealt with.

THE airsEum, LTBRARY, AND ARTS COIMIITTEE. Councillor (Iune:KING in moving the confilination of the minutes of the Museum, Library, and Arts Committee A ObSerVed that Vie members would notice that several im- poTtant donations had been made to the institution, which
the Committee had received with thanks and acknowledged. Councillor BURGESS seconded the adoption of the minutes, whict were carried.
TIIE CEMETERY. On the motion of Councinor Snows, seconded by Alderman HAnnisos, the minutes of the Cemetery Com- mittee were passed.
THE IMPROvEMENT OF THE PARK: PERSONAL RECRIMINATIONS. _
The MAYOR moved the adoption of the Town Hal!, Park, and Baths Committee's minutes, and Councillor PLATT seconded the motion.

Councillor MACKIE asked whether the time had not nearly approached when the Town Council should ta';:, some other steps towards completing their part of the we which they undertook in connection with the public Park. They all remembered that marvellous manifestation of what might really be called mediteval munificence, when two gentlemen gave such a large sum, in connection with that Park, to the town. They remembered the exertions of Mr. Alderman Davies and others, and he personally remembered Mt. Hy. White when he spoke many, many years ago of what the Park might be made for the people of Warrington. He thought that after ten years' trial the time had probably now come, or was within " measurable distance," when something should be done to render the Park really more than it at present was, the people's Park, or the Park of the people of Warrington. He pointed out that it re- mained walled round to a great extent, and those outside could not observe what was going on inside. He contended that the gates were too far apart, remarking that trove one gate on one side they had to walk for seven minutes before they came to the next. He there- fore suggested that the committee be asked to consider the matter. As far as his opinion was concerned, he thought £250 would be quite sufficient, although he might be wrong in'the amount, to carry out the improvements. Councillor WALLINGTON said he had been requested to ask if the Carpenter memorial could wit be put in a better condition for drinking purposes. It was very difficult for persons who were thirsty to obtain any water, and to drink they had to put their lips to the tap, which was very incon- venient. _ _ _

Alderman HARRISON did not know that he could say very much with reference to the suggestions made by Dr. Mackie, but he had a great deal of sympathy with them. There was a large stone wall and a mound which shut out entirely from the roadway the view of the Town Hall, and be thought it would be a great improvement to the street if they were removed. The Town 11.111 would then more resemble a Town Hall than it did at present, and if the alterations were made they would be an immense improvement to the town. _ _ _

----- Councillor WHITTLE: It would to the Gua)qian office— not to the town. (Laughter and hear, hear.") Alderman HARRISON: I thi3ak no man would be stupid enough to say it would not improve the present appearance of this town. (Hear, hear.) ' Councillor 'MACKIE: Allow me, Mr. Mayor, to call your a' tention to this gentleman's (Councillor Whittle's) conduct. I say if we are to conduct business here as gentlemen-- Councillor WHITTLE: Mr. Mayor, Dr. Mackie has already spoken once. I call your attention to that. (Hear, hear.) Councillor MACKIE: I rise for an explanation. This Council's dignity is impugned if you allow remarks of this kind to pass unheeded. Why should I, as the representative of a particular ward in Warrington, be laid open ts charges of this kind?

The MAvon : I think you are fully entitled to an expla- nation, Dr. Mackie, but you cannot make a speech after you have once spoken. I would ask Councillor Whittle what he means by the statement he made. Councillor Mac= said Councillor Whittle meant some- thing which was very painful to him after his long residence in the town, and after be had done all he could for its im- provement—long before Councillor Whittle was born, and when he was playing with the childish playthings of boy- hood. (LaugP,hter and "fear, hear.") Councillor JEANS said he thought that Dr. Mackie's ob- servations to a certain extent were worth consideration at the hands of the Council. Improvement in front of the Town Hall would much improve the garden itself. He sug- gested that it would be a great convenience to the inhabi- tants of a certain portion of the town if they could gain access to the Park without having to go up Sankey-street. (Hear, hear.) He did not speak in his own personal interest, but be thought it would be a great convenience if they could get into the Park somewhere near the corner of Crosfield- street, and it would be a great improvement as well as con- venience if there was another entrance near Messrs. Williams and Clay's works at the other end of the street. Alderman DATIES observed that he had sympathy with any movement that had for its object the improvement of the town, but very likely Dr. ',Mackie was not aware why the Park was enclosed in the way it had been. At one time they had other openings and entrances, and the result was they found the Park was made use of as a near approach from one part of the town to another. In consequence of that what they wanted to preserve was really and indeed destroyed, and a marked footpath was seen at an angle across the Park, which became regularly used as a footpath. It was found desirable and -absolutely necessary in order to preserve it from further trespass at various points to enclose the Park. He thought the time would -came—and he did not care how soon it did—when they should see improve- ments about the Town Hall, but ho wanted Dr. Mackie to understand why it was, after due consideration, that the Town Hall and Park Committee found themselves bound' to enclose it. (Hear, hear.) Alderman IiTEIssTER said the question had been before the committee, but the expense was found to be so serious, and I the rates would be affected to such an extent, that it was al- ways agreed to postpone the consideration of it from time to timeu,ntil they should have more money in hand. As to the statement that £250 would be sufficient it was simply absurd : six times that amount would be nearer the mark.

Councillor PLITT said he quite agreed with Dr. Mackie as to the front of the Town Hall being shown to greater advantage, and also that a view of the park from Sankey- street would be a considerable improvement, but at the present time the rates were sufficiently high without under- taking work of the character indicated. There were other and more pressing matters which should be taken first. When the Sanitary Committee, instead of spending was adding to revenue, then would be about the time for under- taking such work. The MAYOR said this question had been before the com- mittee often for the last three or four years. The only difficulty was the money. He thought the whole of the committee were unanimous in their idea that the wall next to Sanhey-street should come down, and something like a xquare formed with seats around. Aldermen Webster, he beiidvc-d, had suggested that more trees should be planted, or that there should be a kind of shrubbery in the centre, with seats around, but that meant the expenditure of a. considerable amount of money, and that was the only diffi- culty which prevented the committee from mahing the al ter.a- Lions which were so desirable. With respect to the remarks of Mr. Wallington about the Carpenter memorial, the committee were waiting for the action of the Waterworks Company. Mr. Longdin informed him that cups bad been added to the fountain, but they were now taken away. With reference to the inlets to the Park, as Mr, Alderman Davies had said, a thoroughfare had been made from one gate to another round one side in order to make the Park more retired, but if there were more openings—four instead of the present number—the Park he thought would deteriorate, and the women, nurses, and children who now so much enjoy its retreat, would not for obvious- reasons be likely to go there so much as they did at present. As re- garded thoroughfares he considered it would be better to leave the Park as it was. The minutes was then confirmed.

div.head: MAP XETS.
div.p: THE MAP XETS.
On the motion of Councillor LITTON, seconded by Councillor GREENING, the proceedings of the Markets Com- mittee, which contained no items of special interest, were confirmed, without discussion.

div.head: DEATH OF MRS. CROSFIELD.
div.p: THE DEATH OF MRS. CROSFIELD.

Alderman BURGESS, in moving the adoption of the minutes of the Sanitary Committee, said the members had passed a res Aution sympathising with Mr. Crostield in his bereavement, and he would only add that the letter con- veying that sentiment was duly forwarded to Mr. Crostield.

Councillor NON KS seconded the motion. The MAYort said he was very sorry to hear of Mr. Cros- field's bereavement, and he was very glad the Sanitary Com- mittee—at the meetings of which he was so often present and took a great interest—had sent to him the letter which they had done.

Alderman WESTER observed that the tender r.f Mr. It Whitlow for the purchase of the horse manure ii-Lide at the Corporation stables had been accepted, and he expressed the hope that the committee had stipulated for the manure to be removed regularly, as it was injurious to the vegetation in the gardens. • Alderman BURGESS said the committee had made a stipu- lation for the removal of the manure regularly and fuquently, and he added that it was at a serious loss to the Corporation, for if the manure were allowed to remain as in other places it would fetch twice or three times the amount of money it did. The person whose tender had been accepted was tinder an engagement to remove it at least once a week. The committee did not think that vegetation suffered, but they quite understood that if the manure was offensive to people in the Park, it was perfectly right that they should minimise that offence as much as they possibly could.
The proceedings of the committee were confirmed. REDUCTION IN THE PRICE OF GAS. •

Alderman HoLmEs moved the adoption of the proceedings of the Gas Committee, the chief item in which was a recommendation to !educe the price of gas 3i. per 1,000 fut. such reduction to take place from the 25th March last. He observed that a meeting of tbe Ratepayers' Association liad been held a few days ago, at which a suggestion had been made that the price of gas should be reduced by dd. per thousand feet. They, as Members of the Gas Committee, like the members of the RliepayerS' Aszociation, were con- sumers of as ; and in common with the members of the Ratepayers' Association, the numbers of the Gas Commtttee liked t(-) have their, gas as low as they could ; but in the reduction they had made they had gone as far as they dare go, and he thought when he had read some figures to them they would think the committee had no other alternative. The total profits of the gas works during the year amounted to £12,813, out of which the committee had to pay to the Corporation, in rEsly.ct of interest to bondholders and annui- ties, and also in respect of the Sinking Fund (which pro- vided for the repayment of the purchase of the works), the sum of £10,637, leaving a surplus profit of £2,175; The reduction in the price wou!d mean a Ices to the revenue of about £2,000----that was to say, if the amount of consump- tion was the same as in the past, the only basis on which they could safely base their calculations. He thought, therefore, they would be of opinion that the committee had

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 8, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 8, 1882.

gone as far, he repeated, as they dare go in reducing the price. Of course, they hoped that by the reduction in the price there would be a considerable increase in the consumption; and he was glad to be able to infoem the Council that by the offer they had made to the inhabitants of putting down gas cooking apparatus without any cost, a large number of persons were adopting the gas stoves, and the committee hoped to have in a very short time a considerable increase of consumPtion in that way. Those were the reasons which had induced the committee to bring forward the recommendation, and he hoped they would be satisfactory to the Council ; if they could have gone further they would have been glad to do so. He might add that the discount to the urge consumers of gas as set forth a few months ago would be continued in exactly the same ratio as at present. Councillor 'MILNER, in seconding the motion, took the opportunity of calling the Council's attention to the fact that the next reduction in the price might most liLly erise from the increased daylight consumption of gas. As the gas came to be more extensively used during the day they should get double the work out of their plant, and therefore, if that was the case, there would be a considerable reduction under the head of fixed charges. That, he expected, would be the result of the large use of gas fur cooking and other purposes during the day. Councillor MACKIE said he had been asked by the Rate, payers' Association to support a greater reduction in the price of gas, but after the statement of Mr. Alderman Holmes, he thought there was very little that could be urged in favour of their view of a reduction of more than 3d. Still he thought it would be well to hold out a promise to the ratepayers that as the gas works did increase-their pro- fits a further reduction would be made, and that under no circumstances would they entertain the idea of making pro- fits out of the gas merely to relieve the general rates. The cost of the gas, he reminded the Council even with this re- duction, was as they very well knew, still higher than in the majority of towns in the district. It was however pleasing to know that the gas woiks were making a profit, aud all that he wished at present was to impresiLupon the commit- tee that the interests of the large consumers of gas in War- rington, and of those who intended to be large consumers, were hound up in having the price as low as it could be had in any other town in the neighbourhood. He did net think it was wise for the Council to stick up for too high a price. Alderman DAVIES thought it was well that they should caution the public from anticipating a further reduction in the price of gas at the present time. He thought after hearing what Alderman Holmes had said that they ran quite near enough to the wind to reduce it 3d. per .1,000. There was a special reason why they must not lead people to be- lieve that another reduction would follow, because the pre- sent profits were obtained 1)3, an abnormally low price of coal. Coal was, he believed, lower now than ever it was before since the gas works were in existence, therefore, as far as the new Material went, the gas was produced at the eminimum. He also re- minded them that they were paying not only the interest to the landowner!, but that they were paying for the gas works as well, and that the time would come some day when posterity would benefit by what they were now doing. He thought, too, the Ratepayers' Association ought to be taught a lesson from what had passed that night, and that they ought not to pass such resolutions as they had done in Parliament assembled. It was utterly impossible to reduce the price by 6d. per 1,900 feet, and they ought to have made some inquiry before passing such a resolution. Councillor MACKIE said the Ratepayers' Association only made a request, and that it was very kindly doce. Alderman DAVIES thought the Council would agree with him that the resolutions of the Ratepayers' Association were not always couched exactly in the language of a request. He also thought there had been more than enough in the Council Chamber of persons—he would not mention any names—getting up and stating they were speaking in the interest of the ratepayers, but he found that that class of people really did very little for what he called the real pro- gress of the town, the wotk of the town and the work of the Corporation. It was most painful to him and to others who bad spent a great deal of time in the interests of the borough to hear those observations from these gentlemen, as if they alone stood up in the interests of the ratepayers, and he hoped his remarks would not be thrown away. Councillor FarevEouou called attention to a recom- mendation of* the committee "Plat the proposal from the Boiler Insurance Co. for the insurance, under the Employers' Liability Act, 1880, of the v;orkpeople employed at the Gas Works for the sum of £5 65. per annum, be accepted," and observing that the sum seemed a small one, said lie wished to inipress upon the chairman that when the policy comes down be should scan it very carefully, as there were many loopholes in these policies whereby the insurance people could get out of any accident. Alderman BußGess: The Town Clerk will take care of that.

Councillor DIXON pointed out that after meeting their liabilities the Gas Committee had only in round figures .E 2,000 at their disposal at Ode present time. fie pointed oat that this was obtained by fuel being low; in face of the fact that they got their labour as cheap as anybody else, and that they obtained for their by-products a larger ‘,:um than for years back. Ho asked what was to become of the profits if the committee had to contend with a rising market in fuel ? It was clear the price could not be reduced below the paltry sum of gd. per 1,000 cubic feet, yet he maintained they ought to have a good light at is. 101. per 1,000 feet. He hoped the chairman of the committee would not under these circumstances go in opposition to the other tradesmen of. the town by offering too many facilities for erecting the gas stoves. Councillor WALLINGTON said he had nut down one of the gas stoves for cooking purposes and that it answered ad- mirably. He hoped they would be largely taken advantage of.

Councillor MONKS hoped the chairman would not hold out any hope for a further reduction. He (Mr. Monks) and some of his colleagues en the committee had yielded to the present reduction, but they could not shut their eyes the fact that there were two or three causes outside the gas question which might very materially affect the gas works of the profits. He referred to the question of electricity. Some months ago it had been a question with them at the concern with which he was connected as to whether they should put down an electrical machine, and light the works with electricity, which would have cost Very little ; and if there was any chance of the iron works now large contribu- tors to the gas profits relinquishing gas for electricity, then they might find themselves in a position in which they might eventually have to raise the price of gas. He did not therefore for one moment wish to encourage the hope that the price of gas would be further reduced. Alderman HARRISON thought that even if the ratepayers did become somewhat clamorous for a reduction in the price of gas they should not be too severe in their strictures upon them, because before the Council purchased the-works a very rosy picture wa's drawn of the great advantage which would accrue to the ratepayers from the purchase. They were promised a reduction in the rates and ales a reduction in the price of the gas itself. If coal, however, had been the price now that it was when the works were purchased, the present reduction could not have been effected. They ought not, therefore, to be uncharitable if the ratepavera seemed to be clamorous for a further reduction. With reference to the gas stoves, the worthy alderman expressed himself satisfied with one be had bad for years. and added that they were conducive to cleanliness and economy. Alderman DAVIES held that some of the promises made to the ratepayers, when it was proposed to purchase the gas works, had been more than realised, and the committee were now proposing to reduce the price of the gas. The MAYOR said one thing had been lost sight of by the previous speakers, and that was that every year an amount was paid in capital which reduced the interest the ratepayers had to nay. He should have been very glad himself if they had had a reduction of 6d. in the price of gas, but Alderman Holmes had gone into the matter thoroughly with the other members of the committee, and he believed they had acted wisely in the course adopted. (Hear, hear.) He believed the more they reduced the price- of gas the more gas would be consumed. _(Heer, hear)

Councillor PI,XTT asked what was done with what he might call the surplus profits—the profits left after provid- ing for annuities and sinking fund. It was promised that the fund should be applied towards reducing the rates, and he swished to know what was done with those profits. Alderman DAstrs : That money is found very useful in- deed as working capital. We derive considerable advantage in paying ready money for everything we require. . The MAYOR: You get your material cheaper. Councillor PLAIT: Exactly ; but may I ask what it amounts to at the present time, Alderman DAVIES : we require abut £lO,OOO to keep us going over and above the capital sunk in the works. Councillot'PLATT : How far do you propose to carry that process? Alderman DAVIES : There are two answers to that. The first is, as the gas works continues to increase it will require more capital ; and the second is, if it becomes in- sufficient we shall hand it over to Mr. Chorley. Alderman Hor,stEs, replying to Councillor Dixon, said if that gentleman had friends in the trade, either in Warring- ton or elsewhere, who wisheol to supply gas cooking' apparatus, the committee would be very glad of them as additional feeders to their business. As to Councillor Fair- dough's question about insurance, he forgot to say when he moved the adoption of the minutes that the arrangement was that they charged a certain percentage on the annual was:es paid, and for that anneal percentage they took the responsibility of paying for accidents which arose among the men, and for which the employers would be responsible under the Employers' Liability Act. Councillor PLATT presumed the policy referred to accidents through boilers only. Alderman H0r.,7.4F.5: It is for accidents occurring from whatsoever cause to the men in the works that they take the responsibility. Councillor FAIRCLOn'm suggested that Alderman Holmes should read the policy over carefully, and see that there was nothing wrong in it. Alderman Ilor,,,tEs in answer to Councillor Mackie, said the Corporation could make gas for considerably less than the price now charged •, but bearing in mind that they bad interest to pay for bondholders, and also that they had to pay surplus fund, they were saddled to that extent. He had no doubt by a reduction in the price of gas they would have a large increase in the consumption, and the- very object they had in reducing the price of gas was to promote the sale of it. He mentioned that some time ago, and he-Was very glad to see they were now arriving at the point they sought to attain. Ile had no doubt whatever, in his own mind, that the profi!s derived from the gas works had very much more than realised the anticipations set forth. (Hear.) The minutes were agreed to. TUE rnorosFn TIDAL NAVIGATION.
Alderman DA.viEsTremarhed that no doubt ninny of them

had read about the intended tidal navigation between Man- chester and Liverpool. (Hear, hear.) He might state that the Mayor and himself attended the very important meeting held that day week in Manchester, when the matter was brought before what he might call the cream of the Man- chester merchants, by wham it was received very favourably. He might also say that what had taken place since that meeting pointed to the circumstance that tidal navigation to Manchester might yet be an accomplished fact. (Hear, hear) Looking at the circumstance that if such a thing were brought about of what vital importance it would be to the borough of Warrington, he thought even at this stage he might say at the proper time they would have an opportu- nity of promoting it. He thought on the following day the City Council at Manchester would have the matter brought before them for the .first time with the view of seeing if the interests of Manchester would not only be served from a commercial point of view, but if it would not be the means of saving Manchester, Salford, and other adjoining towns from the serious difficulty of floods. If there was one town more than another affected by floods it was Warrington, and he thought it would be to their interest to forward the scheme in every possible way. He saw the Local Board of Eccles was supporting the scheme, and he thought nothing would be lost in pushing it forward. THE CORPORATION AND THE WATERWORKS. The MAYOR moved the confirmation of the minutes of the General Purposes Committee, and observed that the gentle- men named waited upon the directors of the Waterworks Company, and had a very favourable reception. They decided to take water .from the company on certain terms, but the question as to what the future payment should be was left in embryo. The General Purposes Committee would have another meeting in a few days, and they would not only go into the question of the quantity of water required and the price, but they would also see if they could not come to some terms for the purchase of the Waterworks. (Hear, hear.)__
Alderman' HARRISON seconded the motion, which was carried. The Council then rose.
We may add that the proceedings of the various commit- tees appeared in last Saturday's Examiner.

That being the case, the Bench wciuld dismiss I both cases, each party to pay his own costs.

div.head: ALLEGED ASSAULT ON A RUNCORN
div.p: ALLEGED ASSAULT ON A RUNCORN
CONTRACTOR.

Thomas Probin, residing in Surrey-street, was at the Runcorn Police-court on Saturday brought up in custody barged—before Mr. Alfred Thomas and Mr. Bankes--witii assaulting Jas. Cliff, nightsoil contractor to Runcorn Corn- missioners.—Mr. Lake, solicitor, appeared -for the prisoner, who pleaded not guilty.—The prosecutor said the prisoner was a carter, and bad been in his employ for nearly four years. On Thursday evening he (the prosecutor) was at home, 'and whilst reading the newspaper he bad fallen asleep in the chair. When he awakened he was lying on the ground and the prisoner was raining blow 'after blow up- on cirri. He stopped him as well as he could, and his wife went to fetch some one. Mr. Booth and Mr. Howard went to his assistance, but it was some time before the prisoner would desist. He (witness) never struck the prisoner.— 'The Deputy Clerk (Mr. Johnson): Had you any conversa- tion with him before he committed the assault? No, I had rest seen him from dinner time until then. Has he dis- figured your face in the way it is now? Yes Was he ' sober? I hardly think he was.—Mr. Lak6, in applying for a remand, said ha had applied for a cross summons, and he thought it desirable both charges should be triidtogether. —Deputy Clerk (to prosecutor): How many times did he strike you ? Witness thought about a dozen times whilst he was on the floor. He knew no reason why the prisoner should attack him. The prisoner knocked him off the - chair, and when the parties came to his aid he was on the kitchen floor.—la answer to Mr. Lake, Mr. Johnson said the Bench saw no reason for adjourning the case. Mr. Lake represented that at present he could not put the prisoner in the box, which he should be able to do when he got a cross summons. He had good grounds for one, and the case would be put much better before the Bench, who would be able to render justice in the matter.—Mr. Cliff: I never had a wrong word from him, and I never gave him one that I know of.—Mr. Lake slid he should be able to call evidence to contradict that of the prosecutor, and show that Instead of his client being the aggressor that the prosecutor was.— After a short consultation the Bench intimated they had decided to remand the prisoner, and Mr. Lake applied for hail.—The Prosecutor: I have nothing at all against. him, but I object to him being admitted to bail. Let the case go on to-day.—Mr. Johnson: The magistrates have decided to remand him until Monday.—The Chairman :'We shall not accept bail.—The prosecutor's face bore signs of recent ill- usage, and his eyes were discoloured. The case again came on for hearing at the Patty Sessions on Monday, before Mr. James Reynolds (chairman), and Mr. Alfred Thornas.—Mr. Lake appeared for the-prisoner, and Mr. Burton appeared on behalf of the prosecutor, a cross-summons having been obtained.—The evidence of Mr. Cliff showed that on the 29th ult. the prisoner entered his kitchen, while he was asleep in a chair, and without the slightest warning seized hold of him by the coat collar, at the same time dealing him several very severe blows about the face-and head with his. fist. Probin then dragged com- plainant into his sitting-room, end there similarly assaulted him. A scuffle ensued, and prosecutor was dragged back again into his kitchen. The fighting still continued, and when Probin was striking prosecutor he sent his band ' through two panes of glass cutting himself very severely.— Cross-examined by Mr. Lake, complainant said be had had three or four glassts of beer. He did not curse Probin, nor did he rush at him with a bread knife and cut him across the hand. Probin cut his hand when he hit the window. • After the scuffle Probin came for his bat and asked him for his wages, and said that prosecutor had cut him with a knife- -Re-examined by Mr. Burton: There had been no ill- feeling between him and defendant, nor did he know that there was- any ill-feeling between his wife and prisoner.l —Mrs. Cliff was called, and she corroborated her husband's I statement, and added that when the row bad attained a .serious height, she called Mr. Howard and Mr. Booth in. , She then left the house.—Cross-examined by Mr. Burton,l she said two windows were broken. There were no knivei about. They were all deposited in the dresser drawer.—By Mr. Lake : She did 'not see her husband take up a bread knife.—Mr. John Howard, 46, Greenway-road, said Mrs. Cliff came running to him when he was standing at his front gate. She told him that one of the men was ill-using her husband. He went through prosecutor's yard and into his kitchen. When he get into the kitchen he saw the pri- soner holding prosecutor against the kitchen window. He was demanding his money. He asked prisoner what he was ill-using prosecutor for? and be replied that it was all through Mrs. Cliff coining into the stable and interfering with him. Prisoner again struck prosecutor, andlhey both rolled on the floor. Mr. Booth subsequently came in and parted them.—Cross-examined, he said he saw no knife about. He stood near the back kitchen door, and he did not notice that prisoner's hands were bleeding, nor did he hear Probin say that a knife had been used. • Mr. Booth got prisoner away -from prosecutor, and he went outside the gate. He saw him afterwards go hack again, but he (witness) did not go near again.—By the Chairman : He did not see prisoner's hand go through the window.—By Mr. Burton : He did not . think the break in the window was done by Mr. Cliff's head ; it would be above it. The break was a round One.— Mr. Joseph Booth, police-constable in the employ of the Bridgewater Navigation Company, observed that Mrs. Cliff came for him and asked him whether he would go inside and stop prisoner from Musing her husband, and he re- plied that he would have nothing to do with them. Mr. Howard then came up and they went in together. When be got inside the house Probin had hold of prisoner with his right hand and was striking him with his left hand. He got hold of prisoner's hand and stopped him striking prose- cutor. He then said to him "Tom give over and go home like a good lad. Th'all he sorry for all this in the morning." He then got Probin away from the premises and he pulled the yard &or to. He saw Probin again after that getting over prosecutor's wall and he begged of him to go back, which he did. He saw no blood about Mr. Cliff's face; but Probin's band was covered with blood. He beard no com- plaint about a knife.—This concluded the evidence for the prosecution.—Mr. Lake, for the defence, contended that the c-aseeirose out of another case when Mr. Cliff was summoned by his wife. Probin on that occasion was called as a wit- ness on behalf of Mr. Cliff in order to show up the drunken habits which his wife was guilty of. Since that case Mrs. Cliff had taken every opportunity of making herself un- pleasant to him and he had made up his mind to leave Mr. Cliff's employ. He maintained it was very absurd to say that a men would go into his master's house and knock him off the chair. He simply went for his wages, and finding his ir:vder asleep, lie took hold of him by the shoulder to wake him. The first thing Cliff did on waking, was to seize a bread knife, and he inflicted several gashes on prisoner's right hand. During the struggle they both fell to the ground, and Cliff got a good thrashing, which, he submitted, he deserved.—Thomas Probin, in giving evidence, said that prisoner's wife sent her daughter nto the stable on the i evening in-question to ask him whether he had any picks or 110-lc:vele, and to urge him on with his work, whereupon be told her to tell her mother that he should not do any more work. When he went into the kitchen aud after he had awakened prosecutor, Cliff picked up a breadknife and struck him over the hand. He then got hold of prosecutor and they both fell down together on the mat at the door, prpsecu• tor again cutting him on the hand. They then rose ad another scuffle ensued, and be knocked prosecutor's bead through the window. Mr. Booth and Mr. Howarth then came in and separated them. During the row he lost his cap and went back .again for it, and he said he was sorry that the job had occurred. On the following morning prosecutor sent a person down to Iris house to ask him to come up to arrange matters. He went to see prosecutor, and was by hint asked what had caused the bother, and he replied that it was all through his wife. Prosecutor made no reply, and prisoner aelezd him for his cap and also his wages. Prosecutor then told him to leave his house, which he did.—Cross-examined by Mr. Burton, he said that his band never w:ent through the window. The panes were broken by the head of prosecutor. Cliff struck the irst blow. He admitted that be was drunk when the fight took place.—By the Bench : He took the knife out of prosecutor's hand and threw it under the table. It was an ordinary bread knife with is white‘handle.—Dr. McDougall stated that he examino.d the prisoner's hand. He was of opinion that the wounds could not have been inflicted by smashing a window, because they were at the back of the hand ; but had been cat, be, a sharp instrument.—Mrs. Cliff was re-called, and asked *by Mr. Burton how: many bread knives she had in •the hou;e, when she replied that she had only one with a brown handle.—The Chairman said it appeared that that was one of the unfortunate rows in which there was a good deal of conflicting evidence. As it had been put before them they thought it was a bad case for both of the parties. They had taken the law into their own bands. As far as the

div.head: EXTRAORDINA NY WOUNDING CASE
div.p: EXTRAORDINA NY WOUNDING CASE
AT WIDNES.
TRYING TO THROW A MAN INTO THE CANAL.

At the Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, before Messrs. W. N. Heald, and H. S. Hall, Peter Quinn, John Lane, Mary Mannion, and William McNamara, were all (ex- cept the latter) charged, on remand, with unlawfully wounding John Norton, a flatman, who resides on the Old Marsh, Widnes.—Mr. Beasley, solicitor, appeared to defend the prisoners Lane and McNamara.—The prosecutor, John Norton, who appeared in court with a plastered head, in giving evidence, said that about eight o'clock on Sunday night the 25th ult., he was in the Commercial Hotel, on the Old Marsh, Widnes, which is kept by a man named Mark Wright. He had occasion to go into the back-yard, and on returning to the house he met a man named John Hannan, who asked him what sort ot a man he was. Prosecutor replid that he did not know. He then went into the public house and was followed by Hannan, who tried to get hold of him. Thinking he was going to be molested he went through the kitchen and again into the backyard. Whilst there he picked up a liir of iron, about two feet long and about two , inches thick, and let himself out by the back door. He then came round to the front door of the house holding in his hand the bar of iron, which he had picked up for the pur- pose of defending himself on his way home, when he was met by the man Hannan, the prisoners, and a large crowd. The prisoner Quinn threw a brick at him, and the crowd encircled him, whilst McNamara got between his legs and flung him to the ground. He was then rushed upon by Hannan and several others, who pulled and rolled him about 15 yards towards the canal which is in the vicinity. Whilst lie was on the floor he was kicked most unmercifully about the head, ears, and body, until he was readered insensible. He did not remember any more of the affair until he found himself in bed on Monday morning, where he remained until Thursday. He was attended by Dr. McLennan. He did not give either the prisoners or Hannan any provocation for the assault, nor did he know why they had attacked him.— Cross-examined by Mr. Beasley: He would swear that he did not say to anyone that all the, Irish ought to be killed. He • had had no whiskey and beer during the afternoon, and did not go to Mr. Wright's public-house at 6-0 p.m. He had been out for a walk along the river side, and only arrived at the Com- mercial Hotel about eight o'clock. He neither saw Mrs. Lane in the tap-room nor in any other part of the house, nor did he strike the prisoner Lane and knock him down; in fact, he never saw him there at all. Mrs. Lane did not say that her husband was a cripple with only one leg and he a big strong man. He did not recollect seeing the Lanes at all, and he could not say whether Mrs. Lane had taken her husband home. He saw no one in the public-house but Hannan.—A piece of iron was produced by Mrs. Lane at this point, but prosecutor said he did not think it was that which he threw away. He hit no one with the iron. It was thrown away from the crowd altogether. He saw John Kiilala about half-past twelve in the morning, but he made use of no foul language to him, nor did he make use of any offensive language condemnatory of the lush. He did not see Mrs. Stokes at the time the affray took place, but he might have seen her in the middle of the day. He did not say in her hearing that he would kill the first man who came near him.

Mary Norton next entered the witness box, and said she was the wife of the last witness, and resided with her hus- band on the Widnes Old Marsh. On the night of the 25th ult. she was standing against the bridge of the Old Marsh about eight o'clock, knowing at the time that- her husband was inside the public-house. She saw her husband come out of the side door and enter again through the front door. When her husband went into the public-house a sound time she went towards him, and getting close to him, she heard Hannan, whom she had known for: many years, ask her husband what sort of a man he was. Prosecutor entered the house, and shortly emerged through the back door carrying a small bar of iron in his hand. She saw the whole of the prisoners standing near the front door. The prisoner McNamara on seeing her husband got between his legs, and Hannan seized hold of him round the neck with his arms. She then saw the prosecutor throw the bar of iron away. McNamara and Hannan threw her husband to the ground, and whilst he i'fras down McNamara kicked him about the legs several times. The ftisoner Quinn kicked him about the body also when he was down, and Lane, who came round the street corner, said "Just let me have one kick at him." He:kicked prosecutor-twice on the side. The female prisoner Mannion had a brick in her hand, and stand- ing astride her husband she dealt him two blows on the head with it. She attempted to strike him a third time, but the brick fell oat' of her hand. She also saw two other men whom she did not know bit her husband about the face and body with sticks, and heard some one call out that "they would make a worse job of him than was made of Cavendish and Burke." When she saw her husband so cruelly beaten, and apparently in an unconscious state, she screamed for assistance, and hearing her screams Mr. William Walmsley appeared on the scene. He lifted her prostrate husband up from the ground and carried him home. Blood was flowing very freely from his head, face, and ears. She then went for Dr. Paterson, who attended prosecutor, and he was subsequently attended by Dr. McLennan, who has attended him up to the present time.— Cross-examinecl by Mr. Beasley, witness said that Mr. Walmsley brou,Yht her husband home. When her husband threw the bar of iron away it Lit no one. She could not say whether the piece of iron produced was that which prosecutor threw away. She did not know that Lane had been knocked dawn, nor did she know that Mrs. Lane had been kicked. Lane kicked her husband with his wocrlen leg. She did not see Mrs. Stokes there. She thought there were about 20 or 30 persons round. She was sure McNamara was there.

Donald iltquahart Lennan said he was a physician and surgeon, carrying on business in Widnes. He was sent for on Monday, the 26th June and visited prosecutor. He examined him in bed, and found him affected with an incised wound, about two inches long, on the right temple, which penetrated to the bone. There were several scratches on his face his right and left ears were bruised and blackened, and both his upper and lower lips were bruised. Norton also complained of a pain -iirsbis side, but he could find no external marks of violence on his side. He had lost a considerable quantity of blood. The bruises might have been caused by kicks, and the scratches on his face by being pulled and pushed along the ground. The other wounds migbt have been caused by his head coming in contact with the ground, or blows from a-stick. The wound on the fore- head was of a dangerous character by its position. He saw the prosecutor on Saturday last, and he was then unfit for work; and was very weak from the severe bruises he re- ceived. He must have met with -considerable violence. Dr. Paterson had been to see Norton before he (witness) got there, and had dressed the wounds. Hannah lieogh, the wife of Patrick Keogh, and who also resided on the Old M'arsh, gave corroborative evidence, and added that she saw Quinn throw a brick at Norton which missed him. Hannan was assisted by the female prisoner to take off his coat. and vest. When Norton was on the floor she saw Hannah pick him up and carry him to the railings by the side of the canal over which he tried to throw the prosecutor into the canal. James Smith. labourer, residing on the Old Marsh, also gave confirmatory evidence, and said that after Mary Man- nion had struck prosecutor with a brick and deposited it on a heap of rubbish near to Mr. Walmsley's house, he went for a police constable, but when be ft ndlhe police constable had arrived both the mob and Nortan bad removed. Wm. Walmsley, flatman, living on the Old Marsh, spoke to having carried Norton home.—Cross-examined by Mr. Beasley, be said prosecutor threw the bar of iron as if he was trying to hit someone Witt it, but he could not , say whethtr it bit anyone or. not. He did not hear Norton say anything about the Irish; but he was excited and said he would hit the first man who came near him.

P.C. Barker said that from information he received he ap- prehended Peter Quinn and Mary Mannion about a quarter to seven o'clock on the following night; and on Tuesday night, the 27th ult., he apprehended John Lane. When at the police wation he charged them altogether with unlaw- fully wounding one John Norton, on Sunday, the 25th inst., by kicking and striking him. They all replied "I never kicked him." When he apprehended the prisoner Quinn 111 found that the skin of. his third knuckle was turned up and the back of his hand very much swollen. P.S. Robinson deposed that He apprehended the prisoner William McNamara, on the 4th inst., and when charged he replied "I neither kicked him nor struck him.
The prisoners were all committed to take their trial a t the next Liverpool Assizos,bail being refused to all except Lane, who was bound over himself-in £2O and two sureties in 10 each.
