SUDDEN DEATH OF A MARRIED WOMAN AT EARLESTOWN. FOUND DEAD ON THE BEDROOM FLOOR.

Maria Harrop, 54 years of age, wife of Edward Harrop, a labourer, residing at 173, Lower Leigh-street, Earlestown, was found dead on the floor of her bedroom, under some- what singular circumstances, at seven o'clock on Sunday morning last. It appears that the deceased was a dress- maker, and finished a dress on Saturday night, which she took to the owiaer about eight o'clock. On her way home she called at the Oddfellows' Arms Inn, Earlestown, and had a glass of whisky in her husband's company. She afterwards went home, and sent her son, ten years of age, to the Viaduct Inn for a pint of ale. This ale and a quan- tity of bread and cheese, she had for her supper. Seating herself in a chair by the fire she commenced to smoke a pipe, and drink the 'ale. At twelve o'clock her husband, who is employed at the Oddfellows' Arms Inn, came home, and she was still seated in her chair, and appeared to be quite healthy and in good spirits. He sat with her until one o'clock, when he retired to bed, leaving her alone, and sitting in the chair, still smoking. Nothing further was heard or seen of her until about seven o'clock the following morning, when her son John, who slept in the same room as his parents awoke and saw his mother in a kneeling position by the side of her bed. He at once awoke his father, who found his wife to be quite dead. She had one of her hands on the bed and another.on the floor. She had not undressed herself, but had put her night cap on. She. had for a day or two complained of a pain in her stomach, but no doctor was called in to see her. INQUEST ON THE BODY.
An inquest on the body of the deceased was held before the deputy-coroner, Mr. Barker' at the Viaduct Inn, Earle- street, on Tuesday afternoon. The following evidence was given _ _ _

Edward Harrop, a labourer, deposed that the deceased was his wife, who . was 54 years of age. She had been in the habit of smoking and drinking. When he went to bed on Saturday night she was left alone in the house. He fell asleep soon afterwards, and was not disturbed until his son awoke him between six and seven o'clock the following morning. He found her on the floor beside the bed. She had her hands on the bed. She was quite dead. She was not undressed, but had her nightcap on. She was preparing for bed as she had pulled ber apron off. He had previously seen her have one or two fainting fits, the last one about six months ago.- She had complained of a pain in her stomach. She was a very stout person. She did not take drink regularly every day. Sometimes she would have some and sometimes not. He had seen her the worse for drink. The last time he did so was about eight days ago. She had not had a doctor for two years. She was then attended for a bad cold—not for anything in connection with the heart so far as he wes aware.
The Foreman asked why he retired to bed leaving his wife sitting alone in the chair.

The witness said he had done it regularly. She was in the habit of sitting up sewiqg when he went to bed. In reply to further questions, he said that she had been drink- ing for the last few days. She had been on the "spree" for abput a week. He had no reason to think she had taken anything else besides drink. There had been no quarrel between them, and they parted on good terms when he went to bed. •

John Harrop, son of the last witness and deceased, stated that he went to bed at one o'clock on Sunday morning with his father. His mother was then sat on a chair smoking a pipe. When he got up the following morning he saw her at the bedside with one hand on the bed and the other on the floor. She was not undressed. His father was asleep in bed and he awoke him. He did not speak to his mother be- cause he had never seen her in that position before and he thought she was dead. No cne else was in the room besides he, his father, and his mother. He fetched a pint of beer for his mother on S..turday night. She drank it herself. His father was sober when they went to bed. His mother was not sober. He had seen her drunk many times. Mary Jackson said she lived near Mr. Harrop. 7=Bhe had known the deceased for more than a dozen years. She never heard her complain ef anything with the exception of a pain at the bottom of her side caused with sitting while sewing. She took a little drink sometimes. Witness had never seen her the worse for drink, although she had seen her a "little elevated " and a "little forward" at times, through taking drink. She did not see her on Saturday. She was called in on Sunday morning and found the de- ceased at the bedside quite dead. The body was quite cold and stiff. She must have been dead for some hours from the position and condition she was in. Witness washed and laid out the body. There were no marks of violence upon it. The deceased and her husband had lived comfortably together. Deceased had never complained to her about the conduct of her husband.

The Deputy-Coroner, in summing up, remarked that be thought they could fairly assume that death had resulted from natural causeq, and his opinion was that it was from heart disease, though they could not exactly ascertain unless a post-mortem examination of the body was made, and that he did not think necessary.
The jury then ,returned a verdict to the effect that the deceased died from natural causes.

div.head: WIDNES SCIMOL B)ARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCIMOL B)ARD.

On Thursday, the monthly meeting of this Board was held at the Offices, Victoria-road. Mr. T. S,Timmins pre- sided, and there were also present the Rev. T. Finegan, R. H. ravies, H. Shaw, H. W. Deacon, and G. H. Danby (clerk). The District Education Committee reported that during the month of June (two weeks) there were 76 applications for payment of fees, and 67 persons were summoned to attend before the committee for contravention of the Educa- tion Act. Fees were recommended in each case in which application was made. One boy had been sent to an indus- trial school% During the holidays thA attendance officers were employed is taking a census of the children of the dis- trict, the results of which were now submitted to the Board in a tabular form. Table No. 1, showing the number of house and school going children and the accommodation in Public Elementary schools in Widnes, 1882, stated that in the East district there wer_e 109 empty houses out of 677. There were 874 children between the ages of 13 and 3 in the district ; there was accommodation for 809 at Warrington- road school, and in attendance 637 ; being an excess of accommodation over attendance of 172. In the West district were 2,541 houses, 450 of which were empty, while six were in course of erection. There was school accom- modation for 2,391 scholars; and out of 3,072 children, 2,239 were attending school, 152 below the accommodation. South district contains 1,873 houses, 70 being empty, and 21 in coursa, of erection In the district were 2,290 children ; 1,669 were attending. school ; and there was an excess of accommodation over at- tendance of 188. The totals for the whole town were 5,091 houses, of which 829 were empty, and 29 were in course of erection. The total school accommodation was 5,057, an excess of 512 over the attendance, while the children be- tween 13 and 2 years of age numbered 6,236. The second tablegave the number of children in June 1882, in Widnes, between the ages of 3 and 13 and the schools they attend. As stated in the other table the children number 6,216, and of these 844 at'end. West Bank, 404 Warrington-road, 920 Simms' Cross, 411 Faruworth National, 565 St. Mary's National, 589 St. Patricks, 760 St. Marie's, 341 St. Bede's, 125 attending private schools, 1,277 attending no school, and 1,415 are children from 3to 5 years of ape. The third table states there are 5,274 children who ought to be on the rolls of the public elementary schools, the actual number being 5,080, showing there are 194 not on the rolls, an im- provement on last year of 135. An apparent ommission in the taking of the census was ( xplained in table 4, which stated there were 85 children attending school who did not live in the town. The school-going children in proportion to total population in 7875 was 1 to 5; in 1878, 1 to 5 2t; in 1881, 1 to 552; in 1882 (estimated population 26,000) 1 to 5.72. -
_ On the proposition of the CHAIRMAN, the report was adopted, and the thanks of the Board tendered to the corn-

Tbe.School Management Committee recommended that the resignations of the following head mistresses be ac- cepted :—Mrs. M. Davies, infants' department, West Bank ; Miss Bransom,junior girls department, West Bank; Miss Henderson, infants' department, Simms Cross; the resigna- tion to take effect from the 30th September next. In moving the adoption oF this minute, the Rev. F. FINEGAN explained that Miss Henderson had resigned to take an appointment, wWch the managers of the West Bank school bad offered her. Domestic affairs ware the cause of the other resignations. The minute was passed. CENTRAL CLASSES TO 13E ESTA7IIISHED.

On the recommociation of the School Management Com- mittee, the Board It cidcd that central classes be established for the collective instruction of pupil teach IN and monitors to commence September 1, 1882, at Simms Cross schools; and that the classes be open to pupil teachers and monitors .of denominationals at a small fee; teachers of these schools to be eligible for appointment as teachers under the new system.

FARNWORTH GRAMMAR :SCHOOL. Mr. H. R. DAVIES, in accordance with notice given at the last meeting, moved, "That Mr. T. Sutton Timmis, of Clevely, Allerton, near Liverpool and Widnes, be and is hereby appointed one of the governors of Farnworth -Grammar School." He remarked that they would all agree with him that the Board could not possibly appoint a more admirable representative than the gentleman he had named. Mr. Sivaw seconded the motion which. was carried, and-the CHAIRMAN returned his acknowledgements, remarking that be would do all he donld to push forward the school.

div.head: COOKERY SC^ITOOL.
div.p: THE COOKERY SC^ITOOL.

Mr. DEACON said he should be -gra-dTo—know whether the School Management Committee were taking any steps to open cooking classes at the Simm's Cross scho)l. The CHAIRMAN Said be was glad Mr. Behan had men- tioned this matter; it was a thing which had been present in his mind for some time. He believed the latellx. Deacon was really the originator of. the cooking sellool at Simm's Cross, but when it was built he (the chairman) was not a member of the Board, and the committee, no doubt for very good reasons, dilnot open the classes. Siace then there had been a good many alterations in the composition of the com- mittee, and the prospeet had never been fully developed. Now that the committee would sit without alteration until the present term of the Board expired, he hoped they would deal with the question. There was no part of her education which would be of so much use to a girl as learning how to cook a plain dinner, and he believed men would be far more likely to be sober if they could have a supply of good and well cooked food. At present he was sure the workingmen's

tare, wives were most lamentably ant, helpless orea not from want of inclination, Ihnrfrom Want of knowledge. Here they had a school 'whereiu that instruction could be gl,v_ep. to children, and he trusted the committee would bring.i.o.tb ward a comprehensive scheme for its utilization, viror miraticrla would include all the schools in Widnes, denoilel D otherwise, on certain terms. div.head: – RUNCORN FREE PUBLIC LIBRARY.
div.p: - RUNCORN FREE PUBLIC LIBRARY.
ITS ORIGIN A'IND FORMATION.

The ceremony of Thursday last, in which Sir James A. Picton was the central figure, and the inhabitants of Run- corn the chief particip dots, will mark the commencement of a distinct epoch in the history of Runcorn; an epoch, we believe, in which the future historian will have to chronicle the greatest advancement of its people, socially, morally, and intellectually. Education, within cornpara.tively recent years, has become easier of attainment, by all classes of the community, in the numerous public elementary schools established ever the length and breadth of the country; but the knowledge so attained falls far short of whet every English- man and Englishwoman ought to possess, and, as a rule, desire to possess. The passing of the Public Libraries Act was an honest and successful effort to afford facilities for acquiring this increased knowledge; and viewing the matter in this light a short account of the adoption of the Act by the township of Runcorn may not be unacceptable. The honour of being the first to demonstrate to his towns- men the advantages of a free public library belongs to Mr. Wen. Handley, a gentleman foremost in every movement having for its object the benefiting of the public, who in 1879 read a piper before the members of the now defunct Literary Institute. In that paper he strongly advocated the adoption of the Act, but failing, apparently, to impart to his hearers the enthusiasm which animated himself, no action immediately followed. But the seed then sown did not fall wholly on barren ground, and, although for a period it lay hidden, it brought forth fruit about two years ago. At that time numerous letters were addressed to the local newspapers urging ' the authorities to take up the question; while the journals also gave the subject their consistent advocacy. This re- vival seemed doomed to end without any practical issue, when a circumstance occurred which operated greatly in favour of the movement. For a considerable period the Literary Institute had been labouring in a state of much eraharrassment, and its moribund condition now led the managers to discuss the desirability of closing their doors. A calm contemplation of their position showed the financial affairs of the Institute to be far from satisfactory, and with- out any prospect of improvement. It was consequently re- solved to close the establishment. a decision the more readily arrived at bee 'use it was estimated that the proceeds from the sale of the furniture and books would enable the com- mittee to meet all liabilities. Tne dissolution of this edu- cational agency—for so it must be regarded—furnished another strong argument to the advocates for the formationl of the Free Library; but of still more importance was the fact that the committee were the custodians of abent 1,000 volumes, which had previously formed the Runcorn Public Library. It was feared that these mementos of an old in- stitution, would, to use a common metaphor, be scattered to the four winds. To avert this undesirable consummation prompt action was taken. The Press attempted, not unsuc- cessfully, to shosethe necessity of preserving these relics, and a memorial from the ratepayers was presented to Dr. Steele, the eliairman of the Board of Commissioners, requesting him to call a town's meeting for the pur- pose of consideting the advisability of adopting the Free Libraries Act. Meanwhile, a committee, with Dr. McDougall as chairman, was formed to negotiate with the committee of the Institute for the purchase of the books they were entitled to sell, numbering about 300 volumes. Yielding to the desire of the petitioners, Dr. Steele, calk(' a town's meeting, which was held on the 19th December, 1881. Dr. McDougall, Mr. J. Simpson, Mr. G. S. Hazlehurst, and ether gentlemen ably advocated the adoption of the Act. Like almoet every other measure aiming at the public good, the movement was opposed, but by a vote which was prac- tically unanimous the Act was adopted. Since then the project has gained in popularity, and it would now be diffi- cult to and a single opponent to the scheme. No gentlemen exceeded Dr. McDougall in his full appreciation of the ad- vantages which would accrue to the townspeople by the for- mation of the Library, and great praise is due to him for the energetical efforts he put forth to secure them. The ratepayers havinggiven their favourable decision,it was important that it should be carried out as early as possible, and a committee was formed consisting of the following gentlemen :—The Rev. Canon Barcley, M.A., chairman; Dr. Finlay McDougall, vice-chairman ; Dr. Mat Steele, Win. Handley, Thos. Riley, Geo. S. Hazlehurst, Jno. Simpson, J. R. Frith. Peter Briscoe and Geo. Rhodes. Mr. John Daniel Janes wos appointed librarian, Mr. R. A. Charlton treasurer, and Mr. Wm. Brookes secretary. The maximum rate allowed to be laid for the purposes of the Library is a penny in the X, which produces about £l7O, and the committee had to be careful in their measures to keep their expenditure within that sum, as Tinny expenses occur during the first year which will not have to be borne again. It was important, in the first place, that a building suitable for the purposes of the Library should be secured. Waterloo House was suggested, but dis- carded as impracticable at this period, and eventually, on the 23rd May, it was decided, in public meeting, to as-le the Commissioners to allow the Library to be located in their offices. Permission was granted, and the committee went vigorously to work. They were assisted and encouraged by several donations of books, and many gentlemen residing in the neighbourhood generously aided the movement by hand- some donations of money. The books which had formed the library of the Literary Institute were purchaaed at is. per volume; charge was taken of the 1,000 volumes previ- ously referred to, and the committee added several hundred valuable and desirable new works. Thus, with a compara- tively small expenditure, a library of about 2,000 volumes has been formed. For several weeks Mr. Jones, the librarian, has been busily engaged arranging the hooka and drawing lap' the catalogue. He has accomplished the work very satisfactorily, and the books as they crowd the shelves of the bookcase present a neat appearance. Works of fiction naturally predominate, and include such authors 'as Scott, Dickens, Thackeray, George Eliot, Braddon, Bronte, Ains- worth, Kingsley, dze, while history is represented by Macau- lay, Hume, Green, and Freeman. Every other branch of literature is represented to some extent, and the Library cannot fail to be a boon to all who use it. The Library is in the Board-room of the Commissioners, the bookcase occupy- ing a space of about three-fourths of the wall on the right hand side. The wall is hung with a copy of the rules and regulations printed on parchment, and framed and signed by each member of the committee, and the librarian and secre- tary. This was presented by Dr. McDougall. They state the Library will be open on Tuesday from 7 to 10 o'clock in the evening, and on Saturday from 2 to 10 o'clock p.m., and shall be open to readers free of charge. The most important clause states : "Borrowers must be either resident or rate- payers within the Improvement Act district of Runcorn. All ratepayers shall be entitled to borrow books on their own responsibility. Persions not rated shall'be required to obtain the signature of a ratepayer, to a voucher, which must be renewed annually. All borrowers will be required to sign a voucher and to obtain a borrower's ticket, for which two pence will be charged. The ticket to be renewed annually. Printed voucher forms may he had on application to the librarian, who will also issue the borrower's ticket." The effectual working of the Library in minor details is fully provided for in a way which evinces the thoughtful consi- deration the committee have bestowed upon the drawing up of the regulations.

THE OPENING CEREMONY AND PROCESSION. The idea of accompanying the inauguration of the Library with an outdoor demonstration was happy in its conception, andn-despite the unfavourable conditions, suc- cessful in its accomplishment. Sunshine and showers were most inauspiciously blended during the whole of Thursday, but about an hour before the time fixed for the openbig ceremony, the sun sent forth its rays from t blue sky. At half past five rain was falling heavily, but the streets were nevertheless crowded with spectators, Fountain Square pre- senting a scene of much animation. Flags were there sus- pended acioss the road, and in several other places on the way which the procession was to traverse, while frbm every available spot banners, soaked with water, made attempts to flutter in the breeze. Entering the Town Hall, the walls of the staircase leading to the Library were draped with flags of a variety of hues, and the room itself was resplendent with a coat of new varnish. Assembled there, anticipating the arrival of Sir Jas. A. Picton, F.S.A., of Liverpool, who was to declare the Library open, and than whom could not have been chosen a gentleman more fitted to perform the care- were the following., gentlemen :—The Revs. E. W. Preston, J. J. Bryant, J. Lockwood, J. Nowell, J. Billington, R. Edwards, Jos. Piclewell, Dr. McDcugall, Messrs. H. Cole- burn, W. Handley, J. Handley, T. Handley, W. Whittaker, P. Briscoe, T. Norman, P. Speakman, E. Timmins, J. R. Frith, W. Fisher. 0. Leak, Cowell (Librarian Liverpool Library), Madeley (Warrington Library), Wilcock (Chester Library), F. Fairhurst, G. Bellamy, J. W. Woodland, A. Campbell, W. H. Grice, E. Aaron. J. Unsworth, H. Hindle, P. Smith, T. Marmsen, &c. Precisely at a quarter to six, Sir James was escorted into the room by the Rev. Canon Barclay (chairman of the Libtary Committee), Dr. Steele (chairman of the Board of Commissioners), and Mr. John Simpson (vice-chairman of the School Board). A short introductory ceremony having been gone through, .The Bev Canon BARCLAY, addressing Sir Jas. A. Picton, said he very much wished the office which had fallen upon lam had been entrusted to abler and worthier hands, but haying by the courtesy of the members of the committee been elected their chairman for this year, it became his duty, and pleasant duty, so far as be (Sir James) was con- cerned, to ask IHT to fort-nail inaugurate the opening of the Library. Doubtless .he was acquainted with the pre- liminary proceedings winch must precede the formation of such an institution; he knew he (Sir James) had spent many years upon those preliminaries; suffice it to say there. fore, that a requisition according to Act of Parliament, was addressed to the Chairman of the Commissioners, who thereupon called a meeting, and at that meeting the Free Libraries Act was adopted almost unanm iously ; at all events by a large majority. That important step having been taken, the Improvement Commissioners elected a committee, partly of members of their own body and partly of others outside. He might say that i on that committee, the interest of each class n the town was fully represented. The committee set to work with a will, and had many difficulties to surmount. Those d Iffi- culties having been surmounted, they were in a position that day, on a small scale he granted-, to open the Library. He was very sorry he could not ask Sir James to open a magnificient building of architectural proportions, an I pretensions, but they might hope that if Runcorn progressed for the next thirty or forty i years as t had progressed during the last:and was now —many improvements had been effected which the last generation would not have dreamt of, and many of them

div.head: EXAMINER, S A T URDAY, JULY 8, 1882
div.p: THE EXAMINER, S A T URDAY, JULY 8, 1882

who lived at the present day scarcely hoped to see—they might hope, he said, that some future generation would re- quest another Sir James A. Picton to open such a building. (Applause.) It devolved upon him h )wever, not to open such a building as he had mentioned, but with that silver key, not silver in the metaphorical sense of the term, to open that case. (Loud applause.) The Canon then presented Sir James with a prettily- chased silver key, bearing the following inscription on the handle:—" Presented to Sir James A. Picton, F.S.A. Run- corn Free Public Library, July 6, 1882." It was enclosed in a beautiful morrocco case lined with velvet. Sir JAMES A. PICTON said he scarcely knew how to express himself, he felt so flattered by their kindness in requestinc, him to come to perform that ceremony, and also by the reception they had accorded him. He did not feel at all worthy of it by any means, but he accepted it in the spirit in which it was given. (Applause.) The demonstration which he had seen outside, anct the enthusiasm which was visible all around, were extremely creditable to the town of Runcorn. (Applause.) It was not mere external show, nothing to excite or gratify the sense or to make a great ostentatious appearance, but it was the real object of the proceeding, the honest intellectual value which was attrac- tive, and it sh3wed that there was an appreciation in the minds of the Runcorn public of what a library really meant.

(Hear, hear.' He hop:d by and by to have a little to say on that subject, which he would not then attempt to ex- patiate upon. He could only say he was very much gratified by their kind reception, aud in response to what Canon Barclay had said, he trusted that the institution might so progress that in no very great length of time to come thep might have a larger and nobler building to be opened—(ap- plause)—by some one much more worthy than the present humble individual. (A laugh.) Then their future build- ing would exceed the one they had now devoted to this purpose. (Loud applause.) Sir JAMES then unlocked the door of the bookcase, which was completely full, a great number of volumes being arranged on an adjacent table, and also upon the top of the case. He said : I see before me a goodly array of books, which I have no doubt will be both useful and accept- able, and I now in the name of the Chairman of the com- mittee of the Institution declare the Library open and free to all. (Hear, hear, and loud applause). The audience gave three rounds of cheering with hearty enthusiasm' Sir James afterwards remarking that Air. the librarian of the Liverpool Library, would be de- lighted to afford to the committee any assistance and advice, and he could promise on behalf of the committee that if they I would accept a copy of the catalogue, they should be most happy to present it. (Applause). Some amusement was now caused by the town crier, who was dressed in complete uniform, readiec, the following pro- clamation to the people assembled in the square below :- 4 Oyez ! oyez! oyez! I, James Shepherd, town crier of the ancient town of Runcorn, do hereby give notice, to all whom it may concern, that a free public library for the use of the inhabitants of the district comprised within the limits of the Runcorn Improvement Act, 1882, has this day been opened by Sir James Allanson Picton, Knight. God save the Queen ! " The proclamation was received with great cheering. It may be stated that the office of town crier has been fulfilled by the family of Shepherd from time immemorial. Canon BARCLA.Y, having filled a voucher, asked for book No. 41 C, which was discovered to be "Lay sermons, afliresses, and reviews," by Professor Huxley. In handing to him the book, Sir James said : It is a valuable book, which contains the most advanced statements in science, and a book that will, I trust, have a powerful influence in joining what are too often separated, science and religion. (Applause.) While the ceremony described above was proceeding, the various bodies which were to take part in the out-door de- monstration were forming into procession. They now imme- diately started in the following order, headed by Mr. Super- intendent Williamson, who was mounted on a handsome horse :
Detachment of County Police. Town Crier. Band oi the 2nd Cheshire Earl of Chester's Rifle Volun'.eers.
