The Rev. and 83r J. A. Picton, P.S.A. Detachment of County Police. The following bands also occupied positions in the proces- sion :—Runcoru National School, Star of Widnes, Mill Brow, and Sons of Temperance, Weston. The route taken was from Fountain Square to Delph Bridge, returning to the square; thence up High-street, Lowlands-road, Waterloo- road, Church-street, to the Public Hall. The weather was fine as the procession left the square, but when crossing Waterloo-bridge, rain descended in torrents, continuing for about five minutes. This had the effect of clearing the streets of the many thousand spectators who had assembled, only for a time, however, for when a slight cessation oc- curred, so crowded were the thoroughfares that it was almost impossible to proceed. Notwithstanding the un- favourable state of the weather, the demonstration passed off with considerable eclat, and will be long remembered by the inhabitants of Runcorn. The arrangements were carried out without a hitch, and their completeness reflects great credit upon the committee which had them in hand, and which was composed of Messrs. gr. S. Hazlehurst, Wm. Handley, P. Briecoe, T. Riley, J. R. Frith, and G. Rhodes. Messrs. S. C. Beckett, W. H. Chadwick, and Samuel Ravenscroft were the decoration committee. THE PUBLIC MEETING.

At 6-30 tea was provided in the Public Hall. The accommodation was, however, insufficient, and Bethesda school-room was brought into requisition. About 850 persons were present. All, or nearly all, the trays had been given, the number being about 70. The admirable arrange- ments prevented any undue bustle, and when the tables had been cleared away a public meeting was held in the large room, which had been profusely decorated. Drapery was tastefully arranged behind the platform, a centre piece b2ing formed of the words " Reading makes a full man," painted white on a blue ground. Flags were disposed in various parts:of the hall, and round the front of the gallery in white letters on a blue ground, were the names of men famous in English literature. The body of the room was crowded with an enthusiastic audience, and each speaker as he rose to address them was accorded a hearty reception. The Rev. Canon Barclay, M.A., presided; and he was supported by Sir James A. Picton, Revs. W. Preston, M.A., J. Lockwood, J. Nowell, J. J. Byrant, Edwards, E. Williams, Dr. Steel, Dr. McDougall, Messrs. G. S. Hazle- hurst, John Simpson, E. Timmins, J. Norman, G. Rhodes, 1 P. Briscoe, W. Whitaker, P. Speakman, J. J. Speakman, W. Handley, J. Handley, J. R. Frith, P. Cowell, S. Taylor, 0. Leak, Frederick Risty, Middy and others. The Cuirnmerr, who was warmly applauded on rising, said he would simply express his satisfaction at having been one of those who for the last 38 years had been engaged in various schemes for the benefit of the parish in general, some of which, by God's blessing, had succeeded,' and many more of which had failed. He was very pleased indeed to congratulate the inhabitants of Runcorn upon the inauguration of an institution which was not dependant on the liberality of subscribers, or the caprice of members, but which was likely to be a permanent institution in the town. They had books of poetry, history, science, travel, biography, and so on, by authors whose names were round the room: and he was sure the Library would be a wonder- ful benefit to the people of Runcorn. There were books of every sort written in their own mother tongue, that glorious English language which was rich with the spoils of time, the language which Milton sang and Shakespeare wrote, the Language in which Wilberforce, Peel, Brougham, Pitt, Fox, Newton, Wesley, Wellington, and Washington gave utter- ance to those thoughts which had rendered their names famous for all generations. As the poet said :

Stronger by far than hosts that march With battle flags unfurled, It goes with freedom, thought, and truth To rouse and rule the world, Mark, as it spreads how deserts bloom, And error flees away, As vanishes the mists of night Before the star of eay. • But grand as are the vie t.-•ri,?s Whose rnonume:lts wa see, Tlr.se are bus, as the dawn—it speaks— Of noontide yet to be. When earth's oppressed- and savage tithes Shall cease to pine or roam, All taught to prize those English words Faith, Freedom, Heaven, and Home.

(Loud applause.) Dr. STEELE, in the absence of Mr. Charles Wigg, !roved the first resolution, "That this meeting, representing the inhabitants of Runcorn, tender their heartiest acknow- ledgments to Sir J. A. Picton, F.S.A., for the honour he his conferred upon them in opening the Runcorn Free Public Library." Mr. JOHN SIMPSON seconded the resolution. He said he certainly felt that that was a red letter day in the history of Runcorn; and he could not but think that the establish- ment of the Free Public Library, which had been brought to so happy a consummation that evening, was one of the ' happiest events which had taken place in Runcorn for a very long time past. They had now a Free Public Library- in which any one might go and sit and read during the whole of the time that the Library was open, without any restric- tion at all, and where all ratepayers and residents might borrow books and take them home to read. That was a boon which he thought would be appreciated more and more as time went en. Even since the passing of the Free Libraries Act, now some 30 years ago, he had hopd that some time or other the day would come when Runcorn . would adopt the Act, and when they would afford to the in- habitants of Runcorn and neighbourhood the privileges of a free public library. The question had been brought before the Runcorn people for the last few years again and again, and he thought those gentlemen who had been so persistent in

the matter deserved their very best and warmest thanks. (Applause.) After an appreciative reference to the services which Mr. Wm. Handley had rendered to the Library, and to Sir J. Picton, the speaker concluded by relating the fol- lowing anecdote about the latter gentleman. Sir James many years ago had been addressing an assembly composed partly of bricklayers, and after the meeting the following conversa- tion was overheard. The first speaker said, "I say, he's a good un,"—(laughter)—the second one said, "He's a brick," —(renewed laughter)—and the third one said, " Well, then, he's not a common un." " No," another man said, " for he's a picked un (Picton)." (Much laughter and cheers). Sir JAMES Picroer, who was received with loud applause, then rose and spoke as follows :—I feel honoured by the in- vitation to be present on this occasion, which will be a memorable one in the annals of Runcorn. The commence- ment of any undertaking is always a source of interest—the planting of a tree, the launching of a ship, the rearing of a house, the birth of a child, the marriage of a young couple, all give rise to feelings of anticipation and speculation. Surely, then, an undertaking like the present should draw rai our warmest sympathies. It is not connected with sect or party. It is not intended for any particular class. High add low, rich and poor, Catholic and Protestant, Whig and Tory, may equally participate in its advantages, and should equally share in its support. (Ap- plause.) Your little town can boast a high antiquity. It is nearly a thousand years since the Royal Lady Ethelfleda laid its foundation and built its castle; but I question if, during the past millennium, any more important transac- tion, on more affecting the future well-being of the in- habitants than the present, has ever occurred. Think for a moment what is implied by the establishment of a good library, free and open to all. The battle between the sword and the pen has long been decided, and in future, comnauni- ties will take rank, not so much by the extent of their possessions or the success of their arms, as by their progress in wisdom, knowledge, and the liberal arts of life. (Applause.) Indeed, it has been so already. In searching the pages of history for those comuunities which have made their mark on the world and stamped their impress on the coming generations, we do not find them in Assyria, with its vast extension of empire, nor in Egypt, with its art and civilization, extending back into the fabulous night of antiquity; but our minds are insensibly directed to Athens, to Jerusalem, to Florence, to Venice, 1, cities comparatively small and feeble, but which have exer- ' cised an all-powerful influence in determining the course of the world's progress in literature, science, art, and religion. And so it will continue to be in an ever-increasing ratio. The empire of mind is based upon knowledge, and know- ledge can only be accumulated and perpetuated by means of books. Books are not the original source of knowledge, which must come from observation and the exercise of the mental faculties; but they are the storehouses of thought; they are steps in the progress which enable each generation to make the accumulations of one age the starting point of the next. Books have become so familiar to us that it re- quires an effort of mind fully to realise their relation to our daily life. They are become like the air we breathe—if we breathe it not we die. Without books the advance of society if it existed at all would be halting and feeble, and liable at any time to interruption and defeat. Books lend wings to its progress, and prevent the possibility of retrogression of any truth once established. Now let us consider what is implied in the existence of a free public library. I have found in this regard very erroneous notions in the minds of many well-meaning people. They consider that it merely means a collection of current cheap literature for the use of the working classes. Thirty years ago I had great difficulty in struggling against this prejudice, and I am sorry to say it is not yet entirely extinct. My idea of a free public library is something very different from this. It ought to be a collection of the noblest thoughts of the wisest men in all ages of the world—an assemblage of the best books on every subject of human inquiry. We sometimes think what a privilege it would have been to have been able to converse with Shakespeare, or Chaucer, or Bacon, or Milton, not to go back to Homer, or Virgil, or Dante. Well, in a good library we do converse wtth them. We ask them questions, and they reply to us in their choicest language and most precious thoughts. The modern spiritualists tell us that they can establish correspondence with the departed worthies and received communications from them. The result is not happy. If it were true we do not need it; we have the precious jems and the pure gold, and want no deteriorated alloy. And what a range there is! We feel in contemplating the vast and ever-increasing extent of litera- ture as if standing on the verge of an illimitable ocean, which needs a guide and compass to direct our course; or, to change the figure, it is like a vast garden in which there grow
Flowers of all hues and without thorns the rose.

Let us pick out a few. First, I would allude to ancient literature, the classics as they are called, meaning works of the highest class of the period which produced them. There has been of late considerable difference of opinion as to the study and value of the Greek and Roman writers. It is maintained by many that life is too short, and the number of practical subjects too vast, to allow of time being wasted on the study of writers who wrote in languages now dead, on subjects the interest of which is gone by, and in a state of society altogether different from what now exists. There is much truth in this. but it is not the whole truth. Everything depends on the standpoint from which we look. To the vast majority who are engaged in the active business of life, earning their bread by the sweat of their brow, no doubt it would be a profitless occu- pation to spend years over an acquirement which when learned would be of no immediate value in the round of their daily labour. But there is something beyond this. The intelligent daily labourer likes sometimes to escape from Lis common-place surroundings, and to refresh his mind by contact with higher and nobler thoughts. Those who thus cater for his pleasure and recreation require themselves to go to the fountain head of literature, and drink inspira- tion from the fresh and vigorous springs of antiquity. Especially is this the case with what is called style in writing. There is a simplicity and freshness about the early writers which moderns in Vain attempt to • equal. This ' arises in part from circumstances in the nature of language which I cannot now enter into, but it is a fact which must be taken into account. It would be a had day for modern literature if the study of the classics were suppressed. Tho classics,therefore, ought to form a portion of every public library. I have spoken of the working man as being almost necessarily ex- cluded from studies of this kind ; and yet it is not so. I could produce many instances in which the love of learning has broken through the barriers of circumstance, and opened the doors of the inner sanctuary to the humble but diligent student. (Applause.) I will merely mention one. A working joiner, who was fond of reading, met with a few words in a book which he could not understand. He in- quired, and found they were Latin. He procured a grammar, and set himself diligently and successfully to work. One thing led to another. I have not time to go through the whole process; suffice it is to say that in the course of a few years the journeyman joiner emerged as Professor Lee, who tilled the chair of Oriental Literature in the University of Cambridge. (Applause.) I therefore claim in , the interests of all classes, and not the least in that of the working class, that ancient literature shall have its place in your free public library. What shall we next pick out in this garden of sweets? I would place before all other studies that of the world we live in, the investigation of nature in all its various relations. Contemplate its vast sweep and compre- hension at the one end of the scale, the measurement of worlds, the searching out of the component elements of the suns, planets, and systems, the divine: into the depths of time and space, to an extent which sometimes makes the brain reel with the tension find excitement; and at the other end, the microscopical investigations which trace many of the functions and most of the diseases of the human frame, and of nature generally, to creatures so minute as hardly to he visible to the highest power known. Look again at geology, and the light it casts on the changes in our globe, from a period too remote for human thought. Turn to the study of the products of our globe, to botany, zoology and natural history, in all its branches and development. Science in its various depart- ments takes hold of and utilizes all this knowledge, and applies it to the radical needs of our daily life. Now, I do not say that all this knowledge can be derived from I books. The student of nature and science must go out and fight the battle for himself ; but I do say that without books all his investigations would be fruitless. The results of science are there recorded and stored up for future use, and without them progress would be impossible. Look at what science has done for us within the last two or three generations—the steam engine the railway, the steam boat, the gas light, the electric light, machinery in its various application to man's comfort and enjoyment. All these never could have come into existence with- out books. Shall I give you instances of the value of public libraries in the encouragement of scientific pursuits? I could multiply them, but a single one shall suffice. A few years ago, a young Scotchman was a working engineer, in the employ of Messrs. Fawcett, Prestons and Co. He was a steady attendant during hi i leisure hours at our free public library, where he met with scientific works which he could not otherwise have procured. Circumstances opened his way to an appointment in India, for which his acquired knowledge had qualified him. He has risen from stage to stage, and now fills a very important appointment as civil engineer under Government at a high salary. I am happy to soy he has not forgotten the institution OP which he owed so much, and has shown his gratitude by sending home very valuable donations, some of a character almost unique. (Ap- plause.) I will now turn to some departments in which hooks are more especially themselves the subjects of study. The study of the human race from its first appearance in the pre-historic period when it contended with the beasts of prey, in the dens and caves of the earth, in its gradual development, is only practicable from the dire weries recorded in books. And when we emerge from this dim twilight into historical day, what a vast fund of information we find stored up in books ! What lessons we learn, what romances we witness, what vicissitudes are recorded ! Take the history of our own country. What English heart does not glow with pride at the glorious record of the noble deeds of our ancestors. The fields of Cressy and Agincourt, the defeat of the Spanish Armada, the noble and prolonged resistance to the power tof nll Europe wielded by the Emperor Napoleon, are events which invest the books in which the story is told with a radiance which will never grow dim. (Applause.) Again, from books and books only we get our biographies of great and good men and women in all ages. From their example we learn lessons of patient perseverance and suffering in a righteous cause, of noble effort and brilliant success, of wisdom and courage, and philanthropy and self-denial, which stimulate our lagging efforts and teach us to be "not slothful but fol- lowers" of those who by faith and patience have accom- plished such glorious results. Let me say a word or two

about voyages and travels. When the world was not so well known as it now is, there was a wonderful charm about the narratives of our old travellers and voyagers, such as Marco Polo, Sir John Mandeville, and later on in the voyages of Drake, Hudson, Dampier, Anson, and Cook. That novelty has passed away, but there is still an amazing amount of interest and freshness in such narratives as those of Living- stone and Stanley. (Applause.) Philosophy, in its various branches, should form an important department in a free public library. I mean by philosophy the study of the human mind in its workings, and in its search after truth, mental and moral. To many minds, this has an irresistible charm; and though not so popular as some other studies, its importance must always he recogni3ed. Llosely connected with this is the department of theology, both natural and scriptural. The science, as it is now termed, of religion is investigated in a different spirit and by different methods to those formerly employed, and the results formerly looked upon with jealousy and suspicion are now hailed as contributing valuable aid to the cause of rational piety. It is desirable that your library should acquire the hest hooks in this department of literature, which is comparatively new. I have not hitherto alluded to works of imagination, which in most libraries form by far the greater part. (Applause.) Poetry must, of course, occupy a prominent place. No language, ancient or modern, possesses a richer store of true poetry than the English. Look at the grand array of English masters of song, from Chaucer down through Spenser and Shakespeare and Milton Dryden, Pope, and the almost countless multitude of modern poets, who stand ready in their works to elevate the mind, purify the taste, and raise eur thoughts and Of' 3tions from the sordid surroundings of ordinary life to revel in a high region• of beauty and imagination. (Applause.) What could we do without our poets? Life would indeed be flat, stale, and unprofitable without their cheering and ennobling influence. I say then, let your readers have the opportunity of enjoying to the full the rich intellectual banquet thus so profusely provided for them. I have now to say a word:on another sphere of the imagination, that of prose fiction. There is in the human mind a craving for works of imagination. We see it developing in youth, by the instinctive love of stories by children, and at every period of life it is a privilege to escape from our every day anxieties and vexations into an ideal state of things. Sensational it may be where the virtuous hero and heroine, after marvellous vicissitudes and escapes, thrilling the nerves, and filling the mind with astonishment, are at last rewarded and made for ever happy. (Laughter.) You quit your business, it may be at the close of an anxious and harassing day, and steal a quiet hour for study. If you are one of the right stamp, you undergo an entire transformation. There is Nothing in you but doth change Into something rich and strange.
The four walls of your chamber disappear from your mind's eye:—
You can call spirits from the vasty deep, And they do came when you do call for them

Now you are in the leafy shades of Arden, watching the moody Jaques and the motley fool in the forest ; anon the Wizard of the North transports you to the heath-clad bills of Scotland. Rob Roy, Fergus Mclvor, Jeannie Deans pass in review before you. Again you are absorbed in the fortunes of Adam Bede or the gentle Dorothea. Mrs. Poyzer dis- charges her incisive epigrams, the inimitable Mr. Pickwick and Sala Weller—(applause)—again play their parts in the cause of Bardell versus Pickwick. The scene. changes and you are wandering with - - •

Him who walked in glory and in j.,y, Following his plough along the mountain side. You cross the ocean with Childe Harold, and visit under his guidance the fading glories of Venice and Rome ; or in the far East you revel in the gorgeous imagery of the thousand and one nights. This is a fairyland of which no circum- stances can deprive the healthy well-informed mind :

Strong walls do not the prison make Nor Lon bars the cage. The body may be restricted, but the mind in its acquisitions and temperament can overcome the most unpromising circumstances. Provide, then, freely in your library for the cultivation and development of the imagination, but with two provisos. Let your works of fiction be pure and healthy. Do not, for the sake of any amount of ability which they contain, give admission to works which would contaminate the youthful mind or palliate vice in any form. (Cheers.) And further, do not for the sake of popularity give an undue preponderance to this class of literature. It is pleasant to be fed for a time with delicacies which stimulate the appetite; but for the elyetern to beliCelthy we must revert again to homely and useful fare. Your committee and managers will have to exercise a wholesome discretion in this regaiiel. The literature, the various departments of which I have brought under' your notice, is in our own language, the resources of which are rie doubt rich and varied, but no library would be complete nor afford the aid to eudy which modern exigencies require, withotti g fair proportie:2 of foreign literature, especially that of Italy, France, and (he - many. Translations, of course, will do a great deal to eupply the lack, but no translations can °lye in their in- tegrity the delicate shades of meaning, the peculiar style , which each language appropriates to itself, which, like the aroma of the flower. is lost in the artificial imitation. The attempts, for instance, to translate our Shakespeare into , French often result in ludicrous blunders and the .humour of Sam Weller or Sairey Gamp read through a German medium loses its flavour and becomes an absurdity. Of course the result is the same with a converse rendering of foreign works into English. The glorious mediaeval litera- ture of Italy, Dante, Boccaccio, Tasso, &c., must be studied in the original to be of any value. The delicate and spark- ling wit of Moliere becomes coarse in translation, and the rich and varied treasures of deep thought and profound in- vestigation found in the modern German writers can only be fully appreciated in the language in as hich they were written. I think, therefore, that in your provision of literature a fair proportion should be given to foreign works. I have not vet mentioned the subjects of the fine arts. If the public taste is to be improved and a love of the beautiful diffused through the community, some attention must be paid to this department, and a selection of the best books on the subject provided. I may have by-and-bye to add a word or two in relation to another aspect of this question. It might at first sight seem rather odd to add music as one of the departments of a free public library; but it has been found from practical experience elsewhere that no portion of a collection of this kind attracts more interest and diffuses more pleasure than a provision of well-selected music. (Applause.) It is, of course, used for copying and study. The .cultivation of musical taste has of late attracted much attention, this being a department in which our own country has been con- fessedly behindhand, and every facility ought to be given in an institution of this kind in recovering our lost ground. I have thus far sketched in a rapid and cursory manner what appear to me the most desirable features in a free public library ; but if I were to stop here, I should give but a very imperfect view of the comprehensive nature of the institution which you are now founding. The Act of Parliament from which your authority is derived does not limit you to the mere provision of books. It has been ex- panded to embrace a much wider sphere, and gives power to add to the library a museum and gallery of art. And here I come to the practical mode of carrying out your purposes on which I wish to add a few word. First, I would say, let your general scheme be broad and comprehensive. (Ap- plause.) Very probably only a small portion of it may be carried out at once, but let it be so arranged that any addi- tional feature will easily drop into its proper place. Do not attempt too much at once, but what you do, let it be done well. It is far better to have a choice and select library of the best books than to be tempted to swell out your collection by works of indifferent quality. Fortunately, the masterpieces of our literature in poetry, history, science, philosophy, and fiction are to be had at extremely moderate prices, and more expensive works may be waited for until opportunity offers. Let me for your encouragement give you a resume of the history of the kin- dred institution in Liverpool, with which I have been con- nected for more than thirty years. (APplause.) It is true that the extent and population of a great city like Liverpool provide resources which do not exist in a smaller commu- nity, but the demands are in proportion equally great. The example may not be without its use. Little more than thirty years ago, no public library ever existed in Liverpool to which the mass of the people could have access even to con- sul t a dictionary or a directory. Some attempts have been made on a small scale, but they did not meet with success. In January,.lBso, the subject was brought before the Com- mon Council by one of the members, and a committee was appointed to inquire and report thereon. The report was favourable, and a public meeting was called, which resulted in a subscription amounting to £1,680. With this the com- mittee set to work, and commenced the library, laying down as a peinciple that the object should be to obtain the best books on every subject of human inquiry. At this time Ewart's Free Libraries Act did not exist, and it was necessary to go to Parliament to obtain power to levy a penny rate. The library being founded a second department soon presented itself. The valuable collections in Natural History made by the 13th Earl of Derby were bequeathed to the town. and formed the bulk of what is now the magnifi- cent Derby Museum. It became now necessary to provide a local habitation for these two departments, and the task was undertaken by the late Sir William Brown, Bart., at a cost of about £40,000. (Applause.)Then came* the noble and priceless gift of a collection of historical artistic treasures almost unequalled, made by a man of whom Liverpool is proud, Joseph Mayer, who, I am happy to say, still lives in honoured age to enjoy the respect and gratitude of his fellow-townsmen. The subject of art next presented itself for recognition; the annual exhi- bitions began to be held and resulted in a great succese. To give them a local habitation and a name another generous benefactor stepped forward and erected the buildiug which bears his name—the Walker Art Gallery—at a cost of about £35,000. (Applause.) Many other hand- some donations have been presented—of money for books, money for pictures, and of pictures and books themselves, and several sums have been at different times voted by the Council, and valuable sites given for the buildings, the penny rate being devoted exclusively to the annual ex- - Pens• es In this way, besides the maintenance, about £250,000 have been contributed and expended in the build- ings, sites, and collections. (Applause.) Now, I do not give this history in a spirit of boasdne, or for a moment to suggest such ambitious ideas to Runcorn; but I say that if Else peo;frle of Runcorn do their duty and show themeelves in earnest, there will be found generous benefactors to second their efforts and give them support. The establishment of a Free Public Library is not quite new to the neighbourhood of Runcorn. It is recorded in the annals of Cheshire that in the 17th century a sum of money was contributed to provide a library of books in the parish of Halton free and open .to all. Whether this library is still maintained I do not know, but it is evidence of the taste for literature in this neighbourhood in the 17th century. Your
library is now established and opened, and I trust its prestige will be maintained. (Applause.) Your two branches of the reference and circulating library will assist eaCh other; _ . _ . . . .

but I would strongly recommend that they be kept separate and distinct, otherwise I fear some disappointment will be experienced by the readers. Your library being in opera- tion, your next aim will be towards the founding of a museum of natural science, antiquities, and the industrial _ _ _
. . . arts. You need not be in a hurry about this or have any doubts of its success. If you provide ..a suitable building _ .

and proper care and attention you will find that donations will begin to flow in, and acquisitions will multiply to an extent which will surprise you. Then as the crowning grace will come the gallery of art. (Applause.) In this we are far behind our continental neighbours. There is scarcely a town in France of anything like the importance of Run- corn which does not possess its gallery of pictures, of which the people are proud. It is strange what a con- tagious influence generosity imparts. A donation or two to commence with sets the example, and are soon fol- lowed by others. Attention is called to the subject and an interest created which opens the fountains of liberality. In order to follow up the pperations of the several branches of your institution, you will find the establishment of lectures a valual4le auxiliary. They stimulate inquiry, create a thirst for study and thought, and promote the boat practical use of your books and collec- tions. I think I have now, perhaps somewhat lightly, passed in review the objects, purposes, and mode of action of in- stitutions like this, and must bring these remarks to a close with one additional hint. It is well that yob should cele- brate with éclat and enthusiasm the opening of a means of instruction and improvement not confined to one particular class, high or low, offering its benefits freely to all, but its Success must depend upon continued vigorous effort. Diffi- culties will arise, enthusiasm may grow cold, lassitude and laxity may creep in, and your present noble effort result if not in failure, yet in perfunctory feebleness, but I hope for better things. I trust succession of earnest managers may be found, who will continue from generation to generation the noble work this day begun, increasing and adapting as circumstances may require. lhe true secret of success con- sists in constant vigilance, patient perseverance and untiring exertion. Without these no cause can ultimately succeed, but with their exercise you may look forward to a glorious future. (Cheers.) The Rev. W. PRESTON (vicar of Holy Trinity) moved the second resolution, "That this meeting believes the in- creased incentive to the acquisition of knowledge afforded by the Runcorn Free Public Library will powerfully stimulate our moral, intellectual, and commercial life, and be an in- estimable boon to the youth of our population." The Library, the speaker said, was designed to cure idleness and dispel the ignorance of the people. To the attractions of the public-house the Library would lia7e a counteracting influence, and the committee must take care that it really was so not only in point of appearance and comfort but in the plentiful supply of mental food. In time, too, it was to be hoped they should have newspapers and periodicals; and as the lives of the great men of our race were read, might the words of America's great national and lately deceased poet find an echo and realisation,—
Lives of great men all remind us We can make our lives .üblime ; And. departing, leave behind us Footprints on the sand of time.

(Loud applause.) The Rev. JOHN NOWELL seconded the resolution, and said be was convinced the town took a wise and beneficial step in adopting the Free Libraries Act. (Hear, hear, and ap- plause.) "Knowledge is power," whether used in work- manship, in the counting-house, the warehouse, or the pulpit; and its power was of the highest kind. The intelli- gent man had always an advantage over the ignorant man; the educated man had always an advantage over the illiterate. Mr. Nowell drew a comparison between the work- ingmen of the north and south of England, remembering that the former bad sharper intellects and were more pleasant than the latter: and he concluded by saying that if they wanted to save the men of the town from all that was low and degraded, let them not only promote their interest, but show them better methods, that there were higher aims than those they were pursuing. And'in the establishment of that Library they were taking an effectual step towards that end. (Ap- plause). Mr. G. S. HAZLEHURST, supported the resolution in a vigorous speech, and it was carried unanimously. Dr. MCDOUGALL proposed the next resolution, which was as follows ;—" That this meeting acknowledges with grati- tude all gifts, don tions, and services ip connection vith Olt , establishment of the Free Public Library." He gave an in- teresting description of the commencement of the movement for the establishment of the Library, and traced its subsequent development, culminating that evening in a demonstration, the significance of which no person could possibly mistake. He trusted the time was, not far distant when they should have a reading room in connection with the Library open to All who conformed to the rules. (Applause.) In taking a retrospective view of what had been accomplished, he took the opportunity to state that be himself issued a circular letter to the leading people of the district, and in response they had a large sum of money forwarded to them. They , had also something like 133 volumes added to the Library, I sup the committee had purchased 313 new volumes. He was in hopes that a better state of things was beginning in Runcorn; that they should be hearing of their merchant princes establishing exhibitions at the large universities in order to enable young men, who, from no fault of their own, were pursuing a course of study such as be knew happened in that part of the British Empire to which he belonged Some of the people in the neighbourhood who were in pos- session of fortunes could not better perpetuate their name or fame than by sparing a little of it to aid those who were unable- to raise themselves in a social position in life. He concluded amid applause by making an appeal for donations of books and money. Mr. W. HANDLEY seconded the resolution, which was carried. Mr. J. R. Emu, in appropriate terms, proposed a vote of thanks to all those who had contributed to the success of the demonstration. Mr. RHODES seconded the motion, and it was carried by acclamation. The Rev. J. LOCKWOOD proposed a .vote of thanks to Canon Barclay for presiding. Mr. COLEBURN (chairman of the Burial Board) seconded the resolution, which was unanimously carried, and the Rev. Canon Barclay ,replied. Mr. G. S. HAZLEHURST came to the front of the platform, and said he wished the meeting to pass, by acclamation, a resolution that this meeting desires the Commissioners to grant the Library Committee the full use of the Free Library at as early a day as possible. (Loud cheers long continued.) Dr. McDouGALL seconded the motion in a few energetic remarks, and it was carried with much enthusiasm. The proceedings then terminated with the singing of a verse of the National Anthem. A large quantity of provisions remaining at the conclusion of the tea, the committee decided to give them to the poor, and Dr. McDougall, Mr. Shaw (seaman's missionary), Mr. Wright, and Mr. Bowyer, were entrusted with their distribu- tion.

div.head: WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS.
WEDNFSDAT.—Defore Messrs. W. N. Heald (chairman) and H. S. Hall.

DRUNK AND CREATING A DISTURBANCE.—A man named Peter Riley was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Queen-street, on the Ist inst., and also with committing a breach of the peace by fighting with Michael Malone in Waterloo-road, on the 10th June last. It was his eleventh appearance.—P.C. Thompson proved the cases; and for the first offence he was committed for one month's imprison- ment with hard labour, and for the second he was bound over in £lO and two sureties in £5 each to keep the peace for three months.

MISCELIANEOUS.—A woman named Rachel Hunt made her 21st appearance on a charge of being drunk and dis- orderly in Water-street, on the 3rd inst., and she was sent to prison for a month.—Martin Grady pleaded guilty to a charge of being drunk and creating a disturbance in Milton- road, on Sunday night, and also with assaulting P.C. 185. drunk and in the custody of the officer the prisoner became very riotous, created a great disturbance, and kicked and struck the constable when being brought to the police- station. The prisoner is an old offender, and he was sent to gaol for two months.—Patrick Smith for being drunk and disorderly in Elizabeth-street, on the 26th ult., was fined 103 and cosrs,.or in default 14 days' hard labour. Mary Fildes was mulcted in the sum of 5s and costs for being drunk and causing a disturbance in Ann-street West, on the 24th ult.—Mary Mcllermot and Mary Ann Killala were charged with committing a breach of the peace on the Old Marsh, Widnes, on the 25th ult , and were bound over each in the sum of £lO, and one surety of £5 to keep the peace for one month, with the alternative of 7 seven days' impri- sonment.—A man named Robert Bell was fined 7s 64 and costs for keeping a dog without a licence.—James Beesley for discharging a double-barrelled gun in Timperley-street, on the 27th ult., was ordered to pay a fine of 26 6d and Costs. THE DOG AND THE POLICEMEN.—A young man, named William Palin, was summoned for allowing his dog, which was a very ferocious one, to be at large in Ann-street West, on the 24th ultimo.—P.C. 268 stated that when he was on duty on the day in question the dog "flew " at him and bit his leg. He called the defendant's attention to the fact, and he replied that it had also bitten P.S. Clarkson and P.C. Strickland on previous occasions.—Defendant was fined 20s. and costs. • _ _

_ THEFT OF A TAME RABBIT.—Two boys, named Patrick Hogan'and James Riley, aged 13 and 14 respectively, were charged with stealing a tame rabbit, the property of Ellen Jones, 12, Lugsdale-road, at an early hour on Sunday morn- incr.—The prosecutrix saw that the rabbit was safe in a cote in her backyard on Saturday night, and when she went to examine the cote on Sunday morning it was missing.—P.C. McGuinness said that he saw the prisoners carrying the rabbit about 5-30 on Sunday morning. He asked prisoners where they had got the rabbit from,and they told' him they had found it in a field. Not be:ng satisfied with prisoners' explanation, he took them to the police station.—They were each fined 55. and costs, with the alternative of 10 days' im- prisonment with hard labour. CHARGE AGAINST A DEESSMAiER.—Margaret Burns, a dressmaker, was charged with pawning a dress, the property of a young woman named Elizabeth McFarlane, on the Ist inst.—From the evidence of the prosecutrix,it appeared that on Thursday' the 29th inst., she took her dress to defendant to be altered, and was told by defendant that it would be finished on Saturday. When she went for the dress it was not ready, and she did not go for it again until Sunday morning, when defendant then told her that her sister (Mrs. McKenna) had been for it. Mrs. McKenna said that her

mother owed her some money, and gave her instructions to call for her sister's dress, which she pawned in order to re- coup the money which her mother owed her.—After hearing the evidence, the magistrates dismissed the case. AN INCORIZIGIBLE.—A lad named Jahn Molyneux was sent to prison for seven days, with hard labour, for begging in Kent-street, on the previous day. He had been imprisoned on many previous occasions, and had also served five years in a reformatory _school.

BEGGING.—John Cooney, 13 years old, was charged with asking for alms from a gentleman, and also from a constable who was wearing plain clothes, near the Central Station on the previous day.—The case was dismissed.

ALLEGED ASSAULT.—.Mary Flinn was charged. with violently assaulting a man named Patrick Quinn by strik- ing him OR the back with a brick.—lt seemed that Quinn's wife went into defendant's house and took a jar of beer which defendant's lodger had paid for. Defendant then went to complainant's house and asked for the beer which his wife had stolen. Complainant there and then threw the beer into the street, and a squabble ensued, when he received a blow on the back with a brick.—The case was dimissed. SERIOUS ASSAULT.—A woman named Ann Cannon was charged with assaulting a labourer named John Townshend, of 95, Travis-street, on Monday.—Mr. Beasley, solicitor, appeared for the complainant.—About four o'clock on Mon- day afternoon the defendant, who lives next door to com- plainant, came out of the house holding a glass bottle by the neck, and without the least provocation struck the complainant on the face with it. The blow was such a severe one that the bottle was completely smashed. Blood flowed very profusely from the wounds inflicted on the com- plainant's face, and he had to go to Dr. O'Keeffe to have them dressed,—Defendant was tined 10s. and 10s. 6d. costs, or in default, 14 days' imprisonment with hard labour.
- RUNCORN POLICE COURT. .Continued from page 6. FRlDAY.—Before Mr. W. Banke.

ALLEGED ROBBERY FROM A SCHOONER.—A youth named Richard Collingwood, was charged with stealing about LI the property of Joseph Ralphs. The presecutor is a seaman on board the schooner Jane, of Preston, and the prisoner was,employed on the same vessel. On Thursday morning the prosecutor had a guinea in his trousers which were locked in his chest. During the afternoon the money was missed and the prisoner was subsequently apprehended by P.C. Price, who found an old purse and sovereign upon him. —lnspector Hollingworth said the prisoner was a dis- charged induste.al school lad, and asked for a remand that inquiries might be made.-The prisoner was remanded until Monday. THEFT or ROPE.—Eleanor Rynolds, a boatwoman, was charged with stealing a hauling line of the value of about 25., the property of Jessie Bibby, the captain of two canal boats, lying near the Old Qurky. On Wednesday the rope was missed from the forecastle of the boat, but on Tuesday, it was subsequently ascertained, the prisoner had sold the rope to Mr. Lavelle, marine store dealer, Mersey-street.—P.S. Whalley deposed to apprehending the prisoner on Thursday. She admitted stealing the]rope, and as she had a long black list against her, she was committed for trial.

div.head: PRESCOT RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: PRESCOT RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The monthly meeting of this Authority was, held at the Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday morning, when there were present :—Messrs. Meadows (in the chair), Newsome, Hall, Leatherbarrow, Legh, W. B. Longton, Gilbody, Sykes, and the Revs. T. Chamber, and Barnacle, together with Mr. Hartley (clerk), and Mr. Twist (surveyor).

div.head: TRH DRAINAGE OF ECCLE STON PARK ESTATE.
div.p: TRH DRAINAGE OF ECCLE STON PARK ESTATE.

The CHAIRMAN said the first business arising from the minutes would be Mr. Newsome's notice that he would at that meeting move that Mr. Goldsworth in conjunction with Mr. Twist should report as to the drainage of Eccleston Park Estate.

Mr. NEWSOME said he would make a motion in accordance with that notice. There had been a well attended meeting at which three and twenty ratepayers came to the unani- mous conclusion that Mr. Goldsworth in conjunction with Mt. Twist should make a report not only on Eccleston Park Estate but EO/33 on that part of the district as well.
Mr. GILBODY secontled tl* proposition, which was anani, mously carried;

kEGLEftrED NOTICRS. A letter wag tcdd front Messrs. Thomas Leas and Son stating that as notices had been served on the occupiers of Mrs. Sutton's cottages at Whiston, they were giving up the property, as they did not feel disposed to incur expenses of drainage for property which might be taken frorr. them at any moment. The other cottages (Roscoe's), and the one in Church-row, were being attended to..

The SURVEYOR said nothing had been done vet. Mr. HALL said they would not put the cottages in proper sanitary condition; he would move that they be forced. What was the use of playing with those things. The CHAIRMAN: Of course not.
Mr. HALL sAid that thing hhd been going on so long they were the laughing stock of the whole country. It had been going on for the last 12 or 18 months, and they were then as far as ever.

Mr. NEWSOME asked if notice had been given. The CHAIRMAN: Oh, yes. Mr. NEWSOME thought that if Mr. Twist had the power he ought to put it in force. The CHAIRMAN: We will take the proper course. In answer to Mr. Leatherbarrovr, the SURVEYOR said that notices had lnen served on Messrs. Leas and Sons, as they had received the rents.
It was agreed that the proper notices should be given.
THE QUALITY OF THE WATER.
Some discussion took place with respect to the quality of the water which had been analysed by Dr. Brown. Dr. HALL said it seemed to be of good quality if properly filtered.

The SURVEYOR There seems to be a lot of iron in it. Mr. Hata,: Iron is very good to take, isn't it, doctor? Dr. HALL: Yes, if you don't take too much of it. The SURYEYOR said it was good simply for domestic purposes, but he was afraid that the analysis had not been taken at the proper time. It was ultimately agreed that another sample of water should be analysed within the next three months, the sample to be taken at a more favourable time by the surveyor.

div.head: LORD- DERBY NEGLECTING THE BYE-LAWS.
div.p: LORD- DERBY NEGLECTING THE BYE-LAWS.
The SURVE FOR reported that some houses had been erected by Lord Derby at Knowsley without plans having first been submitted.

Mr. HALL proposed that action should be taken apinst Lord Derby, although it was probable Lord Derby knew nothing at all about it. There was more trouble fro m Knowsley township than from any other in the union. Mr. Leslie knew perfectly well that plans ought to have been deposited, and if he did not do so, he (Mr. Hall) thought Lord De:by ought to be 'peppered "the same as other people. The CLERK said it would be hard if Lord Derby should be punished for what he knew nothing about.. Mr. HALL said it would be very unfair if other people were punished and Lord Derby go free. The CHAIRMAN suligested that the Surveyor write to Mr. Leslie.

Mr. HALL suggested the Mr. Hale should also be written to, and told that Mr. Leslie knew the law very well, and in- formed that if such a thing should again occur proceedings would be taken. He (Mr. Hall) thought Lord Derby should be treated like other people. _ _
The CLERK said he. would 'write on the matter, and draw their attention to the fact that they caused the same trouble in connection with the water act.
This was agreed to.
TIU CLERK'S SALARY.

The CLERK said he had hithel to been paid on the basis of the last settlement, and the Guardians always fixed the amount of his salary at the end of the twelve months, but the auditor now said he must draw nothing on account, and therefore it would be necessary for them to make-a fixed salary. The Clerk having retired, Mr. CHAMBERS moved that his salary be fixed at £l5O a year. Mr. LEA.THERB.tREOW seconded this proposition, which was carried unanimously.

div.head: VIE MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.
div.p: VIE MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.

The MEDICAL OFFICER (Dr. Hall) reported as follows : With the exception of the measles, the health of the dis- trict has been very satisfactory since your last meeting, and these have been chicily confined to Whiston. There have been no more deaths from this cause in Rainhill. One death has occurred there from fever of a simple character. I can find no fault with these premises, except that the midden ashpit is not roofed over, is too deep, and nothwithstanding that a few years ago it was drained under the moist principle is wet. The whole now are in just the same state when nearly empty of ashes, it' would be well to have them converted in conformity with our bye-laws. There has also been a death from fever of a simple character at Hall Bank in one of the houses re- ported upon-at the last meeting; the same conditions apply as then reported, and the same remedy as ordered will answer the purpose. The place has been disinfected. The water sent to Dr. C. Brown from Tarbock Smithies appears to be of good quality if it is properly filtered.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS.

WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. H. Bleckly and S. Rigby. Sarah Jane Bradshaw, wife of a forgeman, residing at Orford, was bound over to keep the peace for three months for rasing threatening language towards a married woman named Winifred Ann Seals.

James Olewerth, an elderly man, W 2•5 summoned for having left his horse and trap on the highway at Houghton ort the 20th ult. without any person in charge for an unreasonable time, and he was fined 103. and coats. Three lads named James Hill, Richard Lawless, and James Higham, were charged with stealing a duck, value 3s.' the property of William PenuingtQn, of Orford, on the 519th June. Several of the prosecutt;r's ducks were in a brook or pond, and the prisoners were seen near the place. A short time afterwards one of the ducks was missed, and the lads were followed into Warringtrar, where they were apprehended. They then admitted haying taken the duck. The lads were throwing stones to see which of them could hit the ducks, when one of them was killed, and one of the prisoners picked it up and left it in a field, where it was found by P.C. Whit- tingham. They were each fined ss. and costs or 7 days, the Bench observing that the prisoners bad got off very leniently. •
